leads.caseName: Matter of Zero Waste Ithaca v. thaca City Planning & Dev. Bd.
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
Matter of Zero Waste Ithaca v thaca City Planning & Dev. Bd. 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06600 
 November 12, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Third Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 In the Matter of Zero Waste Ithaca, Appellant, 
 v 
 Ithaca City Planning & Development Board et al., Respondents. 

 Decided and Entered:November 12, 2026 
 CV-25-0783 
 Calendar Date: September 16, 2026 
 Before: Reynolds Fitzgerald, J.P., Fisher, Mcshan, Mackey And Corcoran, JJ. 

 Pace Environmental Litigation Clinic, Inc., White Plains (Todd D. Ommen of counsel), for appellant. 
 Victor J. Kessler, City Attorney, Ithaca (James F. Kenniff of counsel), for Ithaca City Planning & Development Board, respondent. 
 Cornell University, Ithaca (Jared M. Pittman of counsel), for Cornell University, respondent. 

 [*1] 
 Mackey, J. 
 Appeal from a judgment of the Supreme Court (Mark Masler, J.), entered April 28, 2025 in Tompkins County, which dismissed petitioner's application, in a proceeding pursuant to CPLR article 78, to review, among other things, a determination of respondent Ithaca City Planning & Development Board adopting a negative declaration of environmental significance. 
 In December 2023, respondent Cornell University applied to respondent Ithaca City Planning & Development Board (hereinafter the planning board) for site plan approval in connection with a development project to expand the recreational mixed-use athletic facilities available to students on campus (hereinafter referred to as the project). Located in central campus and bordered by other buildings and facilities owned and occupied by Cornell, the project included the replacement and expansion of existing outdoor natural grass and synthetic turf fields with an updated outdoor synthetic turf field and an indoor synthetic turf field with accompanying facilities housed in a nearby 90,000-square-foot building. The planning board reviewed the project over the course of several months at several board and committee meetings, allowing public comment and directing Cornell to provide information in response to issues raised by the public regarding the environmental and health risks associated with synthetic turf due to the potential presence of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (hereinafter PFAS), semi-volatile organic compounds (hereinafter SVOCs), volatile organic compound (hereinafter VOCs) and microplastics found in the component materials. Cornell furnished the planning board with the requested information and, following further discussion, the planning board approved a final version of the full environmental assessment form identifying the relevant areas of environmental and health concerns and concluding that the project did not pose a significant risk of harm to people or the environment. The planning board then issued a negative declaration pursuant to the State Environmental Quality Review Act ( see ECL art 8 [hereinafter SEQRA]) and approved Cornell's application, contingent upon Cornell subjecting the synthetic turf ultimately selected for the project to third-party testing for PFAS. 
 Petitioner, a volunteer not-for-profit organization dedicated to promoting zero-waste policies and advocating against the use of materials that contain pollutants and toxic chemicals, thereafter commenced this proceeding pursuant to CPLR article 78. Petitioner alleged that the planning board's determinations were arbitrary and capricious in that they overlooked the documented dangers of certain chemicals used in components of synthetic turf by issuing a negative declaration for the project and concluding that there was no significant risk in that regard, thereby obviating the need for an environmental impact statement (hereinafter EIS) pursuant to SEQRA. Petitioner's subsequent attempt to obtain a temporary restraining [*2] order and a preliminary injunction enjoining Cornell from continuing construction of the project was denied. Oral argument ensued, after which Supreme Court dismissed the petition, finding that the planning board had complied with the requirements of SEQRA in issuing the negative declaration. Petitioner appeals. FN1 
 "This Court will not disturb a SEQRA determination so long as the lead agency identified the pertinent areas of environmental concern, took a hard look at them and advanced a reasoned elaboration of the grounds for its determination" ( Matter of Binghamton Plaza, Inc. v City of Binghamton, N.Y. , 228 AD3d 1041, 1044 [3d Dept 2024] [internal quotation marks and citations omitted]; see Matter of Schaller v Town of New Paltz Zoning Bd. of Appeals , 108 AD3d 821, 822-823 [3d Dept 2013]). In reviewing such determination, "it is not the role of the courts to weigh the desirability of any SEQRA action or choose among alternatives, but to assure that the agency itself has satisfied SEQRA, procedurally and substantively" ( Matter of Save Southard Rd. Neighborhood Coalition v Town of Saratoga Planning Bd. , 35 AD3d 1017, 1019 [3d Dept 2006] [internal quotation marks, brackets and citation omitted]; see Matter of Riverkeeper, Inc. v Planning Bd. of Town of Southeast , 9 NY3d 219, 232 [2007]), and "[a] court may only annul an agency's determination to issue a negative declaration where it is arbitrary, capricious or unsupported by the evidence" ( Matter of Creda, LLC v City of Kingston Planning Bd. , 212 AD3d 1043, 1047-1048 [3d Dept 2023] [internal quotation marks and citations omitted]; see Matter of Hohman v Town of Poestenkill , 179 AD3d 1172, 1174 [3d Dept 2020]). In meeting SEQRA's mandate, "[a] negative declaration may be issued, obviating the need for an EIS, if the lead agency determines that no adverse environmental impacts will result or that the identified adverse environmental impacts will not be significant" ( Matter of Village of Ballston Spa v City of Saratoga Springs , 163 AD3d 1220, 1223 [3d Dept 2018] [internal quotation marks, ellipsis, brackets and citations omitted]; see ECL 8-0109 [2]; 6 NYCRR 617.3 [c] [1]), and a type I action — such as this — "does not, per se, necessitate the filing of an EIS" ( Matter of Gabrielli v Town of New Paltz , 116 AD3d 1315, 1316 [3d Dept 2014] [internal quotation marks, brackets and citation omitted]; see 6 NYCRR 617.4 [a] [1]). 
 The record before us is extensive, detailing the various studies and expert examinations and recommendations relied upon by the planning board in identifying and evaluating the relevant areas of health and environmental concern of the project. Over several months of an open and deliberative process, the planning board reviewed engineering and architectural reports prepared by various consultants, several scientific reports, as well as Cornell's application materials, and actively invited public comment thereon. Of note, a memorandum prepared by H & A of New York Engineering and Geology [*3] , and submitted by Cornell, examined the risks associated with certain synthetic turf components. To this end, the H & A memo noted two studies conducted by synthetic material producers finding that "fewer PFAS compounds were detected in synthetic turf, and at lower concentrations, than those that are present as a background condition in soil" from the growing prolific use of PFAS in everyday items. In a study that also tested for SVOCs, it was similarly observed that "[m]ost SVOCs were not detected, and those that were detected were below standards and screening levels." The H & A memo thus concluded that "synthetic turf systems are safe for contact by people and will not harm groundwater or surface water." Another report cited five peer-reviewed studies that the use of synthetic turf would not cause adverse effects to human health above safety levels determined by the US Environmental Protection Agency and European Union, and that VOC emissions from synthetic turf were generally not detectable. Other peer-reviewed studies similarly concluded that exposure to rubber infills was not harmful to people or ground water. The planning board further highlighted a federal multiagency research study finding that, due to the small amount of chemicals released from the infill and turf, there was only marginal if any difference in the presence of chemical metabolites in study populations as compared to background samples or the general population. 
 Notwithstanding the foregoing, the planning board called for further information from Cornell, including how it planned to alleviate any potential health concerns raised in public comments. Cornell accordingly submitted additional materials consisting of its own reports and those of various project consultants, emphasizing that "more than 110 technical studies conducted by a variety of trusted scientific authorities, including the US EPA, Washington State Department of Health, US Department of Energy and Environment, and more" have concluded that "[a]rtificial turf has been shown to pose no health risk." In nevertheless addressing the environmental concerns associated with the use of synthetic turf, Cornell articulated its plan for preventing microplastic pollution through a storm water management process — including a filtration system equipped to filter out microplastics down to particles 0.212 millimeters in size — and it further agreed to third-party testing of the synthetic turf ultimately chosen for use in the project for PFAS. 
 The record thus amply demonstrates that the planning board made a careful and deliberate consideration of the relevant areas of health and environmental concern, took the requisite hard look, and made a reasoned elaboration in issuing a negative declaration; thus, we find no basis to disturb its determination ( see Matter of Creda, LLC v City of Kingston Planning Bd. , 212 AD3d at 1048-1049; Matter of Schaller v Town of New Paltz Zoning Bd. of Appeals , 108 AD3d at 822-824; Matter of Save [*4] Southard Rd. Neighborhood Coalition v Town of Saratoga Planning Bd. , 35 AD3d at 1019-1021; Matter of Defreestville Area Neighborhood Assn., Inc. v Planning Bd. of Town of N. Greenbush , 16 AD3d 715, 721- 723 [3d Dept 2005]; compare Matter of Bigelow v Town of Willsboro Planning Bd. , 243 AD3d 979, 983 [3d Dept 2025]; Matter of Clean Air Action Network of Glens Falls, Inc. v Town of Moreau Planning Bd. , 235 AD3d 1124, 1127-1129 [3d Dept 2025]). The requirements of SEQRA having been met, we will not disturb the determination. 
 Alternative grounds for affirmance advanced by Cornell have been rendered academic in light of our determination. 
 Reynolds Fitzgerald, J.P., Fisher, McShan and Corcoran, JJ., concur. 
 ORDERED that the judgment is affirmed, without costs. 

 Footnotes 

Footnote 1
 Petitioner sought a preliminary injunction pending the instant appeal enjoining the construction and installation of synthetic turf fields at the project site, which motion this Court denied (2025 NY Slip Op 75957[U] [3d Dept 2025]).

leads.caseName: Atwood v. Lamar Obie Co., LLC
leads.text:
516 November 12, 2026 No. 1089
IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF THE 
STATE OF OREGON
Jim A. ATWOOD, 
in his capacity as trustee of the Jim A. Atwood Trust 
dated August 10, 2017; Jim A. Atwood, an individual; 
and J.A. Atwood Corporation, an Oregon corporation,
Plaintiffs-Respondents,
v.
LAMAR OBIE COMPANY, LLC, 
a Delaware limited liability company,
Defendant-Appellant,
and
ONDISPLAY ADVERTISING, LLC, 
an Indiana limited liability company;
Michael H. Maloney, an individual; 
Alec Dille, an individual; Bradley Williams, an individual; 
and James Derby, an individual,
Defendants.
Multnomah County Circuit Court
20CV29502; A181594
Katharine von Ter Stegge, Judge.
Argued and submitted October 15, 2025.
Drew L. Eyman argued the cause for appellant. Also on 
the briefs were Clifford S. Davidson and Snell & Wilmer 
LLP.
Nicholas A. Kampars argued the cause for respondents. 
Also on the brief was Wildwood Law Group LLC.
Before Ortega, Presiding Judge, Joyce, Judge, and 
Hellman, Judge.
ORTEGA, P. J.
Affirmed.
Cite as 354 Or App 516 (2026) 517
518 Atwood v. Lamar Obie Co., LLC
 ORTEGA, P. J.
 Defendant Lamar Obie Company, LLC (Lamar) 
appeals from a general judgment entered for plaintiffs 
on their claim for breach of the implied duty of good faith 
and fair dealing and awarding damages of $1,237,191.92. 
Plaintiffs own a building and have historically leased a 
large, exterior wall of that building to advertising companies 
to sell commercial advertising space for large signs. In June 
2015, for the first time, plaintiffs were required to obtain 
a permit from the Oregon Department of Transportation 
(ODOT) that allowed that use. The company leasing the 
wall from plaintiffs at that time, OnDisplay Advertising 
Services, LLC, obtained the ODOT permit which, contrary 
to plaintiffs’ instructions, ODOT issued solely in the name 
of OnDisplay. Around the same time, OnDisplay sold the 
lease with plaintiffs to defendant Lamar and ODOT trans -
ferred the permit to Lamar. Plaintiffs were not aware at 
the time that they were not named on the permit. In 2019, 
plaintiffs terminated the lease with Lamar. Among other 
disputes, Lamar refused to sell or transfer the ODOT per -
mit to plaintiffs and instead turned the permit in to ODOT 
for relocation credit that Lamar cannot use and which ended 
plaintiffs’ ability to display commercial advertising on the 
building’s exterior wall.
 As relevant to this appeal, plaintiffs asserted a 
claim for breach of the implied duty of good faith and fair 
dealing against Lamar, and the jury returned a verdict in 
plaintiffs’ favor. Lamar now appeals, asserting nine assign-
ments of error that challenge the trial court’s submission 
of the good faith and fair dealing claim to the jury and the 
jury instructions on good faith and fair dealing and on dam-
ages. In sum, we conclude that, as a matter of law, the par-
ties could have held the objectively reasonable contractual 
expectations that formed the bases of plaintiffs’ claim, and 
that the trial court correctly submitted to the jury whether 
the parties in fact held those expectations and whether 
Lamar’s actions, including with respect to the ODOT per -
mit, were contrary to those expectations. We also conclude 
that plaintiffs’ future damages were not too speculative to 
submit to the jury. Finally, we conclude that the trial court 
Cite as 354 Or App 516 (2026) 519
did not err in any of the ways asserted by Lamar in giving 
the jury instructions on the implied covenant of good faith 
and fair dealing and on damages. Accordingly, we affirm.
I. ASSIGNMENTS OF ERROR NOT 
REVIEWABLE ON APPEAL
 Before turning to the facts of this case and the mer-
its of Lamar’s assignments, we first dispose of those assign-
ments of error that are unreviewable on appeal. In its first 
assignment of error, Lamar argues that the trial court erred 
in denying Lamar’s motion for summary judgment. “In a 
case that has gone to trial, the denial of a summary judg -
ment motion is not reviewable on appeal unless the motion 
rested on a ‘purely legal’ contention.” Freeman v. Stuart, 203 
Or App 191, 194, 125 P3d 786 (2005). “A ‘purely legal’ conten-
tion, as that term is used in this context, refers to one that 
‘does not require the establishment of any predicate facts.’ ” 
Id. (quoting Stilwell v. Seibel, 169 Or App 613, 616, 10 P3d 
319 (2000)). “That means facts are not merely undisputed, 
but immaterial, such as a facial challenge to the constitu -
tionality of a statute.” Id. That is, “the legal theory under -
lying the motion must be that the moving party has a right 
to prevail on any set of facts and that the facts, in effect, 
do not matter.” York v. Bailey, 159 Or App 341, 345-46, 976 
P2d 1181, rev den, 329 Or 287 (1999). The facts of this case 
are material to Lamar’s summary judgment motion, which 
rested on its contention that plaintiffs’ contractual expec -
tations were not objectively reasonable. Thus, Lamar’s first 
assignment of error is unreviewable.
 Lamar’s fourth assignment of error challenges the 
trial court’s denial of Lamar’s motion for judgment notwith-
standing the verdict and alternative motion for new trial. 
However, “[d]enials of those motions made on the grounds of 
insufficient evidence are not reviewable.” Burke v. American 
Network, Inc., 95 Or App 274, 277, 768 P2d 924 (1989). 
Although Lamar attempts to frame the issues as purely 
legal, the gravamen of Lamar’s argument below was that 
the evidence was legally insufficient to support the jury’s 
verdict. Thus, we do not address Lamar’s fourth assignment 
because it is not reviewable on appeal.
520 Atwood v. Lamar Obie Co., LLC
II. BACKGROUND
 In its remaining assignments of error, Lamar 
argues that the trial court erred in denying its directed ver-
dict motions and in its instructions to the jury. “In review -
ing the denial of a motion for directed verdict, we view the 
evidence, including reasonable attendant inferences, in the 
light most favorable to the nonmoving party, here, plain -
tiff[s].” Hudjohn v. S&G Mach. Co. , 200 Or App 340, 342, 
114 P3d 1141 (2005). We recite the following facts with that 
standard in mind. To the extent that Lamar is entitled to 
any different factual inferences with respect to jury instruc-
tions, we will address that in our analysis of those assign -
ments of error. See, e.g., Ossanna v. Nike, Inc., 365 Or 196, 
199, 445 P3d 281 (2019) (“We review a trial court’s failure to 
give a requested jury instruction for errors of law and eval-
uate the evidence in the light most favorable to the estab -
lishment of the facts necessary to require the instruction.” 
(Internal citations omitted.)).
 Plaintiffs are owners of a building located on West 
Burnside in Portland. Plaintiff Jim Atwood is the sole share-
holder of plaintiff JA Atwood Corporation and the trustee of 
plaintiff Jim A Atwood Trust. The west side of the building 
has a large wall, and plaintiffs used the wall to display com-
mercial advertising for decades (the wall sign). Plaintiffs 
would lease the wall sign to advertising companies to act as 
brokers to obtain advertising for the wall sign and gener -
ate revenue. Each lease was for a set period and a monthly 
rental amount, and, at the end of the lease, plaintiffs were 
free to lease the wall sign to another tenant.
 On July 1, 2009, plaintiffs entered into a lease with 
Onsite Advertising Services, LLC to act as the broker for the 
wall sign. That lease was different than prior leases in that 
it provided that the revenue from advertisers would be split 
between plaintiffs and Onsite Advertising. The lease included 
terms that plaintiffs leased the building to Onsite Advertising
“for the purpose of displaying a painted mural, painted 
advertising sign, signage applied by way of other materials 
such as adhesive or flex vinyl products (common for indus -
try), or signage affixed by bolts or screws anchored into the 
building in such a way so as not to damage the bricks or 
Cite as 354 Or App 516 (2026) 521
structure. All holes, if any, shall be filled by Lessee at the 
expiration of the lease.”
The lease also provided that, “Lessee shall take no acts 
which would damage or threaten to damage any portion of 
the building wall.” Atwood testified that he did not want 
any tenants to take any acts that would impair his ability 
to lease the wall sign. The lease was for 60 months, ending 
on June 30, 2014, with an option to renew for 60 months. 
Also in 2009, plaintiffs paid for an illumination system for 
the wall sign that was attached to the building, and later, 
through reduced rent, paid for a cabling system to attach 
vinyl signs.
 After entering into that agreement, in 2010, OnSite 
Advertising assigned its interest in the lease to OnDisplay 
Advertising LLC, in a sale of assets. In February 2014, with 
an effective date of June 30, 2014, plaintiffs and OnDisplay 
executed a lease addendum, which set out the revenue split 
going forward, extended the lease to June 30, 2019, and 
provided that the lease would automatically renew for five 
years, unless either party gave at least 60 days prior notice 
of intent not to renew.
 In 2012, the portion of West Burnside where the wall 
sign is located was designated a state highway by Oregon, 
which made the sign subject to permitting requirements for 
commercial advertising located next to a highway. However, 
ODOT did not require applications for permits until June 
30, 2015. In December 2014, OnDisplay’s representative, 
Mike Maloney, contacted Atwood and informed him that the 
state required a permit for the wall sign and that he needed 
Atwood to prepare a letter to ODOT. Atwood agreed to pro-
vide the letter, so long as plaintiffs owned the permit when 
the lease ended. Atwood provided the letter to Maloney, 
which gave consent to OnDisplay to apply for the permit and 
provided that the permit “shall be in the name of: OnDisplay 
Advertising, J A Atwood, J A Atwood Corporation, their 
successors and assigns, as his or its interest may appear.” 
Atwood included that language to be clear that he was to 
own the permit when the lease with OnDisplay ended.
 In early 2015, OnDisplay began discussions with 
Lamar to purchase OnDisplay’s assets, including its lease 
522 Atwood v. Lamar Obie Co., LLC
with plaintiffs. As a condition of the transaction with 
Lamar, OnDisplay was required to apply for the ODOT per-
mit. Maloney then sent the application to ODOT along with 
Atwood’s letter, which is part of the permit file. Maloney 
also sent the application packet to OnDisplay’s attorneys as 
part of the transaction with Lamar. Lamar’s purchase of 
OnDisplay’s assets closed on June 16, 2015. OnDisplay did 
not ever give Atwood a copy of the application to ODOT or 
a copy of the ODOT permit. Maloney also did not communi-
cate with Atwood about the permit.
 Maloney notified Atwood of the sale of OnDisplay’s 
assets and that it was assigning the lease to Lamar on July 
7, 2015. Atwood did not know prior to that time that the sale 
was occurring, and he was never informed of any terms of 
the sale. He did inquire whether the state permit was com -
pleted, and Maloney told him that the wall sign was now 
state permitted. OnDisplay then transferred the ODOT per-
mit to Lamar, without notice to plaintiffs, and ODOT reis -
sued the permit only in the name of Lamar. Plaintiffs were 
not notified by OnDisplay, ODOT, or Lamar that ODOT had 
issued the permit only in the name of OnDisplay and then 
transferred it only in the name of Lamar.
 After Lamar took over the lease for the wall sign, 
plaintiffs experienced a decline in revenue. In June 2017, 
Lamar’s representative, John Fitzmaurice, emailed Atwood 
his analysis of the Portland market, and stated, “As you 
move forward with whatever company you work with, Jim, 
you might consider going to a long-term fixed rate,” and 
stated that Lamar would be willing to discuss a buyout

leads.caseName: First Care Therapy, LLC and Loodhinssy Lafaille-Paul v. Congress Ave Boynton, LLC
leads.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida
leads.text:
DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF FLORIDA
 FOURTH DISTRICT

 FIRST CARE THERAPY, LLC and
 LOODJHINSSY LAFAILLE-PAUL,
 Appellants,

 v.

 CONGRESS AVE BOYNTON, LLC,
 Appellee.

 No. 4D2025-2466

 [November 12, 2026]

 Appeal from the Circuit Court for the Fifteenth Judicial Circuit, Palm
Beach County; Gregory Keyser, Judge; L.T. Case No.
502025CA001625XXXAMB.

 Dexter F. George of Law Office of Dexter F. George, Plantation, and
Robert Wellington Guerrier of Law Offices of Robert Guerrier, P.A., West
Palm Beach, for appellants.

 Daniel E. Nordby, Alyssa L. Cory, and Kassandra S. Reardon of Shutts
& Bowen LLP, Tallahassee, and Brett R. Renton and Samendio L. Mathieu
of Shutts & Bowen LLP, Orlando, for appellee.

FORST, J.

 In this breach of a commercial lease and guaranty case, Appellants
First Care Therapy, LLC (“Tenant”) and Loodjhinssy Lafaille-Paul
(“Guarantor”) appeal from the final default summary judgment entered
against them and in favor of Appellee Congress Ave Boynton, LLC
(“Landlord”). Appellants contend that the judgment is void because: 1)
Landlord lacked standing and failed to state a cause of action; 2) the trial
court lacked subject matter jurisdiction; and 3) Appellants were denied
due process—both as to the corporate Tenant’s appearance without
counsel and as to the award of unliquidated damages without a properly
noticed trial.

 We affirm the judgment with minimal discussion insofar as it
adjudicates Landlord’s standing, the trial court’s jurisdiction, and
Appellants’ liability. But because the trial court awarded unliquidated
 damages against defaulted defendants without the properly noticed
damages trial which our precedent requires, we reverse the damages
award and remand for a properly noticed trial.

 Background

 In September 2021, Tenant leased commercial premises in Boynton
Beach from SNH Medical Office Properties Trust (“Former Landlord”).
Guarantor executed a guaranty of Tenant’s obligations under the lease. In
May 2024, Landlord purchased the property and Former Landlord
assigned the lease and guaranty to Landlord.

 On February 21, 2025, Landlord sued Tenant and Guarantor for breach
of the lease and guaranty, claiming nonpayment of commercial rent. The
complaint did not allege a sum certain. Landlord instead sought “base
rent, additional rent, operating expenses/common area maintenance, late
fees, real estate taxes, and sales taxes that was due,” together with “the
additional amounts that will [not] come due until the Premises is relet,”
plus fees and costs. Landlord attached to the complaint: the original lease
and guaranty agreements; a “notice of monetary default”; a “lease ledger”
itemizing various unpaid charges totaling $34,337.91; an agreement by
which Tenant would return the premises to Landlord, which would
“attempt to relet the premises”; and the guaranty, wherein Guarantor
agreed to be held liable for any of Tenant’s unpaid lease obligations.
Landlord did not attach the paperwork concerning the lease assignment
from Former Landlord to Landlord.

 Tenant and Guarantor were served with the complaint but did not
respond, and the clerk entered a default against Tenant and Guarantor in
March 2025. Landlord then moved for final summary judgment, asserting
that an attached “Affidavit of Indebtedness . . . liquidates the amount of
damages sought by the Complaint, which totals $85,782.80, through the
date of reletting plus the costs of reletting.” The affidavit, executed by
Landlord’s managing agent, attributed that sum to four components:
$48,480 in rent, $4,222 in “legal fees to draft and negotiate new lease,”
$10,557 in “commission paid to relet,” and $22,523 in “tenant
improvement in relet.” The motion also claimed entitlement to attorney’s
fees and costs.

 The trial court held a summary judgment hearing in July 2025. The
resulting final judgment reflects that, at the hearing, Guarantor appeared
pro se, and no attorney appeared for Tenant. Appellants did not provide
a transcript of that hearing and we can only speculate as to whether
Landlord and/or Guarantor presented witnesses or introduced evidence.

 2
 The final judgment merely states that the court “heard argument.” The
trial court entered final judgment for Landlord in the amount of
$85,782.80 (the exact amount requested by Landlord), plus interest, and
found Landlord entitled to attorney’s fees.

 Tenant’s and Guarantor’s appeal follows.

 Analysis

 “Whether a judgment is void is a question of law reviewed de novo.”
Vercosa v. Fields, 174 So. 3d 550, 552 (Fla. 4th DCA 2015).

 Standing, Jurisdiction, and Liability

 We are unpersuaded by Appellants’ principal arguments—that the
complaint failed to state a cause of action, Landlord lacked standing, and
the trial court therefore lacked subject matter jurisdiction.

 Section 26.012(2)(a), Florida Statutes (2024), vests the circuit courts
with exclusive original jurisdiction over all actions at law not cognizable
by the county courts, which includes this breach-of-contract action.
Appellants conflate subject matter jurisdiction with case jurisdiction. The
former concerns the court’s authority over a class of cases. The latter
concerns the court’s authority to act in a particular case, and a challenge
to case jurisdiction is waived if not timely raised. JJJTB, Inc. v. Schmidt,
415 So. 3d 129, 132–33 (Fla. 2025). Here, the circuit court clearly had
subject matter jurisdiction, and Appellants waived any case jurisdiction
objection.

 The absence of the written assignment from Former Landlord to
Landlord did not defeat Landlord’s standing or render the complaint legally
insufficient. Florida Rule of Civil Procedure 1.130(a) requires only that the
“contracts, accounts, or documents on which action may be brought or
defense made . . . must be incorporated in or attached to the pleading.”
Landlord sued on the lease and guaranty and attached both. Rule 1.130
did not require Landlord to also attach the assignment.
Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.130(a).

 Moreover, by defaulting, Appellants admitted the complaint’s well-pled
factual allegations, including the allegation that Former Landlord had
assigned the lease and guaranty to Landlord. See Donohue v. Brightman,
939 So. 2d 1162, 1164 (Fla. 4th DCA 2006) (“A default terminates the
defending party’s right to further defend, except to contest the amount of
unliquidated damages.”) (citing Kaplan v. Morse, 870 So. 2d 934, 936 (Fla.

 3
 5th DCA 2004)); Fla. Bar v. Porter, 684 So. 2d 810, 813 n.4 (Fla. 1996)
(“[T]he entry of default precludes a party from contesting the existence of
the plaintiff’s claim and liability thereon. Thereafter, a party has the right
to contest damages caused by the party’s wrong but no other issue.”
(citations omitted)).

 That implicit admission established Landlord’s status as assignee—and
thus Landlord’s standing—as a matter of law. The rule that a failure to
state a cause of action is not cured by a default does not help Appellants,
because the complaint stated causes of action for breach of the lease and
the guaranty.

 Finally, Tenant argues it was denied due process when it “could not
have had an opportunity to be heard” at the summary judgment hearing.
Yet, Appellants’ brief acknowledges “[i]t is well recognized that a company,
unlike a natural person, cannot represent itself and cannot appear in a
court of law without an attorney as occurred in this case and reflected in
the Final Judgment.” See Lamaze v. Guthrie, 411 So. 3d 16, 22 (Fla. 4th
DCA 2025). We agree with Landlord that “Tenant’s failure to appear by
counsel does not create a due process violation if [Tenant] does not elect
to appear by counsel.”

 We therefore affirm the final judgment insofar as it determines that
Landlord had standing, the trial court had jurisdiction, and Appellants are
liable for breach of the lease and the guaranty.

 The Trial Court Awarded Unliquidated Damages Without a Properly
 Noticed Trial

 Recently, in Affinity Health Partners, LLC v. Hayes Locums, LLC, 2026
WL 2415958, 51 Fla. L. Weekly D1697 (Fla. 4th DCA Aug. 19, 2026),
relying upon well-established precedent, we held that a trial court errs by
entering a final default judgment for unliquidated damages without a
properly noticed damages trial. Id. at *3. We reversed and remanded for
such a trial on facts materially indistinguishable from those in the present
case. Id. Thus, the same result follows here.

 Whether damages are liquidated or unliquidated is a question of law we
review de novo. Talbot v. Rosenbaum, 142 So. 3d 965, 967 (Fla. 4th DCA
2014). A clerk’s default entitles a plaintiff to liquidated damages, but not
to unliquidated damages—damages are liquidated only where “the proper
amount to be awarded can be determined with exactness from the cause
of action as pleaded,” and are unliquidated where the court must consider
testimony or other evidence to ascertain the facts on which to base a value

 4
 judgment. City of Fellsmere v. Almanza, 380 So. 3d 1199, 1202 (Fla. 4th
DCA 2024) (quoting Bodygear Activewear, Inc. v. Counter Intel. Servs., 946
So. 2d 1148, 1150 (Fla. 4th DCA 2006)). A complaint’s demand for a fixed
sum does not itself liquidate damages. Hartford Fire Ins. Co. v. Controltec,
Inc., 561 So. 2d 1334, 1335 (Fla. 5th DCA 1990). Similarly, an affidavit of
proof does not operate to liquidate them. MacDonnell v. U.S. Bank N.A. as
Tr. for Truman 2013 SC4 Title Tr., 293 So. 3d 585, 590 (Fla. 2d DCA 2020).

 Here, the damages were unliquidated. The complaint pleaded no sum
certain. The ledger attached to the complaint totaled $34,337.91, less
than half of the $85,782.80 which the court ultimately awarded. The trial
court could arrive at the judgment figure only by consulting Landlord’s
“Affidavit of Indebtedness,” which calculated the award from rent, reletting
commissions, tenant improvement costs, and the legal fees of negotiating
a new lease. Because the amount owed could not be determined with
exactness from the pleadings and required the court to weigh evidence,
the damages were unliquidated. See Affinity Health Partners, 2026 WL
2415958 at *3; City of Fellsmere, 380 So. 3d at 1202; Talbot, 142 So. 3d
at 967. The prejudgment interest that derives from that principal is
likewise unliquidated, as are the costs. Affinity Health Partners, 2026 WL
2415958 at *3; MacDonnell, 293 So. 3d at 590.

 Our precedents require an evidentiary hearing or damages trial, noticed
in compliance with Florida Rule of Civil Procedure 1.440(d), before the trial
court could award unliquidated damages against a defaulted defendant.
Affinity Health Partners, 2026 WL 2415958 at *3; Bodygear Activewear,
946 So. 2d at 1151 (“For lost profits or sums expended to perform a
contract, testimony or other evidence is necessary ‘to ascertain facts upon
which to base a value judgment’ and set a damage figure. Therefore, even
though it was in default, Bodygear was entitled to an evidentiary hearing
on the issue of damages noticed in compliance with Florida Rule of Civil
Procedure 1.440.” (quoting Roggemann v. Boston Safe Deposit & Tr. Co.,
670 So. 2d 1073, 1075 (Fla. 4th DCA 1996) (footnote omitted))).

 Here, the July 2025 proceeding was a non-evidentiary summary
judgment hearing, not a damages trial noticed under Rule 1.440. The final
judgment reflects that the court received argument rather than evidence,
and awarded the precise sum which Landlord’s motion had requested.
Summary judgment proceedings are not a substitute for the noticed
damages trial which our cases require. The award of unliquidated

 5
 damages without a noticed hearing was therefore error. 1 See Affinity
Health Partners, 2026 WL 2415958 at *3.

 Further, Appellants’ failure to furnish a transcript of the July 2025
hearing does not compel affirmance without a remand on the damages
issue. The hearing was non-evidentiary, and the error which we have
identified—the award of unliquidated damages through summary
judgment rather than a noticed damages trial—appears on the f

leads.caseName: Yeshiva Ohr Shraga Veretzky v. Town of Highland Zoning Board of Appeals
leads.court: Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
leads.text:
1 
26-638 
Yeshiva Ohr Shraga Veretzky v. Town of Highland Zoning Board of Appeals 

UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS 
FOR THE SECOND CIRCUIT 

SUMMARY ORDER 

RULINGS BY SUMMARY ORDER DO NOT HAVE PRECEDENTIAL EFFECT. CITATION TO A SUMMARY 
ORDER FILED ON OR AFTER JANUARY 1, 2007, IS PERMITTED AND IS GOVERNED BY FEDERAL RULE OF 
APPELLATE PROCEDURE 32.1 AND THIS COURT’S LOCAL RULE 32.1.1. WHEN CITING A SUMMARY ORDER 
IN A DOCUMENT FILED WITH THIS COURT, A PARTY MUST CITE EITHER THE FEDERAL APPENDIX OR AN 
ELECTRONIC DATABASE (WITH THE NOTATION “ SUMMARY ORDER” ). A PARTY CITING A SUMMARY 
ORDER MUST SERVE A COPY OF IT ON ANY PARTY NOT REPRESENTED BY COUNSEL. 

 At a stated term of the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, held 
at the Thurgood Marshall United States Courthouse, 40 Foley Square, in the City of New York, 
on the 12th day of November, two thousand twenty-six. 

Present: 
SUSAN L. CARNEY, 
MICHAEL H. PARK, 
EUNICE C. LEE, 
Circuit Judges. 
________________________________________ 

Y
ESHIVA OHR SHRAGA VERETZKY, 

 Plaintiff-Appellant , 
 26-638 
v. 

T
OWN OF HIGHLAND ZONING BOARD OF APPEALS, 
TOWN OF HIGHLAND, 

 Defendants- Appellees.
* 
________________________________________ 

FOR PLAINTIFF-APPELLANT:
 STEVEN BARSHOV, SBarshov Law PLLC, 
Haverstraw, NY. 

FOR DEFENDANTS-APPELLEES: L EO D ORFMAN, Sokoloff Stern LLP, Carle 
Place, NY.

* The Clerk of Court is respectfully directed to amend the caption accordingly. 

2 
Appeal from a judgment of the United States District Court for the Southern District of 
New York (Seibel, J.). 
UPON DUE CONSIDERATION, IT IS HEREBY ORDERED, ADJUDGED, AND 
DECREED that the judgment of the district court is AFFIRMED. 
Yeshiva Ohr Shraga Veretzky is a New York religious corporation that provides Hasidic 
Orthodox Jewish religious education. The Yeshiva acquired property in Barryville, New York, 
within an R-2 Residential Agricultural zoning district, where “places of worship” are permitted by 
special use permit. The Yeshiva applied to the Town of Highland Planning Board for a special 
use permit to use the property for religious educational programming in the summer and for 
religious retreats during the rest of the year. The Planning Board referred to the Town of 
Highland Zoning Board of Appeals (“ZBA”) the question whether the proposed use qualified as a 
“place of worship” under the zoning code. The ZBA concluded in a written interpretation that 
the proposed use constituted a prohibited “children’s camp” rather than a permitted “place of 
worship.” 
Without first seeking a use variance from the ZBA, the Yeshiva brought this action, 
asserting claims under the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (“RLUIPA”), the 
Free Exercise and Equal Protection Clauses of the U.S. Constitution, and various provisions of the 
New York State Constitution. The Southern District of New York granted Defendants’ motion 
to dismiss on ripeness grounds because the Yeshiva had not sought a variance. See Yeshiva Ohr 
Shraga Veretzky v. Town of Highland Zoning Bd. of Appeals, No. 24-cv-8477, 2026 WL 621872, 
at *10–11 (S.D.N.Y. Mar. 5, 2026). We assume the parties’ familiarity with the underlying facts, 
the procedural history of the case, and the issues on appeal. 

3 
“We review de novo the district court’s dismissal of a claim . . . as unripe.” BMG Monroe 
I, LLC v. Vill. of Monroe, 93 F.4th 595, 600 (2d Cir. 2024). “To be justiciable, a cause of action 
must be ripe—it must present a real, substantial controversy, not a mere hypothetical question.” 
Vill. Green at Sayville, LLC v. Town of Islip, 43 F.4th 287, 293 (2d Cir. 2022) (citation omitted) . 
“Ripeness is a doctrine rooted in both Article III’s case or controversy requirement and prudential 
limitations on the exercise of judicial authority.” Id. (citation omitted). “At its heart is whether 
we would benefit from deferring initial review until the claims we are called on to consider have 
arisen in a more concrete and final form.” Id. (citation omitted). 
The Yeshiva’s claims are unripe because it has not pursued the variance process and it has 
made no argument under Circuit law that it was excused from doing so. In the land-use context, 
the Supreme Court has held that a takings claim “is not ripe until the government entity charged 
with implementing the regulations has reached a final decision regarding the application of the 
regulations to the property at issue.” Williamson Cnty. Reg’l Plan. Comm’n v. Hamilton Bank of 
Johnson City, 473 U.S. 172, 186 (1985). This Court has extended the final -decision requirement 
to other types of zoning challenges . See, e.g., BMG Monroe I , 93 F.4th 595 (Equal Protection 
Clause); Murphy v. New Milford Zoning Comm’n, 402 F.3d 342, 352 (2d Cir. 2005) (Free Exercise 
Clause and RLUIPA). “[I]n order to satisfy the finality requirement under our ripeness doctrine, 
a [plaintiff] bringing a federal claim against a municipality . . . must . . . submit at least one 
meaningful application for a variance .” BMG Monroe I , 93 F.4th at 598 ( emphasis added) 
(cleaned up).
1 But “a property owner is excused from obtaining a final decision if . . . seeking a 

1 See also Vill. Green, 43 F.4th at 296 (same); Sunrise Detox V, LLC v. City of White Plains, 769 
F.3d 118, 124 (2d Cir. 2014) (same); Murphy, 402 F.3d at 348 (same); Williamson Cnty., 473 U.S. at 200 
(“No [final] decision had been made . . . because respondent failed to apply for variances from the 
regulations.”). 

4 
variance would be futile.” Id. at 601 (cleaned up). And “a plaintiff need not await a final 
decision to challenge a zoning policy that is discriminatory on its face,” Vill. Green , 43 F.4th at 
294, or when it “can show that [it] suffered some injury independent of the challenged land- use 
decision,” Sunrise Detox v. City of White Plains , 769 F.3d 118, 123 (2d Cir. 2014) (citation 
omitted). 
The Yeshiva concedes that it has not sought a variance, even though the ZBA has the 
authority to grant one. It disclaims any futility argument, asserting that “[t]his is not a futility 
case,” Appellant’s Br. at 25, and concedes that it has alleged no harm independent of the 
interpretation it challenges, see id.2 It also does not advance a facial -discrimination theory on 
appeal. See State St. Bank & Tr. Co. v. Inversiones Errazuriz Limitada, 374 F.3d 158, 172 (2d 
Cir. 2004) (“When a party fails adequately to present arguments in an appellant’s brief, we 
consider those arguments abandoned.”). The Yeshiva has therefore disclaimed, forfeited, or 
abandoned any argument that the one -meaningful-application requirement does not apply to it. 
Accordingly, the Yeshiva’s federal claims are not ripe under our settled law.
3 
The Yeshiva responds that its claims are ripe because the ZBA’s interpretation of the 
zoning code cannot be altered by the Planning Board. I t relies heavily on a New York state 
decision directly overturning a different zoning board’s interpretation of “place of worship,” under 

2 The Yeshiva does argue that requiring it to seek a variance would force it to abandon its property 
and constitutional rights, but those injuries are not independent of the decision it challenges. And, in any 
event, the Yeshiva may be able to challenge that decision later , once it has availed itself of the variance 
process. 
3 We need not decide whether the Yeshiva’s claim under the New York State Constitution is ripe 
because we decline to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over that claim. This is “‘the usual case in which 
all federal-law claims are eliminated before trial’ such that ‘the balance of factors to be considered . . . point 
toward declining to exercise jurisdiction over the remaining state -law claim[]. ’” Kolari v. N.Y. -
Presbyterian Hosp., 455 F.3d 118, 119 (2d Cir. 2006) (quoting Carnegie-Mellon Univ. v. Cohill, 484 U.S. 
343, 350 n.7 (1988)); see also 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(3). 

5 
a different zoning code . See Yeshiva Talmud Torah Ohr Moshe v. Zoning Bd. of Appeals of 
Wawarsing, 170 A.D.3d 1488 (3d Dep’t 2019). But the finality of the ZBA’s interpretation is 
not the finality required for the Yeshiva’s federal claims here. 
In arguing otherwise, the Yeshiva does not cite a single Second Circuit case in its principal 
brief. It instead relies on three decisions from the District of New Jersey.4 Those decisions do 
not control here and in any event did not consider our “one meaningful application” requirement. 
The district court did not err in dismissing the Yeshiva’s claims as unripe. 
* * * 
We have considered the Yeshiva’s remaining arguments and find them to be without merit. 
For the foregoing reasons, the judgment of the district court is AFFIRMED. 
FOR THE COURT: 
Catherine O’Hagan Wolfe, Clerk of Court 

4 See Congregation Kollel, Inc. v. Twp. of Howell , No. 16-2457, 2017 WL 637689 (D.N.J. Feb. 
16, 2017); Bais Brucha Inc. v. Twp. of Toms River, No. 21-3239, 2024 WL 863698 (D.N.J. Feb. 29, 2024); 
Khal Anshei Tallymawr, Inc. v. Twp. of Toms River, No. 21-2716, 2021 WL 5757404 (D.N.J. Dec. 3, 2021).

leads.caseName: Jesus M. Zeno, P.C. v. Grullon
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
Jesus M. Zeno, P.C. v Grullon 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06552 
 November 10, 2026 
 Appellate Division, First Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Jesus M. Zeno, P.C., Plaintiff-Respondent, 
 v 
 Meglis Grullon, Defendant-Appellant. 

 Decided and Entered: November 10, 2026 
 Index No. 535791/22|Appeal No. 7467|Case No. 2026-00324| 
 Before: Webber, J.P., Moulton, González, Chan, JJ. 

 Nwokoro & Associates, P.C., Brooklyn (Emeka Nwokoro of counsel), for appellant. 
 Jesus M. Zeno, P.C., Brooklyn (Jesus M. Zeno of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 Order, Supreme Court, Kings County (Saul Stein, J.), entered June 2, 2025, transferred to this Court by order of Supreme Court, Appellate Division, Second Department, dated December 12, 2025, which, to the extent appealed from as limited by the briefs, denied defendant's motion to vacate the money judgment in plaintiff's favor dated February 22, 2024, and granted plaintiff's motion for a turnover of defendant's assets and the appointment of a receiver, unanimously modified, on the law, to exclude from the property subject to the turnover order defendant's pension monies that remain in trust and her unspecified real property located in the Dominican Republic, and otherwise affirmed, without costs. 
 Supreme Court providently exercised its discretion in denying defendant's motion to vacate her default under CPLR 317 and 5015(a)(1). Contrary to defendant's contention, her bare denial of proper service is insufficient to challenge the sworn statements in the affidavit of service ( see e.g. San Lim v MTA Bus Co. , 190 AD3d 493 , 493 [1st Dept 2021]; see also Goldfarb v Zhukov , 145 AD3d 757, 758 [2d Dept 2016]). In addition, defendant waived her service defense by filing a notice of appearance in the action without first preserving the defense in an answer or pre-answer motion under CPLR 3211 ( see CPLR 320[b]; see also Capital One N.A. v Ezkor , 209 AD3d 823, 824 [2d Dept 2022]). 
 Even if proper service were in question, which it is not for the reasons stated above, defendant's affidavit failed to establish a meritorious defense to the action for the purposes of vacating her default. With respect to the account stated cause of action, defendant's failure to lodge a timely and specific objection to the billing was "insufficient to rebut any inference of an agreement to pay the stated amount" ( Law Off. of Mark S. Helweil v Karambelas , 190 AD3d 560 , 560 [1st Dept 2021]). Plaintiff established the elements of the claim by submitting evidence in the form of detailed monthly invoices addressed to defendant, together with affidavits stating that the invoices were regularly and timely forwarded to defendant and that she received the invoices. This evidence established compliance with the regular billing requirements in the retainer agreement ( id. ). Plaintiff also submitted an affidavit by defendant in the underlying divorce action, in which she acknowledged that she had incurred at least $52,000 in fees as of that date. The bare assertion that at some point defendant objected orally to the amounts due by requesting an extension of time to pay an unspecified amount at the conclusion of the case does not constitute a meritorious defense ( see Katsky Korins LLP v Moskovits , 198 AD3d 566 , 567 [1st Dept 2021]). 
 [*2] 
 Additionally, Supreme Court providently exercised its discretion in denying defendant's motion under CPLR 317 and 5015(a)(1) to vacate the default judgment against her. Paragraph 7 of the retainer agreement required any modification of its terms to be set forth in writing and signed by the client before taking effect. Thus, any oral modification was ineffective under General Obligations Law § 15-301(1), which provides that an agreement with a no oral modifications provision "cannot be changed by an executory agreement unless such executory agreement is in writing and signed by the party against whom enforcement of the change is sought." 
 With respect to the motion for a turnover of assets under CPLR 5225 and the appointment of a receiver, CPLR 5205(c)(1) and (2) expressly exclude monies held in trust, including pensions, from those assets which may be applied to satisfy a judgment ( see Office Create Corp. v Planet Entertainment, LLC , 140 F4th 96, 103 [2d Cir 2025]). Although this exception does not include the monies defendant has voluntarily withdrawn from her pension, which are no longer held in trust, the order must reflect that under CPLR 5205(c), her pension remains exempt from collection efforts. 
 As to the branch of plaintiff's motion seeking the turnover of unspecified real property purportedly owned by defendant and located in the Dominican Republic, real property does not fall within the categories of property subject to turnover under CPLR 5225(a), which relates solely to personal property ( Gryphon Dom. VI, LLC v APP Intern. Fin. Co., B.V. , 41 AD3d 25, 35 [1st Dept 2007], lv denied 10 NY3d 705 [2008]). We reject plaintiff's assertion that under Koehler v Bank of Bermuda Ltd. ( 12 NY3d 533 [2009]), a judgment debtor or third party in control of a debtor's assets may be ordered to produce real property located outside the State of New York, as Koehler related to out-of-state stocks, which are personal property ( id. at 541 ). Similarly, Hotel 71 Mezz Lender LLC v Falor ( 14 NY3d 303 [2010]) involved collection efforts against "intangible personal property" including "defendants' ownership/membership interests in various out-of-state business entities," which also constitute personal property ( id. at 307 ). 
 THIS CONSTITUTES THE DECISION AND ORDER OF THE SUPREME COURT, APPELLATE DIVISION, FIRST DEPARTMENT. 
 ENTERED: November 10, 2026

leads.caseName: Logrono v. City of New York
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
Logrono v City of New York 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06553 
 November 10, 2026 
 Appellate Division, First Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Luz Maria Intriago Logrono, Plaintiff-Appellant, 
 v 
 The City of New York et al., Defendants-Respondents. [And a Third-Party Action] 

 Decided and Entered: November 10, 2026 
 Index No. 23399/20|Appeal No. 7462|Case No. 2025-07477| 
 Before: Webber, J.P., Moulton, Friedman, González, Chan, JJ. 

 Ginarte Gonzalez Winograd LLP, New York (Anthony F. DeStefano of counsel), for appellant. 
 Mintzer Sarowitz Zeris & Willis, PLLC, New York (Thomas G. Darmody of counsel), for respondents. 

 [*1] 
 Order, Supreme Court, Bronx County (Mary Ann Brigantti, J.), entered on or about October 15, 2025, which denied plaintiff's motion for summary judgment as to liability against defendants the City of New York, Riverbay Corporation, and Xinos Construction Corp. on the Labor Law § 241(6) claim predicated on Industrial Code (12 NYCRR) §§ 23-1.7 (e)(1) and (e)(2), unanimously reversed, on the law, without costs, and the motion granted. 
 As an initial matter, defendants asserted no viable defenses as to their liability other than plaintiff's alleged comparative negligence, which, they incorrectly argue, precludes a determination of ttheir liability as a matter of law. Plaintiff is not required to show her freedom from comparative negligence to be entitled to summary judgment on liability under Labor Law § 241(6) ( see Mather v HFK KIK 30th St. Owner LLC , 244 AD3d 539, 540 [1st Dept 2025]). The record established defendants' Labor Law § 241(6) violations predicated on 12 NYCRR 23-1.7(e)(1) and (2). Therefore, plaintiff's motion should have been granted and the issue of comparative negligence directed for trial ( see Luciano v New York City Hous. Auth. , 157 AD3d 617 [1st Dept 2018]). 
 Plaintiff established that the doorway where she tripped and fell constituted a passageway within the meaning of 12 NYCRR 23-1.7(e)(1). Plaintiff's deposition testimony also established the applicable Industrial Code violation, and defendants failed to challenge plaintiff's testimony as demonstrably false, thus entitling plaintiff to summary judgment under Labor Law § 241(6) ( see Ward v Times Sq. Hotel Owner LLC , 243 AD3d 514, 516 [1st Dept 2025]). 
 As to plaintiff's claimed violation of 12 NYCRR 23-1.7(e)(2), plaintiff's testimony established that the storage area where she fell was a "working area" at the time of her accident. Plaintiff testified that about a half hour before the accident, her supervisor directed her to mix cement, which required her to bring up bags of cement from the subject building's storage room and take them to the yard. Because plaintiff was required to traverse the storage room to access the cement bags before she tripped and fell on the cord of a hammer drill obstructing the doorway, that area constituted "a working area" for the purposes of 12 NYCRR 23-1.7(e)(2) ( see Gonzalez v G. Fazio Constr. Co., Inc. , 176 AD3d 610, 611 [1st Dept 2019]; Canning v Barneys N.Y. , 289 AD2d 32, 35 [1st Dept 2001]). Thus, plaintiff is also entitled to summary judgment on Labor Law § 241(6) predicated upon 12 NYCRR 23-1.7(e)(2) ( see Lester v JD Carlisle Dev. Corp., MD. , 156 AD3d 577, 578 [1st Dept 2017]). 
 THIS CONSTITUTES THE DECISION AND ORDER OF THE SUPREME COURT, APPELLATE DIVISION, FIRST DEPARTMENT. 
 ENTERED: November 10, 2026

leads.caseName: Allison Lauderdale v. Hinds County Mississippi Board of Supervisors, Soul City Storage, LLC and Soul City Energy, LLC
leads.text:
IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF THE STATE OF MISSISSIPPI

 NO. 2025-CA-00566-COA

ALLISON LAUDERDALE APPELLANT

v.

HINDS COUNTY MISSISSIPPI BOARD OF APPELLEES
SUPERVISORS, SOUL CITY STORAGE, LLC
AND SOUL CITY ENERGY, LLC

DATE OF JUDGMENT: 04/11/2025
TRIAL JUDGE: HON. ELEANOR JOHNSON PETERSON
COURT FROM WHICH APPEALED: HINDS COUNTY CIRCUIT COURT,
 FIRST JUDICIAL DISTRICT
ATTORNEY FOR APPELLANT: JOHN PRINCE MARTIN
ATTORNEYS FOR APPELLEES: RAYFORD G. CHAMBERS
 MARIE ELIZABETH ROPER
NATURE OF THE CASE: CIVIL - STATE BOARDS AND AGENCIES
DISPOSITION: AFFIRMED - 11/10/2026
MOTION FOR REHEARING FILED:

 EN BANC.

 LASSITTER ST. PÉ, J., FOR THE COURT:

¶1. In April 2024, Soul City Storage LLC and Soul City Energy LLC (collectively, Soul

City) submitted applications to the Hinds County Planning Commission requesting

conditional use permits for two projects. Soul City sought to build a solar farm and battery

storage facility on property in Hinds County. The property was comprised of approximately

5,800 acres of undeveloped land, stretching from Bolton to an area north of the Natchez

Trace.

¶2. A few weeks later, Soul City “hosted a community meeting and open house” in

Raymond, which “was well attended with over 100 attendees[.]” Soul City was “provided
 a lot of feedback regarding the project” and voluntarily revised its permit applications to

address the community’s concerns. Its revisions included relocation of construction traffic,

a road use agreement, tree and vegetation management, and the use of agricultural fencing

and wildlife corridors.

¶3. The Hinds County Planning Commission held a public hearing on Soul City’s permit

applications in May 2024. The county’s zoning director presented the details of both

applications to the Planning Commission, and representatives of Soul City spoke in favor of

the projects. Members of the public were then given an opportunity to voice their opinions

and concerns. The concerns raised by county residents opposed to the project included a

desire to maintain the undeveloped rural nature of the county and prevent disruption in

wildlife movement.

¶4. Allison Lauderdale was one of the community members present at the Planning

Commission’s meeting. According to transcripts from the meeting, Lauderdale took part in

the hearing as “a designated spokesperson” for the “constituents of Hinds County” and

voiced her opposition to the conditional use permits.

¶5. At the end of the hearing, the Commission remarked:

 Chairman: Commissioners, you heard presentations and also the
 rebuttal and the community concerns and support.
 What’s your pleasure?
 Commissioner: Mr. Chairman, due to the amount of opposition that
 we’ve heard, we feel that we should not grant the
 petitioner their request.

The Planning Commission then unanimously voted to deny both of Soul City’s

conditional-use permit applications.

 2
 ¶6. Soul City appealed to the Hinds County Board of Supervisors, and the Board held a

public hearing in June 2024. Individuals spoke both against and in support of the project. The

mayor of Raymond requested a one-year moratorium on solar projects. During the hearing,

a Board member asked Permit and Zoning Director Henry Davis whether the application

complied with the zoning ordinance. Davis represented that Soul City had followed all the

zoning guidelines and that solar farms are a permissible conditional use.

¶7. The Board of Supervisors approved Soul City’s applications by a 3-2 vote. The order

and minutes further memorialized the Board’s resolution to approve the two applications.1

¶8. Lauderdale appealed the Board’s decision to the Hinds County Circuit Court. She

argued that the Board’s decision was invalid because the Board did not issue written findings

 1
 In Soul City’s appellate briefing, it summarized the attachments as follows:

 Both CUP applications included Supplemental Applications, which provided
 detailed assessments of compliance with the pertinent sections of the Hinds
 County Zoning Ordinance, including Articles IV (General Regulations, as to
 setbacks, street frontage, visibility at intersections, and height regulations), V
 (Agricultural District uses and Conditional Uses in this zoning district,
 including public or quasi-public facilities and utilities), and Article XXIV,
 Section 2406 (specific requirements for the Board to grant a conditional use),
 Section 2408 (site plan review), and Section 2409 (specifications for required
 site plans). (SOULCITY_00010-00083, 00099-00659). Soul City Energy’s
 Supplemental Application also addressed compliance with Article XIX
 (noting that it will not install solar panels within FEMA designated
 floodplains, including a setback from the floodplains). (SOULCITY_00120).
 Appendices to both Supplemental Applications provided further information
 in support of Soul City’s compliance with all requirements: Preliminary Site
 Plans; a Detailed Description of Solar Project Facilities; Zoning Verification
 Letters; Federal Aviation Administration-Determination of No Hazard; and
 Lists of Adjacent Landowners and Zoning Districts (as required for the Site
 Plan) and proof of notification to these landowners.
 (SOULCITY_00039-00083, 00133-00659).

 3
 as required by the zoning ordinance. She further argued that the decision to grant the permits

was not supported by substantial evidence.

¶9. The circuit court, sitting as an appellate court, heard arguments from the parties in

February 2025 and then issued a written order in April. The circuit court found that Soul

City’s supplemental applications and detailed plans were “substantive in nature and

addressed potential adverse impacts, such as odor, noise, road and traffic congestion, and

general compatibility” and “included maintenance of trees and vegetation, along with

protection of wildlife using agricultural fencing and wildlife corridors.” The circuit court

acknowledged Lauderdale’s argument that the Board did not make its decision in writing, but

the court found this was not error. The circuit court ultimately affirmed the Board’s grant of

the two permit applications to Soul City.

¶10. Aggrieved, Lauderdale appeals.

 STANDARD OF REVIEW

¶11. “In reviewing zoning cases, the circuit court acts as an appellate court, not as the trier

of fact.” Elliott Land Devs. LLC v. Bd. of Supervisors of Jackson Cnty., 421 So. 3d 1206,

1212 (¶25) (Miss. 2025). “The circuit court acts as the first-level appeals court, and our Court

reviews ‘the same record that was made at the agency whose decision is the subject of the

appeal, and applies the same review standard to it regardless of whether the circuit court

affirmed or reversed that decision.’” Id. (quoting Thomas v. Bd. of Supervisors of Panola

Cnty., 45 So. 3d 1173, 1180 (¶21) (Miss. 2010)).

¶12. And “[i]f the [b]oard of [s]upervisors’ decision is based on substantial evidence, then

 4
 it is binding on the circuit court and [this] Court.” Id. at (¶26). “For ‘zoning decisions by

boards of supervisors, the order of the governing body will not be set aside unless it is clearly

shown to be arbitrary, capricious, discriminatory, or is illegal, or without a substantial

evidentiary basis.’” Id. (quoting Thomas, 45 So. 3d at 1180 (¶22)).

¶13. “The burden of proof on issues of ‘rezoning rests on the party asserting the invalidity

of the board’s actions, while the board’s actions’ are presumed valid.” Id. at (¶28) (quoting

Thomas, 45 So. 3d at 1180 (¶23)). This Court “cannot substitute its judgment for actions

taken by the board.” Id. (quoting Thomas, 45 So. 3d at 1180 (¶23)). “The zoning authority’s

actions ‘must not be disturbed where the issue is fairly debatable.’” Id. (quotation mark

omitted) (quoting Thomas, 45 So. 3d at 1180 (¶23)). “When there is substantial evidence

supporting each side of the zoning application, the zoning authority’s ultimate decision is

considered fairly debatable, rather than arbitrary or capricious, depriving our Court of the

authority to overturn the zoning authority’s decision.” Id. at 1212-13 (¶28). “A zoning case

must be decided on all of the circumstances of that particular case.” Id. at 1213 (¶28).

 DISCUSSION

¶14. Lauderdale raises one core argument on appeal. She asserts that “[t]he Board of

Supervisors acted arbitrarily and capriciously by approving the conditional use permits

without issuing the written findings and a written certification of compliance as required by

the Zoning Ordinance.” As a complement to that issue, she further argues that the Board and

Soul City “are judicially estopped from argu[ing] that written findings were unnecessary,”

and last, she argues that the reliance on two prior conditional use permit cases was

 5
 “misplaced.”

 I. The Board satisfied the ordinance’s written requirements.

¶15. Lauderdale argues the Board of Supervisors committed reversible error when it failed

to issue the required written certificate, failed to provide any written findings demonstrating

its reasons for granting the applications, and failed to impose any additional conditions on

the permits it issued.

¶16. “Conditional use permits are adjudicative in nature.” Longo v. City of Waveland, 431

So. 3d 693, 696 (¶11) (Miss. 2026) (quoting Barnes v. Bd. of Supervisors, DeSoto Cnty., 553

So. 2d 508, 510-11 (Miss. 1989)). “The burden is upon the applicants to prove by a

preponderance of the evidence that they have met the elements/factors essential to obtaining

the conditional use permit.” Id. at 696-97 (¶11) (quoting Barnes, 553 So. 2d at 511).

¶17. There is no dispute that subsections (a), (b), and (c) of Hinds County Zoning

Ordinance Section 2406 have been satisfied.2 Soul City filed a written and supplemental

application for a conditional use, as well as a supplemental information letter in response to

the community meeting it held. Likewise, Soul City provided a detailed “Site Plan.”

 2
 Hinds County Zoning Ordinance Section 2406 provides the following requirements
for allowing conditional uses:

 (a) A written application for a conditional use[] is submitted indicating the
 Section in the Ordinance under which the conditional use is sought and
 stating the grounds on which it is requested.
 (b) A detailed Site Plan is submitted in accordance with Section 2408 of
 this Ordinance for review of the requested conditional use.
 (c) A public hearing shall be held and notice of such hearing given in
 accordance with the procedures specified in Section 2410 for all public
 hearings relative to this Ordinance.

 6
 ¶18. The section at issue is subsection (d), which requires:

 (d) The Board of Supervisors have made a written decision certifying
 compliance with the special rules governing individual conditional uses
 and that satisfactory provisions and arrangement has been made
 concerning the following where applicable:

 (1) Ingress and egress to property and proposed structures thereon
 with particular reference to automotive and pedestrian safety
 and convenience, traffic flow and control, access in case of fire
 or catastrophe.
 (2) Off-street parking and loading areas where required with
 particular attention to the items noted above and the economic,
 noise, glare, or odor effects of the conditional use on adjoining
 properties and properties generally in the District.
 (3) Refuse and service areas, with particular reference to the items
 noted above.
 (4) Utilities, with reference to locations, availability, and
 compatibility.
 (5) Screening and buffering with reference to type, dimensions, and
 character.
 (6) Required yards and other open space.
 (7) General compatibility with adjacent properties and other
 property in the District.
 (8) Any other provisions deemed applicable by the Board of
 Supervisors.

Subsection (d) does not prescribe a particular form for its decision or require a separate

certificate containing a finding on each consideration.

leads.text:
IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF THE STATE OF MISSISSIPPI

 NO. 2025-CA-01438-COA

VENTURE INVESTORS LLC AND AMRUT APPELLANTS
PATEL

v.

THOMAS LEONARD AND BIRDIA LEONARD APPELLEES

DATE OF JUDGMENT: 11/07/2025
TRIAL JUDGE: HON. JAMES D. BELL
COURT FROM WHICH APPEALED: HINDS COUNTY CIRCUIT COURT,
 FIRST JUDICIAL DISTRCIT
ATTORNEYS FOR APPELLANTS: DAVID RINGER
 BRENTON MATTHEW CARTER
ATTORNEY FOR APPELLEES: THOMAS W. POWELL
NATURE OF THE CASE: CIVIL - CONTRACT
DISPOSITION: REVERSED AND REMANDED - 11/10/2026
MOTION FOR REHEARING FILED:

 BEFORE CARLTON, P.J., WEDDLE AND LASSITTER ST. PÉ, JJ.

 LASSITTER ST. PÉ, J., FOR THE COURT:

¶1. Amrut Patel, through his limited liability company, Venture Investors LLC (Venture),

leased a property at 5124 North State Street in Jackson to Thomas and Birdia Leonard. The

parties’ relationship eventually deteriorated, prompting Venture to file suit in the County

Court of Hinds County, alleging that the Leonards had breached an oral contract for the lease

of the property. Venture later moved for summary judgment. The county court entered

summary judgment and dismissed the complaint as a matter of law, finding that the oral

contract did not satisfy the elements of a valid contract. The circuit court affirmed, and

Venture appealed. After review, we find that a genuine issue of material fact precludes
 summary judgment, and we reverse and remand.

 FACTS AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY

¶2. Venture filed a complaint in the County Court of Hinds County, alleging that the

Leonards had breached an oral contract for lease of property. Venture alleged that Venture

and the Leonards had entered into a non-binding letter of intent (LOI) to lease property. The

terms of the LOI provided that the Leonards would pay Venture “a $4,000 deposit for months

1-10 of the lease and $3,500 for months 10-36.” The Leonards also agreed to make

renovations to the property, totaling $8,468. Venture alleged in its complaint that the

Leonards made an initial $4,000 payment “for months 1-10” and then took control of the

property, but they did not sign a later-presented lease agreement.

¶3. The LOI states that it “is completely non-binding and has no effect on either party

whatsoever until a Lease Agreement has been fully executed by both Tenant and Landlord.”

The Leonards signed the LOI, but Venture did not. The copy of the lease agreement was later

included in Venture’s summary judgment motion, and neither party signed it.

¶4. The Leonards responded to the complaint, arguing only that Venture’s complaint

should be dismissed for failure to state a claim upon which relief could be granted. They also

countersued for reimbursement and admitted “the parties entered into an oral contract,” but

they argued that they took possession of the property after making “a down payment of

$4,000.” They claimed they tried to get permits to repair the buildings, but the City of

 2
 Jackson would not issue them due to code violations.1

¶5. Venture moved for summary judgment, arguing that the Leonards violated “the terms

of the oral contract,” which can be “found or inferred from” the LOI. Venture argued that,

per the oral contract, the Leonards were required to pay, and did in fact pay, $4,000 as a non-

refundable deposit that also served as rent for the first ten months of the contract. Venture

asserted that the Leonards were required through the oral agreement to make certain repairs

to the property and to begin paying $3,500 each month in rent beginning in July 2018 through

August 2020. Venture claimed that the Leonards occupied the property “continuously”

through November 2018 but did not pay the monthly rent of $3,500 or complete the required

repairs. Venture alleged under those facts that the Leonards owed Venture $99,468 for

unpaid rent and incomplete repairs. Venture asserted there were no genuine issues of material

fact to warrant a trial.

¶6. In support of its motion, Venture attached a copy of the non-binding LOI, an excerpt

from Birdia Leonard’s deposition (in which she stated that she and Thomas had been married

and started the non-profit “Pro-Way Youth Sports” together), the unsigned lease agreement,

“receipts” (for $1,905 for unclear items or services; $2,000 for grass cutting on the property;

$750 for work on the fence; $375 and $275.26 for machinery rental); a letter from Venture’s

attorney (letting the Leonards know they were behind on the rent); a cashier’s check (from

 1
 The county court granted summary judgment in Venture’s favor on this claim, but
the Leonards did not cross-appeal.

 3
 Thomas to Patal for $4,000); the Leonards’ non-profit’s marketing material; Secretary of

State documents for the non-profit; the non-profit’s application for a privilege license; and

the IRS revocation for the non-profit.

¶7. Venture argued in support of its motion that the Leonards “planned to operate a youth

sports business” at the property, pointing out that the Leonards had registered the non-profit’s

place of business as 5124 North State Street and that the receipts showed they had undertaken

some efforts to improve the property. Venture argued that the failure to pay the rent, to

complete repairs, and to maintain the property were all “clear breach[es] of the agreement”:

“Stated differently, [Venture has] suffered damages in the amount of $91,000.00, plus the

repairs valued at $8,468.00, which were never completed, and damages for [the Leonards’]

failure to maintain the property resulting in deterioration. Accordingly, there is no genuine

issue of material fact and summary judgment should be entered for [Venture.]”

¶8. Despite acknowledging the existence of an oral contract in their answer and failing

to raise the statute of frauds as a defense, the Leonards responded, arguing that there was no

written contract, and therefore there was no binding lease. The Leonards alleged that they

“were never afforded an opportunity to repair said property due to [there] not being a signed

contract or lease.” The Leonards did not file a cross-motion for summary judgment on

Venture’s claims or move for summary judgment on their counterclaim. Rather, the Leonards

only asked the court to deny the plaintiffs’ motion and set the case for “trial.”

¶9. The county court held a hearing on Venture’s motion, but the transcript of the hearing

 4
 was not contained in the record on appeal. The county court’s order notes that “[a]t the

motion hearing counsel for the parties acknowledged . . . that there were no genuine issues

of material fact requiring a determination by a jury, and that the court could resolve the issues

as a matter of law.”

¶10. The county court found that there was not a valid contract between Venture and the

Leonards and that there was no evidence upon which to support recovery on the competing

claims of unjust enrichment. Venture appealed to the Hinds County Circuit Court, which

affirmed. This appeal followed.

 ANALYSIS

¶11. The interpretation of a contract is a question of law that we review de novo. Gulf

Coast Hospice LLC v. LHC Grp. Inc., 273 So. 3d 721, 734 (¶34) (Miss. 2019). We also

review a trial court’s grant of summary judgment de novo. Id. Summary judgment is

appropriate when “the pleadings, depositions, answers to interrogatories and admissions on

file, together with the affidavits, if any, show that there is no genuine issue as to any material

fact and that the moving party is entitled to a judgment as a matter of law.” M.R.C.P. 56(c).

We view the evidence in the light most favorable to the non-moving party. Id.

¶12. The Encyclopedia of Mississippi Law summarizes what a plaintiff must show to obtain

summary judgment:

 Obtaining summary judgment is hard for plaintiffs who carry the burden of
 proof. Plaintiffs must demonstrate that there is no genuine issue of material
 fact on each element of the prima facie case. Basically, in order for the
 plaintiff to obtain summary judgment, the plaintiff must demonstrate that the

 5
  defendant has no evidence disputing any material fact on which the plaintiff’s
 prima facie case rests or must negate the evidence the defendant/nonmovant
 has. The plaintiff movant must demonstrate that no reasonable juror could
 find for the defendant on any material issue.

Jeffrey Jackson et al., Effect of Burdens of Proof on Movant’s Burden, 2 Encyclopedia of

Mississippi Law § 13:179 (3d ed. Sept. 2026).

¶13. Here, Venture’s motion for summary judgment asserted that the parties “entered into

an oral contract” and that “[t]he terms of the oral contract can be found or inferred from the

Non Binding Letter of Intent to Lease.”2 However, the “Non Binding Letter of Intent to

Lease” expressly stated that it was “completely non-binding and ha[d] no effect on either

party whatsoever until a Lease Agreement ha[d] been fully executed by both [parties],” and

the parties never executed a lease. More important, Venture offered no affidavit, deposition

testimony, or other evidence that the parties orally agreed to any contract terms.3

 2
 The theory of Venture’s motion for summary judgment varied materially from the
allegations of Venture’s complaint. Venture’s complaint seemingly alleged that the “Non
Binding Letter of Intent to Lease” was a valid written contract. Specifically, Venture’s
complaint alleged:

 Defendants entered into a Non-Binding Letter of Intent to Lease (referred to
 herein as “agreement”) with the Plaintiffs. A copy of the subject agreement
 is attached hereto as EXHIBIT “A” and incorporated herein by reference.

 Defendants breached the agreement by failing to pay the Plaintiffs in
 accordance with the agreement . . . .

Venture’s complaint made no allegations regarding an oral agreement.
 3
 Venture submitted no affidavits and only one page of Birdia Leonard’s deposition
transcript in support of its motion. The deposition excerpt had nothing to do with the
alleged oral contract.

 6
 ¶14. The county court held that “[a] breach of contract claim must arise from the existence

of [a] valid and binding contract. As to Venture, it simply never had a signed contract with

[the Leonards].” The court noted, “Of the six elements necessary to establish a contract in

Mississippi, some are missing from the unsigned document and others clash with the [LOI,]

thus prohibiting the cobbling together of documents,” then the court pointed out the

uncertainties inherent in the documents relied on by Venture. The court concluded: “Simply

put, the documents supplied by Venture fail to create a contract under Mississippi law and

hence, the [c]ourt need not delve further into the deficiencies undercutting the breach of

contract claim.”

¶15. A plaintiff moving for summary judgment based on an alleged oral contract, at

minimum, must offer an affidavit or testimony that the parties orally agreed to something.

But Venture offered no evidence that the parties ever orally agreed to any of the terms of the

non-binding LOI—Venture simply asserted, without evidentiary support, that the terms of

the alleged oral contract could be “inferred” from that document. Therefore, the county court

properly denied Venture’s motion for summary judgment because Venture failed to meet its

burden of establishing that there was no genuine issue of fact and that it was entitled to

judgment as a matter of law. M.R.C.P. 56(c). Because Venture’s motion was the only motion

on file, the court should have stopped there.

¶16. The county court should not have gone further and dismissed Venture’s claims

because the Leonards never sought summary judgment. See Sullivan v. Trustmark Nat’l

 7
 Bank, 653 So. 2d 930, 932 (Miss. 1995) (holding that “it would be improper” to render

summary judgment in favor of a non-moving party that “did not seek summary judgment in

his favor and ha[d] not sought such relief [on appeal]”). This is true even despite the parties’

apparent agreement before the county court that
