leads.text:
[Cite as U.S. Bank Trust Natl. Assn. v. Diallo, 2026-Ohio-4464.] 

IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF OHIO 

TENTH APPELLATE DISTRICT 

U.S. Bank Trust National Association, : 

 Plaintiff-Appellee, : No. 26AP-474 
 (C.P.C. No. 23CV-3206) 
v. : 
 (ACCELERATED CALENDAR) 
Mamadou Diallo, : 

 Defendant-Appellant. : 

D E C I S I O N 

Rendered on November 10, 2026 

On brief: Mamadou Diallo, pro se. 

APPEAL from the Franklin County Court of Common Pleas 

EDELSTEIN, J. 
{¶ 1} Defendant-appellant, Mamadou Diallo, appeals from a decision and entry of 
the Franklin County Court of Common Pleas denying his motion to vacate the default 
judgment entered in favor of plaintiff-appellee, U.S. Bank Trust National Association (“U.S. 
Bank”). U.S. Bank did not file an appellate brief. For the following reasons, we reverse. 
I. Facts and Procedural History 
{¶ 2} This matter involves a foreclosure action for real property located on Noe 
Bixby Road in Columbus, Ohio (“property”). On October 13, 2017, Mr. Diallo executed a 
promissory note in favor of JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. , secured by a mortgage on the 
property. (Compl. Ex. A; Compl. Ex. B.) On May 4, 2023, Nationstar Mortgage, LLC, the 
mortgagee by assignment or merger, filed a complaint in foreclosure in rem against 
Mr. Diallo, Fatoumata Diallo, JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., Synchrony Bank, the State of 
Ohio Department of Taxation, and the Franklin County Treasurer , alleging Mr. Diallo 
No. 26AP-474 2 

defaulted on the note and mortgage. The complaint stated Mr. Diallo had filed for 
bankruptcy and had been discharged and released from the indebtedness due on the 
promissory note and, thus, Nationstar Mortgage did not seek a deficiency or personal 
money judgment from Mr. Diallo. (Compl. at ¶ 7.) 
{¶ 3} On August 22, 2023, after obtaining leave of court, Nationstar Mortgage filed 
an amended complaint adding the unknown spouse of Mr. Diallo , if any, as a party 
defendant. Nationstar Mortgage subsequently filed a notice of dismissal of defendant 
Fatoumata Diallo, pursuant to Civ.R. 41(A) , because she is deceased. Mr. Diallo and 
Fatoumata Diallo were married until her September 2021 death. 
{¶ 4} On April 26, 2024, the trial court substituted U.S. Bank as owner trustee for 
RCAF Acquisition Trust as the plaintiff and subsequently granted U.S. Bank leave to file a 
second amended complaint. On June 6, 2024, U.S. Bank filed the second amended 
complaint for foreclosure in rem against Mr. Diallo, JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., 
Synchrony Bank, the State of Ohio Department of Taxation, the Franklin County Treasurer, 
and the unknown spouse, if any, of Mr. Diallo. At the time U.S. Bank filed its second 
amended complaint, Mr. Diallo was incarcerated at Southeastern Correctional Institution 
(“SCI”). After service by certified mail to Mr. Diallo initially failed, U.S. Bank requested 
service by process server on Mr. Diallo at SCI. The process server certified on August 16, 
2024 that substitute service on Mr. Diallo was accomplished by leaving a copy of the 
summons and second amended complaint with the intake officer at SCI. Additionally, the 
docket noted service on Mr. Diallo by certified mail as completed on August 15, 2024 by 
delivery to SCI. 
{¶ 5} On September 17, 2024, U.S. Bank filed a motion for default judgment noting 
service on Mr. Diallo had been perfected by certified mail on August 15, 2024. In an 
October 21, 2024 final judgment entry, the trial court granted U.S. Bank’s motion for 
default judgment and entered a decree of foreclosure in rem. The trial court then entered 
an order of sale for the property on November 3, 2024. On April 8, 2025, U.S. Bank filed a 
notice of sheriff’s sale indicating the property was scheduled for auction on April 25, 2025. 
Sale of the property was completed on April 25, 2025. U.S. Bank filed a motion to confirm 
the sale on July 3, 2025, and the trial court entered a judgment entry confirming sale and 
ordering distribution on August 5, 2025. 
No. 26AP-474 3 

{¶ 6} Approximately two months later, on October 6, 2025, Mr. Diallo filed a 
motion for distribution of excess funds in the amount of $61,060.07 from the sheriff’s sale 
of the property. Separately, on November 5, 2025, the Estate of Fatoumata Diallo (“the 
estate”) filed its own motion for distribution of the excess funds. Following a November 12, 
2025 hearing, the magistrate denied Mr. Diallo’s motion for distribution of excess funds 
and granted the estate’s motion for distribution of excess funds. (Mag.’s Decision at 7-8.) 
The magistrate determined that Mr. Diallo was not entitled to the excess sale proceeds 
because he had been convicted of murdering his wife. See R.C. 2105.19(A) (“no person who 
is convicted of . . . [murder] shall in any way benefit by the death. All property of the 
decedent . . . shall pass or be paid or distributed as if the person who caused the death of 
the decedent had predeceased the decedent”). (Mag.’s Decision at 7.) Thus, the magistrate 
determined the entire balance of excess sale proceeds from the foreclosure and sale of the 
property is owed to the estate. (Mag.’s Decision at 7.) 
{¶ 7} Mr. Diallo filed objections to the magistrate’s decision on December 8, 2025. 
Mr. Diallo disagreed with the magistrate’s factual and legal conclusions but did not raise 
any defenses related to insufficient service of process of the underlying foreclosure action. 
In a December 9, 2025 entry and order, the trial court overruled Mr. Diallo’s objections, 
adopted the magistrate’s decision, and ordered the Clerk of Courts to disburse all funds on 
deposit to the estate. Mr. Diallo appealed the trial court’s December 9, 2025 entry and 
order. This court sua sponte dismissed the appeal on May 26, 2026 for Mr. Diallo’s failure 
to file an appellate brief. (May 26, 2026 Journal Entry of Dismissal, case No. 26AP-16.) 
{¶ 8} On March 24, 2026, Mr. Diallo filed a motion to vacate judgment, raising 
insufficiency of service of process for the first time. That motion was stricken due to non-
compliance with Civ.R. 11 and improper hybrid representation. On April 14, 2026, 
Mr. Diallo filed a common-law motion to vacate the default judgment granting the decree 
of foreclosure in rem and the subsequent sheriff’s sale. Mr. Diallo argued service of the 
foreclosure action was insufficient, he never received a summons or complaint, he was not 
properly served within the timeline required by Civ.R. 3(A), and he did not learn of the 
foreclosure action or the sheriff’s sale until September 15, 2025. U.S. Bank filed a motion 
for extension of time to file a response. 
No. 26AP-474 4 

{¶ 9} In lieu of ruling on U.S. Bank’s motion for extension of time, the trial court 
instead issued a May 1, 2026 decision and entry denying Mr. Diallo’s motion to vacate, 
noting the court did not require any opposition to rule on the motion. The trial court 
determined Mr. Diallo waived the defense of insufficiency of process by failing to raise the 
defense in a timely fashion and failing to explain his delay in raising the defense once he 
learned of the foreclosure action. The trial court specifically noted Mr. Diallo appeared 
before the court several times between October 2025 and January 2026 in his attempt to 
obtain distribution of excess funds from the sheriff’s sale of the property but did not raise 
insufficiency of service in any of those appearances or filings. (Decision and Entry at 2-3.) 
Thus, the trial court denied Mr. Diallo’s motion to vacate judgment and found U.S. Bank’s 
motion for extension of time to be moot. Mr. Diallo timely appeals. 
II. Assignments of Error 
{¶ 10} Mr. Diallo raises the following two assignments of error for our review: 
I. The trial court erred as a matter of law when it determined 
Appellant waived his insufficiency of service defense. 

II. The trial court abused its discretion when it denied the, 
unopposed, motion to vacate without holding a hearing. 

III. First Assignment of Error – Waiver of Insufficiency of Service Defense 
{¶ 11} In his first assignment of error, Mr. Diallo argues the trial court erred when 
it determined he waived the defense of insufficiency of service and denied his motion to 
vacate on that basis without further inquiry. Mr. Diallo asserts he could not waive the 
defense of lack of personal jurisdiction due to insufficient service because the court had 
already rendered judgement in the foreclosure decree before he took any action that could 
constitute waiver of service. 
{¶ 12} To render a valid judgment, a court must have personal jurisdiction over the 
defendant. Maryhew v. Yova, 11 Ohio St.3d 154, 156 (1984); Harris v. Mapp, 2006-Ohio-
5515, ¶ 9 (10th Dist.), quoting NetJets, Inc. v. Binning, 2005-Ohio-3934, ¶ 4 (10th Dist.) 
(“ ‘Personal jurisdiction is the authority of a particular forum to enter judgment 
constitutionally binding on a particular defendant.’ ”) . A judgment rendered by a court 
without personal jurisdiction over the defendant is void ab initio, not merely voidable. 
GEICO Indem. Co. v. August, 2023-Ohio-1196, ¶ 14 (10th Dist.), citing Mun. Tax Invest., 
No. 26AP-474 5 

L.L.C. v. Pate, 2016-Ohio-7791, ¶ 9 (10th Dist.); Columbus, Div. of Income Tax v. Yockey, 
2020-Ohio-3290, ¶ 13 (10th Dist.), quoting Green v. Huntley, 2010-Ohio-1024, ¶ 11 (10th 
Dist.); Third Fed. S. & L. Assn. v. Taylor , 2017 -Ohio-7620, ¶ 11 (10th Dist.) . The 
appropriate method to challenge a judgment as void due to lack of personal jurisdiction is 
through a common-law motion to vacate. Chuang Dev., L.L.C. v. Raina, 2017-Ohio-3000, 
¶ 29 (10th Dist.), citing C & W Invest. Co. v. Midwest Vending, Inc., 2003-Ohio-4688, ¶ 7 
(10th Dist.). 
{¶ 13} Generally, an appellate court reviews a trial court’s denial of a common-law 
motion to vacate for an abuse of discretion. Yockey at ¶ 11, citing Third Fed. S. & L. Assn., 
at ¶ 11. An abuse of discretion connotes a decision that is unreasonable, arbitrary, or 
unconscionable. Blakemore v. Blakemore , 5 Ohio St.3d 217, 219 (1983); State ex rel. 
DeBlase v. Ohio Ballot Bd., 2023-Ohio-1823, ¶ 27. However, the issue of whether the trial 
court acquired personal jurisdiction is a question of law we review de novo. Yockey at ¶ 11, 
citing Star Seal of Ohio, Inc. v. Tri State Pavement Supplies, L.L.C., 2010-Ohio-2324, ¶ 10 
(10th Dist.); Shannon Village Homeowners Assn. v. Miller , 2023-Ohio-1449, ¶ 9 (10th 
Dist.), citing Williams v. Gray Guy Group , L.L.C., 2016 -Ohio-8499, ¶ 18 (10th Dist.) ; 
Kauffman Racing Equip., L.L.C. v. Roberts, 2010-Ohio-2551, ¶ 27. 
{¶ 14} A trial court lacks personal jurisdiction to enter judgment against a defendant 
if the plaintiff fails to perfect service of process and the defendant has neither voluntarily 
appeared in the action nor waived service. GEICO Indem. Co. at ¶ 13, citing Bowling v. 
Grange Mut. Cas. Co., 2005-Ohio-5924, ¶ 27 (10th Dist.); Shannon Village Homeowners 
Assn. at ¶ 10 (“In the absence of service of process or a waiver of service by the defendant, 
a court usually cannot exercise power over a named defendant.”), citing Williams at ¶ 18, 
citing Murphy Bros., Inc. v. Michetti Pipe Stringing, Inc., 526 U.S. 344, 350 (1999). The 
duty to perfect service of process rests with the plaintiff, and defendants have no duty to 
assist plaintiffs in fulfilling this obligation. Gliozzo v. Univ. Urologists of Cleveland, Inc., 
2007-Ohio-3762, ¶ 16, citing Maryhew at 159. In order for a court to render a valid 
judgment against a defendant who has not been properly served with process, “ ‘the record 
must demonstrate that the defendant voluntarily submitted to the court’s jurisdiction or 
committed other acts to constitute a waiver of the defense of lack of personal jurisdiction.’ ” 
Yockey at ¶ 14, quoting Green at ¶ 12. 
No. 26AP-474 6 

{¶ 15} In his motion to vacate, Mr. Diallo set forth two main arguments: (1) he was 
not properly served with the summons and complaint in the foreclosure action w

COURT OF APPEALS OF VIRGINIA

 Record No. 1145-25-4

 OMAR MOHAMMAD EL-RASHED, ET AL.
 v.
 COMMISSIONER OF HIGHWAYS FOR THE COMMONWEALTH OF VIRGINIA

Present: Chief Judge Decker, Judges AtLee and Callins
Argued at Fredericksburg, Virginia
 Opinion Issued November 10, 2026

 FROM THE CIRCUIT COURT OF FAIRFAX COUNTY
 Stephen C. Shannon, Judge1

Brian G. Kunze (Blake A. Willis; Waldo & Lyle, P.C., on briefs), for appellants.

Nancy C. Auth, Senior Assistant Attorney General (Jason S. Miyares,2 Attorney General; Leslie
A. T. Haley, Deputy Attorney General; Christian A. Parrish, Senior Assistant Attorney General;
Scott W. Carpenter, Assistant Attorney General; George R. A. Doumar; Daniel R. Hernandez;
Doumar Martin PLCC, on brief), for appellee.

 PUBLISHED OPINION BY
 CHIEF JUDGE MARLA GRAFF DECKER

 Omar Mohammad El-Rashed and Eliana Eyad Albelbaisi appeal the decision of the circuit

court in favor of the Commissioner of Highways in this eminent-domain case. They challenge the

court’s ruling excluding evidence pertaining to their claim for additional compensation related to a

temporary construction easement taken by the Commissioner over a small portion of their

residential property. Their assignments of error suggest the belief that they were entitled to

compensation not only for the rental value of that temporary easement but also for the amount by

 1
 Judge Patrick M. Blanch ruled on the pre-trial motion in limine. Judge Shannon entered
the final order based on the parties’ negotiated settlement.
 2
 Jay C. Jones succeeded Jason S. Miyares as Attorney General on January 17, 2026.
 which they claim the highway expansion project as a whole permanently reduced the value of their

entire parcel. El-Rashed and Albelbaisi also seek attorney fees and costs “incurred in advocating

for . . . just compensation.” We hold that the circuit court did not err and also conclude that the

appellants have not established an entitlement to financial reimbursement. We therefore affirm the

circuit court’s ruling and deny the request for attorney fees and costs.

 BACKGROUND

 El-Rashed and Albelbaisi (the landowners) owned a home and the parcel of land on

which it was located in McLean, Virginia (the property). Before March 2023, the portion of

Interstate 495 (I-495) in that area was an eight-lane highway, which was separated from the

landowners’ property by a sound wall and a wooded area. The Virginia Department of

Transportation (VDOT) owned a right-of-way adjacent to the landowners’ property, located

between their property and the sound wall. Trees were located on both the right-of-way and the

landowners’ property.

 In March 2023, VDOT initiated legal proceedings under Virginia’s eminent-domain law

to establish a temporary construction easement (TCE) over a small portion of the landowners’

property. It did so by filing a “certificate of take” as defined in Code § 33.2-1000. See, e.g.,

Code §§ 33.2-1016 (outlining the general procedure for condemnation by the Commissioner of

Highways), -1022 (addressing the required contents of a certificate of take). The easement that

VDOT sought covered a strip of land less than ten feet wide at the rear of the property totaling

1,458 square feet.3 VDOT calculated the rental value of the TCE, which was for an unknown

duration, as $29,700. The breakdown of that sum was $1,500 for “[n]atural trees/vines” and

$28,200 for “Temporary Construction Easement (Slopes).” The certificate stated that the

 3
 The property as a whole was approximately 20,198 square feet, meaning that the TCE
property was slightly more than seven percent of the landowners’ parcel.
 -2-
 Commissioner estimated the amount “to be the fair market value of the . . . interest” in the land

and “damages to the remainder, if any.” The related petition in condemnation provided that the

Commissioner attempted to buy the temporary easement, “including any and all damages, from

the owner[s] thereof” but “ha[d] been unable . . . to agree upon the purchase price.”

 The landowners filed an answer to the petition. They alleged that they rejected the

Commissioner’s offer to purchase the TCE because “it did not represent the constitutionally-

required just compensation to which the[y we]re entitled.” They also sought attorney fees and

costs. The landowners received a check for $29,700 while they continued to pursue their claim

that they were entitled to a greater sum.

 During the pre-trial discovery process, the landowners identified appraiser Dennis

Gruelle as an expert witness and provided a summary of his expected testimony. According to

the landowners, Gruelle placed the rental value of the small parcel for an estimated period of five

years at $50,495 and valued “landscaping being acquired by VDOT [at] $3,000,” for a total of

$53,495 related directly to the TCE. He also opined that the TCE and the highway construction

project itself would reduce the value of the entire property by just under $500,000. Gruelle

claimed that factors contributing to that reduction included the “elimination . . . of trees,”

“reconstruction of the sound wall closer to the subject property,” and the “close proximity of the

newly constructed I-495 travel lanes.”

 The Commissioner filed a motion in limine to exclude that portion of Gruelle’s testimony

claiming the almost $500,000 in damages. The Commissioner contended these damages were

“unrelated to the acquisition” of the TCE and therefore were “not compensable.” Put another

way, he argued that because the only “public use” in question was the TCE—not the entire I-495

project—the landowners’ damages were limited to those caused by the TCE. He explained that

the acquisition itself was merely “the temporary rental of a sliver of land,” which would “mak[e]

 -3-
 no permanent changes to the [acquisition] property and caus[e] no damages.” The

Commissioner added that the damages claimed would occur due to lawful activity on property

that VDOT already owned,4 therefore not resulting in a compensable taking.5 The landowners

replied that 2019 amendments to Code § 25.1-230 required considering damages to the

remainder property. Additionally, they argued that the public use was the entire I-495 project,

not simply the TCE.

 At oral argument on the motion, the parties and the court addressed VDOT’s

constitutional and statutory duties. Following argument, the court granted the motion in limine,

holding that Gruelle could not testify about damages “flowing from the overall roadway project”

because only damages flowing from the TCE were recoverable. It also ruled that Gruelle could

“not testify as to non-compensable factors . . . shared by the entire public,” including the “loss of

buffer . . . trees . . . from VDOT’s [p]roperty, roadway or construction noise, vibration, or dust.”

Tracking the language of Virginia’s Takings Clause, the court explained that the law permitted

recovery for “damages to the residue that flow[ed] from the take.” See Va. Const. art. I, § 11, cl.

3 (addressing “damages to the residue caused by the taking”).

 After the circuit court granted the motion, the landowners obtained a revised valuation

from Gruelle. They represented that Gruelle opined that factors flowing solely from the TCE

during the construction project—including noise, dust, vibration, and informal use of the rest of

the landowners’ property as a means of ingress to and egress from the TCE—reduced the value

of the residue by five percent or $124,850.

 4
 The record reflects that some “[n]atural trees[ and ]vines” were on the landowners’
property. The TCE price, though, included $1,500 for the removal of those trees.
 5
 The Commissioner also suggested that the damages claimed to the “neighboring
property,” the residue, were speculative. The landowners disagreed. The circuit court declined
to rule on this argument.
 -4-
  The Commissioner filed a second motion in limine seeking to exclude the new dollar

figure. The landowners again opposed the motion. Prior to obtaining a ruling on the second

motion, however, the parties entered into a settlement. They stipulated that “the value of just

compensation” for the TCE itself was $29,700, but the settlement preserved the landowners’

right to appeal the court’s ruling on the first motion in limine, which had denied their additional

claim for damages to the residue property. The court entered a final order based on the

settlement.6 The order specifically stated that the “judgment for $29,700 [wa]s binding on the

parties, except for any claim for damage to the residue if appellate review result[ed] in a reversal

of th[e trial court’s evidentiary ruling] and a remand for further proceedings on that issue.”7

 ANALYSIS

 The landowners’ assignments of error challenge the circuit court’s ruling excluding

evidence of the reduction in value of their property that they claim was taken or damaged

through eminent domain. They suggest that they were entitled to compensation for the amount by

which the entire I-495 expansion project permanently reduced the value of their parcel as a whole.8

The Commissioner, by contrast, contends that they were entitled only to the amount by which the

TCE reduced that value. The landowners also seek attorney fees and costs.

 6
 Two days after entry of the final order, counsel for the landowners filed a 524-page
proffer, composed of a six-page summary and four exhibits. The Commissioner objected to the
proffer. Neither party requested a hearing on the issue, and the circuit court did not rule on it.
 7
 The order also required the Commissioner to pay $5,441 “for the cost of discovery for
[the landowners’] appraiser” and $2,000 to them for the cost of deposition transcripts.
 8
 The appellate record provides no indication that the landowners sold or wished to sell
their home. It also does not reflect the ultimate duration of the TCE or the I-495 expansion
project. The landowners alleged in the circuit court that, according to their expert, the duration
of the TCE was coextensive with the I-495 expansion project and the estimated duration was five
years from the commencement of the TCE in March 2023. Due to the parties’ stipulation below
to the amount of compensation due for the TCE itself, however, as well as this Court’s decision
affirming the ruling of the circuit court, that duration is not relevant in this appeal.
 -5-
  I. Standard of Review

 “‘[A] trial court’s decision to admit or exclude evidence,’ including in eminent domain

proceedings, is reviewed for ‘abuse of discretion.’” Palmyra Assocs., LLC v. Comm’r of

Highways, 299 Va. 377, 384 (2020) (alteration in original) (quoting Dean v. Bd. of Cnty.

Supervisors, 281 Va. 536, 540 (2011)). “Discretion means a ‘range of choice’ . . . .” Id. (quoting

Reyes v. Commonwealth, 297 Va. 133, 140 (2019)). “This bell-shaped curve of reasonability

governing our appellate review rests on the venerable belief that the judge closest to the contest

is the judge best able to discern where the equities lie.” Palmer v. R.A. Yancey Lumber Corp.,

294 Va. 140, 164 (2017) (quoting Minh Duy Du v. Commonwealth, 292 Va. 555, 564 (2016)).

Consequently, when applying this standard, an appellate court “will not reverse a trial court’s . . .

discretionary decision [unless it] exceeded the ‘outermost limits of the range of choice

available.’” Palmyra Assocs., 299 Va at 384 (quoting Reyes, 297 Va. at 140). Additionally, if a

“trial court’s decision is ‘influenced by [a] mistake of law,’” that court necessarily has “abuse[d

its] discretion.” Comm’r of Highways v. Karverly, Inc., 295 Va. 380, 388 n.7 (2018) (first

alteration in original) (quoting Martin v. Lahti, 295 Va. 77, 88 (2018)). But to the extent that the

assignments of error here present questions of constitutional or statutory construction, the

appellate court reviews these issues de novo. Palmer v. Atl. Coast Pipeline, LLC, 293 Va. 573,

577 (2017).

 II. Co

leads.text:
COURT OF APPEALS OF VIRGINIA 
Record No. 0145-25-2 
THE CITY OF COLONIAL HEIGHTS, VIRGINIA 
v. 
ALPENE LAND, LLC, ET AL. 
Present: Judges Causey, Chaney and White 
Argued at Richmond, Virginia 
Opinion Issued November 10, 2026* 
FROM THE CIRCUIT COURT OF THE CITY OF COLONIAL HEIGHTS 
Steven B. Novey, Judge 
M. Tolley Gwinn (Andrew R. McRoberts; Andrew P. Selman; Hugh P. Fisher, III, City 
Attorney; Sands Anderson PC; on briefs), for appellant. 
S. Keith Barker (S. Keith Barker, P.C., on brief), for appellees. 
MEMORANDUM OPINION BY 
JUDGE DORIS HENDERSON CAUSEY 
 This appeal concerns a dispute over the City of Colonial Heights’ ability to collect penalties 
and interest on certain delinquent real property taxes. In June 2024, the Circuit Court for the City of 
Colonial Heights ruled that the City was not permitted to collect penalties or interest because the 
City’s operative ordinance was ineffective. In August 2024, prior to the entry of the final order, the 
City passed a new ordinance (Ordinance No. 24-13) that purported to retroactively set interest and 
penalty rates at ten percent each. In November 2024, the circuit court ruled that Ordinance No. 24-
13 did not apply retroactively. 
 The City appeals both rulings. For the reasons discussed below, we reverse the circuit 
court’s judgment in part and hold that statewide default rates imposed by the Code of Virginia 

* This opinion is not designated for publication. See Code § 17.1-413(A). 
 - 2 - 
permitted the City to collect penalties and interest on delinquent property taxes. We affirm the 
circuit court’s ruling that the City lacked the authority to retroactively impose the changes set forth 
in the August 2024 ordinance. 
BACKGROUND 
 In December 2022, the City of Colonial Heights filed one complaint against Alpene Land, 
LLC, and another complaint against Barker Investment Corporation and A. Louise Haine (these 
three parties will be referred to collectively as “the taxpayers”). In the two suits, the City sought the 
sale⎯under Code § 58.1-3965⎯of certain parcels of land owned by the taxpayers for allegedly 
unpaid real estate taxes. In July 2023, the City filed a third suit against Alpene Land, LLC, seeking 
sale of a separate parcel under Code § 58.1-3965. The three cases proceeded separately and 
simultaneously under separate case numbers but were ultimately consolidated in the circuit court’s 
final order. 
 In May 2024, the taxpayers sought to “redeem” their property pursuant to the relevant 
statutory mechanism by “paying into the court” the amount that they argued represented the full 
amount “due with respect to [the] real estate” sought to be purchased by the City. 
Code § 58.1-3974. Several grounds of disagreement arose between the parties concerning the total 
amount due. 
 The court’s rulings on two areas of the parties’ disagreement are not challenged on appeal 
but are useful to note as background. First, the parties disagreed as to the total principal amount of 
delinquent real estate taxes due and the years for which such taxes were due. The parties and court 
ultimately determined that the taxpayers’ liability in this case included over $65,000 in delinquent 
real estate taxes incurred over nine tax years, spanning 2016 through 2024 (with the specific years 
applicable varying by property). Second, the taxpayers disputed the City’s right to collect attorney 
 - 3 - 
fees. In a letter opinion issued in June 2024, the circuit court ruled that the City was indeed 
authorized to collect attorney fees in the instant case. 
The court also decided on a third issue in its June 2024 letter opinion: whether the City’s 
ordinance permitted it to collect interest and penalties on the delinquent property taxes. This 
question is at the core of this appeal. On this issue, the circuit court ruled for the taxpayers. The 
circuit court found that City Code § 258-13, the ordinance purporting to authorize certain delinquent 
penalty and interest rates on such taxes, was ineffective and “enacts nothing.” Consequently, it held 
that the City lacked authority to collect penalties or interest. At a hearing on July 11, 2024, the 
circuit court reaffirmed its ruling, rejecting the City’s argument that default penalty and interest 
rates stated under Code § 58.1-3915 and -3918 should have applied. 
On August 13, 2024, prior to the entry of a final order, the City passed an ordinance aimed 
at authorizing it to collect penalties and interest on delinquent property taxes. Ordinance No. 24-13 
(the ordinance). The ordinance stated that taxpayers failing to pay real estate taxes by the due date 
would “incur a penalty of ten percent of the tax” and that “[i]nterest at the rate of ten percent 
annually shall be levied upon the principal and penalties of” delinquent real estate taxes. Id. at (A) & 
(B). Further, the ordinance stated that “[t]he provisions of this section are declarative of current 
policy and shall be applied retroactively to all real estate taxes due on and after May 15, 1992.” Id. 
at (E) (emphasis added). 
The City orally notified the court of the new ordinance at the next hearing, which was held 
on August 22, 2024. The City argued that the ordinance applied retroactively to permit the City to 
collect penalties and interest of ten percent for the period of taxes owed.1 The taxpayers argued that 
pursuant to the Dillon Rule, the City lacked the authority to impose the delinquent real estate 

1 The City stated that it had always interpreted the ordinance that the court found to be 
ineffective to have granted it the authority to impose interest and penalty rates of ten percent. 
 - 4 - 
penalties and interest retroactively. After receiving supplemental briefing from the parties, the 
circuit court conducted a second hearing on the issue in October 2024. 
On November 7, 2024, the circuit court issued a second letter opinion regarding the 
retroactive penalties and interest and again ruled in the taxpayers’ favor. The opinion explained that 
under the Dillon Rule, the City had not been delegated the authority to pass a “tax ordinance 
retroactively applying interest and penalties to previously delinquent property taxes[.]” The August 
2024 ordinance, therefore, was “invalid as applied retroactively and is only valid prospectively from 
when the city passed the ordinance.” 
On December 23, 2024, the court memorialized the rulings from both of its letter opinions in 
a final order. It further established the total amounts due, including principal, attorney fees, and 
certain other costs. Finally, the court denied the taxpayers’ request for attorney fees. This appeal 
followed. 
ANALYSIS 
I. The City’s Ability to Collect Penalties and Interest under the Ordinance 
 In its first assignment of error, the City challenges the circuit court’s first ruling concerning 
its ability to collect penalties and interest. In this ruling, the circuit court held that because the 
ordinance was ineffective, the City lacked the authority to collect interest and penalties on 
delinquent property taxes. The City assigns error as follows: “The circuit court erred in holding that 
the City could not collect interest and penalties on the delinquent real estate taxes at issue when it 
refused to apply the mandatory rates for penalties and interest provided in Va. Code §§ 58.1-3915 
and 58.1-3918.” 
A. Applicable Standard of Review and Principles of Statutory Interpretation 
This first assignment of error requires us to interpret the City’s ordinance and certain 
provisions of the Code of Virginia. In interpreting both the ordinance and the Code, this Court will 
 - 5 - 
apply a de novo standard of review. Bd. of Supervisors v. Cohn, 296 Va. 465, 472 (2018) (citing 
Conyers v. Martial Arts World of Richmond, Inc., 273 Va. 96, 104 (2007)). 
 In interpreting statutes, this Court’s “primary goal . . . is to determine the General 
Assembly’s intent.” Commonwealth ex rel. Fair Hous. Bd. v. Windsor Plaza Condo. Ass’n, 289 Va. 
34, 51 (2014) (citing Sheppard v. Junes, 287 Va. 397, 403 (2014)). “To do this, we examine the 
language contained in the statute itself, if unambiguous, and apply its plain meaning.” Id. The 
same rules guide our review of municipal ordinances. Miller & Rhoads Bldg., L.L.C. v. City of 
Richmond, 292 Va. 537, 541 (2016). 
 In construing tax statutes, this Court construes ambiguous provisions “in favor of the 
taxpayer.” Kohl’s Dep’t Stores, Inc. v. Va. Dep’t of Tax’n, 295 Va. 177, 188 (2018). However, 
“this principle is not an absolute formula that overrides all other canons of interpretation.” Id. at 
188-89. “Statutory language is ambiguous only ‘when it may be understood in more than one way, 
or simultaneously refers to two or more things.’” Ford v. Commonwealth, 86 Va. App. 41, 49 
(2025) (quoting Williams v. Commonwealth, 61 Va. App. 1, 9 (2012)). Therefore, when statutory 
language is not ambiguous, i.e., “when the General Assembly’s intent in enacting a tax statute is 
ascertainable, the principle requiring strict construction does not prohibit us from giving effect to 
this intention.” Kohl’s Dep’t Stores, 295 Va. at 189 (emphasis added). 
B. The Code of Virginia’s Default Penalty and Interest Rates Apply 
 The Code of Virginia establishes a default penalty rate and a default interest rate applicable 
to delinquent property taxes. Under Code § 58.1-3915, a municipality may collect a default five 
percent penalty on delinquent property taxes “[e]xcept as otherwise provided by ordinance under 
§ 58.1-3916.” Similarly, under Code § 58.1-3918, a municipality may collect a default annual 
interest rate of ten percent on delinquent taxes, except “when the penalty or interest on such taxes is 
regulated by ordinance under § 58.1-3916.” Code § 58.1-3918. 
 - 6 - 
 Code § 58.1-3916 permits a municipality to set its own penalty and interest rates. See Code 
§ 58.1-3916 (stating that a municipality “may provide by ordinance penalties for failure to file 
[property tax] applications and returns and for nonpayments in time; may provide for payment of 
interest on delinquent taxes”). Additionally, this code section sets limits for such penalty and 
interest rates: The penalty rate “shall not exceed” certain defined figures, depending on the type of 
penalty and the degree of delinquency. Id. “Interest may commence not earlier than the first day 
following the day such taxes are due by ordinance to be filed, at a rate not to exceed 10 percent per 
year.” Id. Interest may not exceed a different rate in any “second and subsequent year[s.]” Id. 
 The City of Colonial Heights’ municipal ordinance stated, “[I]nterest and penalties on 
delinquent taxes shall be as provided in § 58.1-3916 of the Code of Virginia” (former City Code 
§ 258-13). However, Code § 58.1-3916 does not set an interest or penalty rate; it merely empowers 
municipalities to set penalty and interest rates, while precluding them from setting rates above a 
certain level. Therefore, the City did not set an interest or penalty rate; as the circuit court found, 
this ordinance “enacts nothing.” 
 The circuit court, while noting the ordinance’s ineffectiveness, also held that the default 
penalty and interest rates set forth in Code § 58.1-3916 were inapplicable. The circuit court stressed 
that the ordinance was ambiguous and noted that, under Virginia law, ambiguous tax laws must be 
construed in favor of the taxpayer. See Kohl’s Dep’t Stores, Inc., 295 Va. at 189. Therefore, the 
circuit court concluded that the City was not authorized to collect any interest or penalties on the 
late taxes. 
 The circuit court was correct that the ordinance did not set an interest or penalty rate. 
Consequently, Code §§ 58.1-3915 and -3918 apply. Because the City did not “otherwise provide[]” 
any separate penalty rate, the default penalty rate of five percent was applicable. Code § 58.1-3915. 
Similarly, under Code § 58.1-3918, an ordinance that failed to set meaningful r

IN THE COMMONWEALTH COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA 

Bluetriton Brands, Inc. : 
 : 
 v. : No. 581 C.D. 2025 
 : Argued: April 13, 2026 
Washington Township Zoning Hearing : 
Board and Weis Markets, Inc. : 
 : 
Appeal of: Weis Markets, Inc. : 

BEFORE: HONORABLE RENÉE COHN JUBELIRER, President Judge 
 HONORABLE MATTHEW S. WOLF, Judge 
 HONORABLE BONNIE BRIGANCE LEADBETTER, Senior Judge 

OPINION NOT REPORTED 

MEMORANDUM OPINION BY 
PRESIDENT JUDGE COHN JUBELIRER FILED: November 10, 2026 
 Weis Markets, Inc. (Weis) appeals from the April 3, 2025 Order of the Court 
of Common Pleas of Northampton County (common pleas) that reversed the 
decisions of the Washington Township (Township) Zoning Hearing Board (Board) 
approving Weis’s site plan and granting, with conditions, Weis’s request for a 
special exception to add a Weis Gas-N-Go fuel station (Gas-N-Go or proposed use) 
to its supermarket located in a planned development in a Commercial District (C 
District). On appeal, Weis argues that the Board lacked subject matter jurisdiction 
because no special exception was required to allow for the proposed use, which is 
permitted by right in the C District by the Washington Township Zoning Ordinance 
(Ordinance), WASHINGTON TOWNSHIP, PA., ZONING ORDINANCE (2014) 
(ORDINANCE).1 Weis further argues that when all the provisions of the Ordinance 
are considered, no site plan was required for the proposed use because the use 

1 The Ordinance is available at https://www.washington-township.com/forms/zoning-
ordinance-rev2014.pdf (last visited Nov. 9, 2026). 
2 
constituted “land development” under the Washington Township Subdivision and 
Land Development Ordinance , THE WASHINGTON TOWNSHIP SUBDIVISION AND 
LAND USE ORDINANCE (2020) (SALDO).2 Finally, Weis asserts that even if a special 
exception was required, there are no specific requirements for the proposed use, 
meaning there was nothing for it to prove before the burden shifted to Bluetriton 
Brands, Inc. (Objector), whose evidence was insufficient for it to meet its heavy 
burden under the law. Upon careful review, we reverse common pleas’ Order 
because Weis did not have to submit a site plan given the ambiguous language as to 
that requirement. However, because common pleas did not address all of Objector’s 
arguments in its appeal challenging the Board’s Decision granting Weis a special 
exception, we remand for common pleas to issue a new opinion addressing 
Objector’s remaining arguments. 

I. BACKGROUND 
A. First Proceeding Before the Board 
Weis operates a grocery store via a lease within the Bangor Plaza, a 20.3-acre 
planned development consisting of multiple uses located within the Township’s C 
District (Property). (February 16, 2023 Board Decision ( Board 2023 Decision), 
Findings of Fact ( 2023 FOF) ¶¶ 1 3-14, 23.3) Planned developments are a special 
exception use in the C District. (Id. ¶ 25 (citing Section 3.10.C.11 of the Ordinance, 
ORDINANCE, § 3.10.C.11).) Weis submitted an application for a special exception 
(Application) on June 17 , 2022, to construct the Gas-N-Go on the Property that 
would be subordinate to its grocery store use and replace a previously approved bank 
use that was now vacant . ( Id. ¶¶ 15, 26, 28; Supplemental Reproduced Record 

2 The SALDO is available at https://www.washington-township.com/forms/saldo.pdf (last 
visited Nov. 9, 2026). 
3 The Board’s 2023 Decision is found at pages 7a to 31a of the Reproduced Record. 
3 
(S.R.R.) at 111b.4) Weis provided a sketch plan for the project. (S.R.R. at 6b.) On 
July 5, 2022, Weis filed an application for a zoning permit for the proposed use, 
which was denied the same day by the Township’s zoning officer on the basis that a 
special exception was needed. (Id. at 1b, 111b.) There is no indication in the record 
that an appeal of this determination was filed. On July 25, 2022, Weis submitted a 
site plan to the Planning Commission, along with a cover letter. (Id. at 11b-14b.) 
The Township’s Engineer, Domenick DiPaolo of Ott Consulting Inc., issued 
a letter on September 8, 2022, following the review of the site plan that identified 
various deficiencies where the site plan did not meet the Ordinance’s requirements 
(Ott Letter). (2023 FOF ¶ 17; S.R.R. at 7b-10b.) Weis presented the site plan to the 
Township Planning Commission on September 20, 2022, for its review and 
recommendation, but the Planning Commission did not issue a recommendation 
following the hearing nor request resubmission. (2023 FOF ¶¶ 18-19.) The Board 
held hearings over multiple days, at which Weis presented evidence in support of its 
Application and Objector, which operates a commercial water extraction business 
on property adjacent to and downstream from the Property and whose spring it 
claimed could be negatively affected , presented evidence and argument in 
opposition thereto. 
Weis’s engineer, William Swanick, testified as follows. The proposed Gas-
N-Go use would have six fueling positions at three pumps under a canopy. (Id. ¶ 28.) 
Auto service stations are permitted as a by right use in the C District , and the 
proposed use constitutes a “land development” under the SALDO. ( Id. ¶¶ 29-30.) 
Weis was not seeking a variance , and the proposed use would comply with the 

4 The Board found that Weis filed its Application on July 26, 2022; however, Weis’s 
Application is dated June 17, 2022 . (S.R.R. at 111b.) Weis filed its site plan with the Planning 
Commission on July 25, 2022. (Id. at 11b-14b.) 
4 
comments in the Ott Letter and all other Township requirements. ( Id. ¶ 27.) The 
proposed Gas-N-Go complies with the applicable federal, state, and local standards 
and regulations. ( Id. ¶ 35.) Mr. Swanick explained that Objector’s arguments are 
based on its belief that there is an inherent negative environmental impact of the 
proposed use, even if all regulations are met. (Id. ¶ 37.) He posited that Objector’s 
position was that the proposed use had to meet Objector’s requested modifications, 
but Objector nevertheless acknowledged that there was nothing unusual about 
Weis’s proposal. (Id. ¶ 36.) 
Objector’s Mid-Atlantic Natural Resources Manager, Eric Andreus, testified 
regarding its operations and concerns about the proposed use, as follows. Objector 
has spring water withdrawal facilities in the Township and withdraws groundwater 
from the Greenwaltz Spring as the primary source for its Deer Park brand, and it or 
its predecessors have been operating in the Township for more than 20 years. ( Id. 
¶ 51a-c.) Objector has property interests in 15 parcels of land in the Township , 
including a Conservation Easement or Watershed Protection Agreement in 2 parcels 
that directly abut the location of the proposed Gas-N-Go. (Id. ¶ 51e.) Surface waters 
and groundwater flow southward from the Property down to Objector’s properties 
and the source of the Greenwaltz Spring. ( Id. ¶ 51g.) Objector is concerned that 
leaks and spills , both underground and surface, from the proposed use will 
contaminate its spring source and cause significant economic damage. (Id. ¶ 51h-i.) 
Objector also offered the expert testimony of Matthew Reynolds, a licensed 
professional geologist who testified about the hydrology of the relevant ar ea based 
on his numerous investigations since 2013. (Id. ¶ 52.) Mr. Reynolds described the 
aquifer that underlies the area, including the Property and Objector’s properties, the 
flow of water in the area , and how Greenwalk Creek, which flows through a pipe 
5 
that runs under the Property and into two stormwater basins on either side of the 
Property, ultimately infiltrates the groundwater just north of Objector’s properties 
and the Greenwaltz Spring, among other springs. (Id. ¶ 53a-f.) The reclamation of 
the Slate Hills Quarry site increased the amount of total dissolved solids , sulfate 
concentrations, and calcium in the pit water, which discharged into Greenwalk Creek 
and were detected in Objector’s sentinel wells , resulting in the Pennsylvania 
Department of Environmental Protection ( DEP) ordering the cessation of that 
reclamation, but the impact o n the water quality lingered. ( Id. ¶ 53h-i.) The 
proposed use is located “within feet of [] Greenwalk Creek, along the same surface 
water flow pathway as from the Slate Hills Quarry.” (Id. ¶ 53j.) Weis intends to 
discharge effluent from its oil-water separator, which would capture fuel spills and 
contaminated water runoff, into the stormwater basin that forms an actual segment 
of Greenwalk Creek itself, and that effluent will either infiltrate into the aquifer 
directly and/or flow toward Greenwaltz Spring through Greenwalk Creek. (Id. 
¶ 53k-m.) Gasoline contains chemicals that are known to be carcinogens that can 
contaminate drinking water. (Id. ¶ 53n-p.) Mr. Reynolds opined that the operation 
of the proposed use in the fashion that Weis intends from the Application 

would create a significa nt threat of (a) adverse environmenta l impact 
on surrounding areas by reason of water run -off and groundwater 
pollution, and (b) adverse effects on the use and value of [Objector’s] 
properties and other properties in the area that rely on the aquifer as a 
water source. 

(Id. ¶ 54.) 
Finally, Objector offered the expert testimony of Marcel Moreau about 
petroleum storage and dispensing systems, the frequent violation of regulations, 
spills and releases from those systems, and the mitigation measures needed to reduce 
the environmental risks associated therewith . ( Id. ¶ 55.) Mr. Moreau testified as 
6 
follows. DEP’s regulations do not require site -specific review prior to installing 
these systems, take a “one-size-fits all” approach to release prevention and detection 
requirements, and establish a floor for the environmentally protective measures for 
these systems. ( Id. ¶ 56a -b.) DEP, in 2021, inspected only about 30% of the 
facilities with these systems, which is consistent with the regulations, and only 55% 
were found to be in “significant operational compliance” with the applicable 
requirements. (Id. ¶ 56c-d.) DEP’s website showed that DEP issued Weis notices 
of violations of the storage tank program requirements for approximately one half 
of its Gas -N-Go locations in the Commonwealth , and those violations included 
failure to comply with release detection, containment, and operational requirements, 
failure to investigate and/or report suspected releases, failure to have trained 
operators, and spill and overfill control violations. ( Id. ¶ 56g.) Based on Weis’s 
compliance record, and that of the entire industry, Mr. Moreau believed there was 
“a meaningful chan ce that Weis’s proposed Gas -N-Go facility will experience a 
significant release of gasoline to the environment over its lifetime,” and Weis’s 
suggested protections were not specific, failed to capture contaminants like benzene 
and ethanol, which are dissolved in water, and/or failed to protect from direct contact 
with precipitation. (Id. ¶ 56i-k, p-s.) Mr. Moreau offered alternatives, which would 
address Objector’s concerns, like those implemented by other gas station developers, 
but Weis had not offered any alternatives. ( Id. ¶ 56n -o, t .) In Mr. Moreau’s

  Krasko v. Konkos

 ROBERT J. KRASKO ET AL. v.
 ROBERT KONKOS ET AL.
 (AC 48824)
 Moll, Seeley and Palmer, Js.

 Syllabus

The defendants, owners of certain real property that is subject to a right-
of-way easement benefitting the plaintiffs’ neighboring property, appealed
from the trial court’s judgment ordering the defendants to authorize the
removal of a utility pole that is located in the easement area so that the
plaintiffs could widen their driveway. The defendants claimed, inter alia,
that the court erred in finding that their refusal to consent to the removal
of the pole was an obstruction of the plaintiffs’ easement. Held:

The trial court did not err in concluding that the defendants’ refusal to
consent to the removal of the utility pole constituted an obstruction of the
plaintiffs’ easement, as the court properly applied the reasonable use analysis
articulated in Williams v. Green Power Ventures, LLC (221 Conn. App. 657),
the court’s analysis of whether the plaintiffs’ proposed use of the easement
was reasonably necessary was sound, the majority of the court’s factual find-
ings were not clearly erroneous, and any erroneous findings were harmless.

The trial court did not err by ordering unpleaded declaratory relief as claimed
by the defendants but, rather, properly awarded injunctive relief as requested
by the plaintiffs in their operative complaint, as the judgment directed the
defendants to take a specific action, namely, to authorize the utility companies
to remove the utility pole and to transfer the defendants’ electrical service to
a different utility pole, rather than merely establishing the existing rights
and legal relations of the parties, and the purpose of the order was to stop
the defendants’ interference with the plaintiffs’ use and enjoyment of the
easement, which is a classic purpose of an injunction.

 Argued September 9—officially released November 10, 2026

 Procedural History

 Action seeking, inter alia, an injunction requiring
the named defendant et al. to consent to the relocation
of a utility pole that obstructed the plaintiffs’ ease-
ment, and for other relief, brought to the Superior Court
in the judicial district of Fairfield, where the court,
Stevens, J., granted the plaintiffs’ motions to cite in
Frontier Communications Corporation et al. as party
defendants; thereafter, the named defendant et al. filed
a counterclaim; subsequently, the court, Hon. Dale W.
Radcliffe, judge trial referee, granted the plaintiffs’
  Krasko v. Konkos

motion to cite in Owned Wealth, LLC, et al. as party
defendants; thereafter, the plaintiffs withdrew their
complaint against the defendant Margaret Mary Kane;
subsequently, the court, Hon. Dale W. Radcliffe, judge
trial referee, granted the plaintiffs’ motion to enforce
a settlement agreement, and the named defendant et al.
appealed to this court, Elgo, Moll and Suarez, Js., which
reversed the judgment of the trial court and remanded
the case with direction to deny the plaintiffs’ motion
to enforce the settlement agreement; thereafter, the
court, Hon. Kenneth B. Povodator, judge trial referee,
rendered judgment for the plaintiffs with respect to the
complaint and with respect to counts three through six
of the counterclaim filed by the named defendant et al.,
from which the named defendant et al. appealed to this
court; subsequently, the court, Hon. Kenneth B. Povo-
dator, judge trial referee, dismissed counts one and two
of the counterclaim filed by the named defendant et al.
Appeal dismissed in part; affirmed.
 Alexander Copp, for the appellants (named defendant
et al.).
 Alan R. Spirer, for the appellees (plaintiffs).

 Opinion

 MOLL, J. This long running dispute over a utility pole
returns to us on appeal from the Superior Court follow-
ing this court’s remand in a prior appeal. See Krasko v.
Konkos, 224 Conn. App. 589, 611, 314 A.3d 34 (2024).
The defendants Robert Konkos (Konkos), Chelsea Konkos
(Chelsea), 105 Honeysuckle Trust, dated March 9, 2021,
Owned Wealth, LLC, as trustee, and Owned Wealth,
LLC,1 now appeal from the trial court’s judgment
 1
 “The plaintiffs initially commenced the underlying action against
only [Konkos and Chelsea]. On January 22, 2020, the plaintiffs moved
to cite in Frontier Communications Corporation (Frontier) and Margaret
Mary Kane as defendants in the underlying action. On February 3, 2020,
the [trial] court, Stevens, J., granted the plaintiffs’ motions and added
Frontier and Kane as defendants to the underlying action. On July 6,
2022, the plaintiffs moved to cite in 105 Honeysuckle Trust, dated
March 9, 2021, Owned Wealth, LLC, as trustee, and Owned Wealth,
  Krasko v. Konkos

rendered after a bench trial in favor of the plaintiffs,
Robert J. Krasko and Francis L. O’Neill,2 ordering the
defendants to authorize the removal of a utility pole in
order to allow the plaintiffs to widen their driveway. On
appeal, the defendants claim that the trial court erred
in (1) ruling that their refusal to consent to the removal
of the utility pole was an obstruction of the plaintiffs’
easement and (2) granting unpleaded declaratory relief.
We affirm the judgment of the trial court.
 The following facts, as either found by the court or
undisputed by the parties, and procedural history are rel-
evant to our resolution of this appeal. The plaintiffs are
the owners of real property located at 115 Honeysuckle
Hill Lane in Easton (plaintiffs’ property). The defen-
dants are the owners3 of the abutting property located
at 105 Honeysuckle Hill Lane in Easton (defendants’
property). The properties were originally laid out in a
1978 subdivision map, which designated the defendants’
property as lot 7 and the plaintiffs’ property as lot 8.
Lot 7 adjoins Honeysuckle Hill Lane, but lot 8 does not;
thus, the subdivision map contains a right-of-way over
lot 7, twenty-five feet wide, that connects lot 8 with the
public road. The properties were once commonly owned.
During the period of common ownership, a house was
constructed on lot 7, while lot 8 remained undeveloped. A
utility pole (original pole) was placed on lot 7, close to the
LLC, as additional defendants. . . . On July 18, 2022, the court, Hon.
Dale W. Radcliffe, judge trial referee, granted the plaintiffs’ motion.
On September 20, 2022, the plaintiffs withdrew their complaint against
Kane.” Krasko v. Konkos, supra, 224 Conn. App. 591 n.1. Frontier is
nominally a defendant in the underlying action; however, no claim has
been made by the plaintiffs against Frontier. Frontier and Kane are not
participating in this appeal. In the interest of simplicity, we refer to
Konkos, Chelsea, 105 Honeysuckle Trust, dated March 9, 2021, Owned
Wealth, LLC, as trustee, and Owned Wealth, LLC, collectively as the
defendants.
 2
 Francis L. O’Neill is referred to as Francis Krasko in parts of the
record.
 3
 105 Honeysuckle Trust, dated March 9, 2021, Owned Wealth, LLC,
as trustee, and Owned Wealth, LLC, are the current legal owners of the
defendants’ property, while Konkos and Chelsea are the former owners
and current beneficial owners of the defendants’ property.
  Krasko v. Konkos

center of the right-of-way, to provide utility service to
the house. The original pole is jointly owned by Frontier
Communications Corporation (Frontier), which provides
telephone service, and The United Illuminating Company
(UI),4 which provides electrical service (collectively,
utility companies).
 In 2015, the then owner of both lots, John M. Barry,
as trustee of the Richard A. Barry Testamentary Trust
(trustee), planned to sell lot 8 for development. A sur-
veyor prepared a site plan, dated December 16, 2015 (site
plan), for the development of a single-family house on
lot 8 for Margaret Mary Kane, a prospective buyer. The
site plan indicated that a driveway would be constructed
across the right-of-way on lot 7 to service the new home
on lot 8, with the original pole located in the proposed
path of the driveway. The site plan also contained a nota-
tion stating “EXISTING POLE TO BE RELOCATED”
and included a proposed location for a new utility pole.
The record does not indicate whether the site plan was
shared with the trustee.
 On December 29, 2015, the trustee, as the owner of
lots 7 and 8, executed an Easement and Mutual Drive-
way Agreement (easement agreement). The easement
agreement granted and conveyed “to the owner of [l]ot
8, its successors and assigns, a perpetual easement over,
under and across [the] 25 [foot] Right of Way to [l]ot 8:
a. for ingress and egress to and from Honeysuckle Hill
Lane on foot and by motor vehicle; including the right
to construct a driveway in common with lot 7; b. for the
installation, maintenance, replacement and repair of
all utilities, including without limitation, water, gas,
cable TV, telephone, and electricity . . . .” The easement
agreement further specified “that the owners of [l]ot
7 will at no time obstruct in any manner the owners of
[l]ot 8’s access to [l]ot 8 in, under or over the 25 [foot]
Right of Way . . . .” The easement agreement was duly
recorded in the Easton land records. On that same day,
the trustee conveyed the defendants’ property to Konkos
 4
 UI is not a party to this action.
  Krasko v. Konkos

and Chelsea by warranty deed. The trustee’s deed speci-
fied that the defendants’ property was subject to the
easement agreement, as well as an overlapping utility
easement now owned by Frontier.5
 At some point thereafter, the trustee conveyed lot 8
to Kane. A single-family home was then built on lot 8,
and a driveway was constructed within the easement
area to service the new home. During the development
of lot 8, a new utility pole (new pole), somewhat close to
the original pole, was installed to provide utility service
to the newly built home. The original pole was never
removed or relocated, and it continues to provide util-
ity service to the defendants’ property. Subsequently,
the plaintiffs purchased lot 8 from Kane. The current
driveway servicing the plaintiffs’ property is adjacent
to the original pole.
 The plaintiffs commenced the present action on August
9, 2019. In their operative complaint, dated October 18,
2024, the plaintiffs alleged that they “have a perpetual
easement over, under and across a twenty-five (25) foot
right-of-way to the plaintiffs’ [property] and which ease-
ment burdens the defendants’ [property] as set forth in
[the easement agreement] . . . . The plaintiffs’ ability to
use the easement is obstructed by the location of [the
original pole] owned and maintained by Frontier and
located within the right-of-way that is the subject of

Filed 11/9/26 Todd v. Rocket Mortgage CA4/2 

NOT TO BE PUBLISHED IN OFFICIAL REPORTS 

California Rules of Court, rule 8.1115(a), prohibits courts and parties from citing or relying on opinions 
not certified for publication or ordered published, except as specified by rule 8.1115(b). This opinion 
has not been certified for publication or or dered published for purposes of rule 8.1115. 

IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA 

FOURTH APPELLATE DISTRICT 

DIVISION TWO 

FELISA TODD, 

 Plaintiff and Appellant, 

v. 

ROCKET MORTGAGE, LLC, 

 Defendant and Respondent. 

 E085261 

 (Super.Ct.No. CIVSB2218736) 

 OPINION 

 APPEAL from the Superior Court of San Bernardino County. Thomas S. Garza, 
Judge. Affirmed. 
 Felisa Todd, in pro. per., for Plaintiff and Appellant. 
 Messner Reeves and Heather E. Stern for Defendant and Respondent. 
INTRODUCTION 
Plaintiff and appellant Felicia Todd sued her sister and brother-in-law for fraud 
and elder abuse, alleging among other things, that they fraudulently induced her to take 
out a mortgage loan on her home. Her complaint asserted a single cause of action for 

 2 
quiet title against the beneficiary of the deed of trust securing the mortgage loan, 
defendant and respondent Rocket Mortgage, LLC (Rocket). Rocket demurred to Todd’s 
operative third amended complaint, and the trial court sustained the demurrer without 
leave to amend. We affirm. 
FACTUAL AND PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND 
Todd, who was represented by counsel in the trial court but represents herself on 
appeal, initiated this lawsuit in October 2022. The operative complaint, Todd’s third 
amended complaint (the TAC), asserted elder abuse and fraud-related causes of action 
against her sister, Aida Pahl, Aida’s husband (Todd’s brother-in-law), and Aida’s son 
(Todd’s nephew) (collectively, the Pahls). 
According to the TAC’s allegations, Todd’s husband (Mr. Todd) left her a 
significant inheritance when he passed in May 2016. During their marriage, Mr. Todd 
handled all of the finances. In July 2016, Todd purchased a property located at 58134 
Spring Drive in Yucca Valley (the Property) “free and clear of any liens or encumbrances 
… using the funds she received through life insurance proceeds following her husband’s 
death.” Todd used the Property as her primary residence and allowed the Pahls to live 
there with her. In May 2017, Todd sold the home that she had lived in with Mr. Todd, 
which was located in Antioch. 
At “some point” following Mr. Todd’s death (the TAC does not provide an 
approximate date), the Pahls “took [Todd] to see an attorney regarding the assets.” Todd 
agreed to the meeting because she trusted the Pahls to act in her best interest. At the 
meeting, Todd signed “ ‘a paper,’ ” but she “did not know what type of document it was.” 

 3 
Over the next few years, the Pahls stole funds from Todd’s bank and retirement 
accounts. The TAC alleged that Todd did not learn of the Pahls’ fraudulent conduct until 
“around May of 2020”; however, other allegations in the TAC suggest that she knew or 
should have known of the conduct earlier. For example, the TAC alleged that the March 
2017 statement for Todd’s individual retirement account showed that over $360,000 had 
been withdrawn from the account, and that the December 2018 statement showed an 
account balance of zero. Elsewhere in the TAC, Todd alleged that in April 2019 she 
traveled to the Philippines and thereafter stayed with her brother in Long Beach “because 
she was upset and shocked by the actions of the Pahls and did not want to live at the 
Property with them.” 
As relevant here, the TAC asserted a single claim against Rocket for quiet title. 
Todd alleged that in July 2018, the Pahls fraudulently induced her to take a mortgage 
loan out on the Property for approximately $194,000. Rocket was the beneficiary under 
the deed of trust securing the mortgage loan. Todd admitted that she signed the deed of 
trust, but alleged that, had she known what the document was, she would not have done 
so. Todd also admitted that, by April 2020, “no further regular payments were made 
from [her] accounts toward the loan.” 
In May 2022, Rocket initiated foreclosure proceedings against the property. The 
TAC alleged that although Todd sent Rocket a police report containing her allegations 
against the Pahls, Rocket did not take “any steps to assist [her] in regards to the identity 
theft.” Todd’s quiet title cause of action against Rocket sought to void the deed of trust 
and stop the foreclosure sale of the Property. 

 4 
Because the appellate record contains only the TAC, the first amended complaint, 
Todd’s requests for entry of default against the Pahls, and the judgment of dismissal, we 
glean the rest of our procedural summary from the register of actions. 
According to the register of actions, after the trial court sustained Rocket’s 
demurrer to the second amended complaint with leave to amend, Rocket filed a demurrer 
to the TAC, which Todd opposed. On August 26, 2024, the trial court held a hearing on 
Rocket’s demurrer, at which a court reporter was present. Thereafter, the trial court both 
issued a ruling, and entered an order, sustaining the demurrer without leave to amend. 
On September 30, 2024, the trial court entered a judgment of dismissal in favor of 
Rocket. On December 19, 2024, the trial court entered an amended judgment in favor of 
Rocket, adding costs of $1,255.09 to the judgment of dismissal. The register of actions 
reflects that Rocket filed a memorandum of costs in October 2024 and that Todd did not 
move to tax the costs. 
Todd filed a notice of appeal from the notice of entry of judgment. 
DISCUSSION 
In her opening brief, Todd argues that “[t]he trial court granted summary judgment 
and excluded key evidence that [her] prior counsel failed to present” and that, as a result, 
she “seeks reversal, admission of her excluded evidence, and a remand for a proper 
adjudication of her fraud claims.” 
As an initial matter, the trial court did not grant a motion for summary judgment, 
but rather it sustained Rocket’s demurrer to Todd’s quiet title claim as alleged in the TAC 
without leave to amend. A demurrer tests whether a pleading states a cause of action as a 

 5 
matter of law. (Mendoza v. JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. (2016) 6 Cal.App.5th 802, 
809.) Although our review is de novo, we presume that an appealed order or judgment is 
correct, and the appellant bears the burden of establishing reversible error. (Demara v. 
The Raymond Corp. (2017) 13 Cal.App.5th 545, 552; Mendoza, at p. 809.) To carry that 
burden, “an appellant must supply the reviewing court with some cogent argument 
supported by legal analysis and citation to the record” (City of Santa Maria v. 
Adam (2012) 211 Cal.App.4th 266, 286-287), as well as “an adequate record to assess 
error” (Maria P. v. Riles (1987) 43 Cal.3d 1281, 1295; see generally Cal. Rules of Court, 
rules 8.120, 8.204(a)(1)(B) & (C)). We may treat an issue as forfeited when the appellant 
fails to support their argument with the necessary citations to the record, legal argument, 
or citation to authority. (In re Marriage of Falcone & Fyke (2008) 164 Cal.App.4th 814, 
830; Duarte v. Chino Community Hospital (1999) 72 Cal.App.4th 849, 856.) These rules 
apply to represented and self-represented appellants equally. (Ballard v. Uribe (1986) 
41 Cal.3d 564, 574; Huang v. Hanks (2018) 23 Cal.App.5th 179, 183 & fn. 1.) 
Todd’s appeal lacks merit because she fails to carry her burden on appeal. Todd 
failed to provide the documents necessary for us to review the trial court’s decision to 
sustain Rocket’s demurrer without leave to amend. The appellate record does not contain 
any of the briefing on the demurrer, the transcript of the hearing on the demurrer, or the 
trial court’s ruling or order sustaining the demurrer. Without those documents, we do not 
know the arguments Rocket made to the trial court or the court’s reasons for concluding 
that Todd failed to state a cause of action for quiet title. Because we presume a judgment 
is correct and it is Todd’s obligation to demonstrate error, this failure alone requires us to 

 6 
affirm. (E.g. Hernandez v. California Hospital Medical Center (2000) 78 Cal.App.4th 
498, 502 [“Failure to provide an adequate record on an issue requires that the issue be 
resolved against plaintiff.”].) 
In addition, however, Todd also failed to support the factual assertions in her brief 
with citations to the record. We struck her opening brief twice for, among other defects, 
the failure to support the facts contained in her briefs with citations to the volume and 
page number in the record where they could be found. Although her new opening brief 
contains a handful of citations to the clerk’s transcript, those citations appear to be 
irrelevant to the appealed judgment. The factual assertions that are relevant to her claims 
of error on appeal are not supported by record cites. “ ‘The appellate court is not required 
to search the record on its own seeking error.’ [Citation.] Thus, ‘[i]f a party fails to 
support an argument with the necessary citations to the record, … the argument [will be] 
deemed to have been waived.’ ” (Nwosu v. Uba (2004) 122 Cal.App.4th 1229, 1246.) 
Todd also failed to support her claims of error with cognizable legal arguments, which is 
a ground for treating them as forfeited. (E.g., Badie v. Bank of America (1998) 
67 Cal.App.4th 779, 784-785 [“When an appellant fails to raise a point, or asserts it but 
fails to support it with reasoned argument and citations to authority, we treat the point as 
waived.”].) 
But, even if Todd had provided an adequate record for review and supported her 
factual and legal assertions with proper citations, we would nevertheless conclude that 
her claims lacked merit. Todd argues that the trial court erred by excluding evidence 
demonstrating that she was fraudulently induced by the Pahls to sign the deed of trust. 

 7 
But the purpose of a demurrer is to test the legal sufficiency of a claim at the pleading 
stage; it is not to test whether the claim has sufficient factual support. Thus, when ruling 
on a demurrer, the trial court does not consider evidence but rather treats the plaintiff’s 
allegations as true and determines whether those allegations state a cause of action. (E.g., 
California Commerce Casino, Inc. v. Schwarzenegger (2007) 146 Cal.App.4th 1406, 
1419 [A demurrer “ ‘ “ ‘admit[s] all material facts properly pleaded,’ ” ’ ” and the only 
evidence the court may consider is “ ‘ “ ‘matters which may be judicially noticed.’ ” ’ ”].) 
Thus, the trial court could not have erred by refusing to consider evidence of the Pahls’ 
fraudulent conduct at the demurrer stage.1 Moreover, as Rocket points out on appeal, 
evidence of the Pahls’ fraudulent conduct would have been irrelevant to Todd’s quiet title 
claim in any event because fraudulent inducement by a third party is not a ground to void 
a mortgage loan as to a bona fide encumbrancer for value, like Rocket. (See, e.g., Fallon 
v. Triangle Management Servs., Inc. (1985) 169 Cal.App.3d 1103, 1106 [“A deed 
obtained by fraud, though voidable, is generally not void” as to “bona fide 
encumbrancers for value without notice.”].) 

1 Because any evidence Todd may have of fraudulent inducement by the Pahls is 
irrelevant to Rocket’s demurrer, we deny Todd’s “Motion to Take Additional Evidence,” 
which she filed in this court while this appeal was pending. In opposing Todd’s motion, 
Rocket argues that the motion is frivolous and submits that it has incurred attorneys’ fees 
of at least $1,475 to oppose the motion. Rocket asks us to (1) impose monetary sanctions 
on Todd “in the form of Respondent’s fees on appeal,” (2) “impose monetary sanctions to 
be paid to the Court,” and/or (3) declare Todd to be a vexatious litigant. Although we 
agree the motion lacks merit, we decline to exercise our di

 Christopher M. Wolpert
 FOR THE TENTH CIRCUIT Clerk of Court

AMANDA MIRACLE; CHRISTOPHER
LOVETT; MICHAEL BEHRENS; ROB
CATLETT; CHARLES EMMER;
BRENDA KOERNER; SHERYL LIDZY;
MICHAEL MORALES; LYNNETTE
SIEVERT,
