and

DAN COLSON; MAX MCCOY,

 Plaintiffs,

v. No. 25-3032

KEN HUSH, President; BRENT
THOMAS, Provost and Vice President of
Academic Affairs; KEVIN JOHNSON,
General Counsel; STEVEN LOVETT;
JULENE MILLER; BILL FEUERBORN;
CHERYL HARRISON-LEE; SHANE
BANGERTER; ANN BRANDAU; MARK
HUTTON; SHELLAINE KIBLINGER;
JON ROLPH; ALLEN SCHMIDT;
HELEN VAN ETTEN; CARL ICE;
CYNTHIA LANE; BLAKE BENSON;
DIANE MENDOZA; WINT WINTER;
JOHN DICUS,

 Defendants - Appellants.
  Appellate Case: 25-3032 Document: 34-1 Date Filed: 11/09/2026 Page: 2

 _________________________________

 Appeal from the United States District Court
 for the District of Kansas
 (D.C. No. 5:23-CV-04056-JAR-GEB)
 _________________________________

Dwight R. Carswell, Deputy Solicitor General (Kris W. Kobach, Kansas Attorney
General, and Matthew L. Shoger, Assistant Attorney General, with him on the briefs),
Office of the Attorney General, Topeka, Kansas, for Defendants-Appellants.

J. Phillip Gragson (Amanda S. Vogelsberg, John H. Hutton, and Kara Eisenhut, with him
on the brief), Henson, Hutton, Mudrick, Gragson & Vogelsberg, LLP, Topeka, Kansas,
for Plaintiffs-Appellees.
 _________________________________

Before MATHESON, EBEL, and EID, Circuit Judges.
 _________________________________

EBEL, Circuit Judge.
 _________________________________

 In this interlocutory appeal, we examine whether qualified immunity extends

to personnel at Emporia State University (“ESU”) and members of the Kansas Board

of Regents (“KBOR”) regarding the termination of several tenured professors

pursuant to a suspension of tenure protections. The Plaintiffs, a group of nine

professors, 1 brought a variety of constitutional claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983,

including violations without due process of their protected property interest in

continued employment, their liberty interest in their reputation absent due process,

 1
 Eleven professors sued Defendants in the district court. Since, two of those
professors agreed with Defendants to stipulate that the appeal would be dismissed
with prejudice as to them. See ECF No. 25, Stipulation to Dismiss Plaintiffs-
Appellees Colson and McCoy (July 25, 2025). Therefore, nine professors remain as
Plaintiffs.
 2
  Appellate Case: 25-3032 Document: 34-1 Date Filed: 11/09/2026 Page: 3

their right to freedom of association, and their right to equal protection, stemming

from the claim that they were fired because of their political beliefs and activities.

Defendants, administrative members of the university that terminated Plaintiffs and

members of KBOR—which is responsible for supervising public universities

throughout the state—moved to dismiss all claims against them as barred by qualified

immunity. The District Court for the District of Kansas denied the motion to dismiss

for most claims because it found that Defendants were not entitled to qualified

immunity. Defendants appealed to our court. We affirm in part and reverse in part.

 I. JURISDICTION

 First, we briefly address Plaintiffs’ argument that we do not have jurisdiction

to consider Defendants’ qualified immunity claim at this time. Despite Plaintiffs’

assertion that overcoming qualified immunity is central to their claims, and thus is

not an immediately appealable collateral order, it is well-established that

interlocutory appeals are appropriate to determine whether such claims could be

dismissed on qualified immunity grounds. See, e.g., Ellis v. Salt Lake City Corp.,

147 F.4th 1206 (10th Cir. 2025). One of the primary justifications for allowing an

interlocutory appeal of a decision denying qualified immunity is that government

actors are entitled “not to be forced to litigate the consequences of official conduct.”

See Mitchell v. Forsyth, 472 U.S. 511, 527 (1985). To preserve this entitlement,

courts will review a denial of qualified immunity, to the extent it turns on questions

of law, prior to the claims proceeding to an otherwise final disposition. Therefore,

 3
  Appellate Case: 25-3032 Document: 34-1 Date Filed: 11/09/2026 Page: 4

we have jurisdiction to review the “final” order denying qualified immunity.

Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 672 (2009).

 II. BACKGROUND

 A key to our opinion is that this case comes to us at the motion-to-dismiss

stage. A defendant asserting qualified immunity at the motion-to-dismiss stage faces

a more challenging standard of review than when that defense is asserted at summary

judgment. Luethje v. Kyle, 131 F.4th 1179, 1187 (10th Cir. 2025). “This is because

the court analyzes only ‘the defendant’s conduct as alleged in the complaint’” Id.

(quoting Thomas v. Kaven, 765 F.3d 1183, 1194 (10th Cir. 2014)); see Peterson v.

Jensen, 371 F.3d 1199, 1201 (10th Cir. 2004) (stating that in defendant’s appeal from

partially denied motion to dismiss for qualified immunity “we adopt the facts as

stated in the complaint”). Similarly, at the motion to dismiss stage, we view the facts

and make all inferences in the light most favorable to the non-movant. Frey v. Town

of Jackson, 41 F.4th 1223, 1232 (10th Cir. 2022).

 Plaintiffs were all tenured professors at ESU, a public university in Kansas, as

of January 2021. Defendant Hush was the interim President of ESU, Defendant

Thomas was at times Provost and Vice President of Academic Affairs and Dean of

the College of Liberal Arts and Sciences, and Defendants Lovett and Johnson were

associate general counsel and general counsel, respectively, for ESU. At the time,

ESU policy stated that tenured faculty could only be fired for cause, or if their

program was discontinued, or in the event of financial exigency. To terminate for

cause, ESU would organize a faculty committee to assess the cause for dismissal.

 4
  Appellate Case: 25-3032 Document: 34-1 Date Filed: 11/09/2026 Page: 5

 The Kansas Board of Regents (“KBOR”) is a state body that supervises

postsecondary education institutions in the state of Kansas, and it is made up of

members appointed by the governor. The remaining non-ESU Defendants are

members of KBOR. KBOR has its own policy on terminations—known as the

Workforce Management Plan (“WMP”). Similar to ESU’s policy, the WMP stated

that tenured faculty could be terminated only for adequate cause, “except in the case

of program or unit discontinuance or under extraordinary circumstances because of

financial exigency.” (I Aplt. App. 35 ¶ 47.) However, in a meeting on January 20,

2021, KBOR voted to temporarily amend its WMP. The temporary amendment,

citing the financial pressures caused by COVID-19, stated that “notwithstanding any

other Board or institutional policy, any state university employee, including a tenured

faculty member, may be suspended, dismissed, or terminated from employment by

their respective university.” (Id. at 146 (emphasis omitted).) The amended WMP

also said that universities need not demonstrate nor declare financial exigency before

terminating any employee, “and no existing university policy hearing procedures

shall apply to such decisions.” (Id.)

 Before acting on this new policy, however, the amended WMP provided that

universities had to submit to KBOR a plan for how they would carry out this process.

Originally, universities had forty-five days to get KBOR’s approval for a framework

to terminate employees under the amended WMP. Shortly thereafter, KBOR voted to

extend this window to July 1, 2021. Though neither the district court nor the parties

discussed how many Kansas state universities presented a framework for approval, it

 5
  Appellate Case: 25-3032 Document: 34-1 Date Filed: 11/09/2026 Page: 6

appears that none submitted frameworks in the forty-five-day window and only one

university (not ESU) is shown to have considered submitting a framework following

this initial extension. There is nothing in the second amended complaint (“SAC”)

reflecting whether this other university did or did not submit a framework for

approval. 2 Sixteen months after the WMP amendment, in May 2022, KBOR

reopened the window and removed the application deadline entirely, though the

expiration date of the tenure suspension amendment remained December 31, 2022.

On September 14 and 15, 2022, Hush and Thomas presented a framework to KBOR

for ESU to implement, which had been drafted jointly by the ESU Defendants,

suggesting that 7% of ESU faculty could be impacted. KBOR approved ESU’s

Framework on September 15. The same day, ESU terminated all nine Plaintiffs, to

be effective on May 16, 2023.

 The termination letters Plaintiffs received from interim President Hush,

allegedly drafted along with university counsel Lovett and Johnson, did not state

precise or tailored reasons for the terminations. Rather, the letters generally stated

that Plaintiffs were being terminated “due to extreme financial pressures accelerated

by COVID-19 pandemic, decreased program and university enrollment, continuing

and ongoing increases in the cost of operations across campus, and substantive

changes in the educational marketplace.” (Id. at 46 ¶ 75.) Then, similar to the

approved ESU Framework, the letters listed a series of general, non-specific and non-

 2
 The Second Amended Complaint is the operative pleading document in this
case.
 6
  Appellate Case: 25-3032 Document: 34-1 Date Filed: 11/09/2026 Page: 7

exclusive bases for termination, including: low enrollment, cost of operations,

reduction in revenues for specific departments, current or future market

considerations, necessary restructuring, realignment of resources, performance

evaluations, teaching and research productivity, and low service productivity.

 The SAC alleged that ESU was not facing any financial exigency. In

presenting the ESU Framework to KBOR, it was alleged that President Hush

acknowledged this fact explicitly. ESU was alleged to be experiencing increased

enrollment, was fully funded, had seen a decrease in operating costs, and had recently

reported significant profits and increased enrollment from some of the departments in

which the terminated professors taught—all as revealed during a presentation by ESU

to KBOR entitled “Review Low Enrollment Programs Under Strategic Program

Alignment.” (SAC Ex. 6 (KBOR Meeting Agenda, Mar. 17-18, 2021).) 3 In this

same presentation, the SAC alleges that some Plaintiffs received individual

commendations for their performance, and ESU recommended continuing to fund

their programs—a recommendation that KBOR ratified. 4

 3
 Documents attached to pleadings are “part of the pleading for all purposes,”
and thus may be considered on a motion to dismiss. Fed. R. Civ. P. 10(c).
 4
 “Plaintiffs allege in the SAC that ESU did not qualify for that financial
exigency provision [amended by KBOR] because ESU was fully funded during the
academic year for which Plaintiffs received termination notices. They allege that
overall enrollment had in fact increased, operating revenues had increased, and
operating expenditures had gone down.” (Dist. Ct. Mem. & Order 29 (footnote
omitted).) Additionally, Exhibit 6 to the SAC, a KBOR Meeting Agenda, stated that
the History Program in which some of the Plaintiffs taught brought in a net revenue
of $593,000, was efficiently run, was awarded a “With Excellence” designation by
the university’s Office of Institutional Effectiveness, and had “highly productive”
faculty members. (SAC Ex. 6 (KBOR Meeting Agenda, Mar. 17-18, 2021).)
 7
  Appellate Case: 25-3032 Document: 34-1 Date Filed: 11/09/2026 Page: 8

COUNSEL 
ARGUED: Cindy Rhodes Victor, THE VICTOR FIRM, PLLC, Southfield, Michigan, for 
Appellant. Michael T. Berger, ROSATI, SCHULTZ, JOPPICH & AMTSBUECHLER PC, 
Farmington Hills, Michigan, for Appellees. ON BRIEF: Cindy Rhodes Victor, THE VICTOR 
FIRM, PLLC, Southfield, Michigan, for Appellant. Michael T. Berger, ROSATI, SCHULTZ, 
JOPPICH & AMTSBUECHLER PC, Farmington Hills, Michigan, for Appellees. 
_________________ 
OPINION 
_________________ 
 MATHIS, Circuit Judge. GSL Holdings, LLC owns a parcel of land in an industrial park 
in Lyon Township, Michigan. In late 2020, GSL agreed to build a manufacturing facility on the 
> 
No. 25-1394 GSL Holdings, LLC v. Charter Twp. of Lyon Twp., Mich. Page 2 

parcel for Moba Americas, Inc. GSL promised Moba that the facility would be ready in about 
ten months. But there was a potential problem with this timeline: the property had no public 
sewer access, which meant GSL would need to secure a septic permit from the county health 
division before any on-site construction commenced. 
That would take time. With the clock ticking, GSL and Lyon Township tried to reach an 
agreement that would allow the developer to start building the facility without a septic permit. 
When those negotiations broke down, GSL sued the Township, along with Township supervisor 
John Dolan, bringing numerous claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 for alleged violations of its 
constitutional rights. GSL now challenges the district court’s grant of summary judgment to the 
Township and Dolan on its equal -protection, due -process, and First Amendment retaliation 
claims. We affirm. 
I. 
 GSL Holdings is a real -estate developer in Michigan. It owns a roughly six -acre parcel 
of land in an industrial complex in Lyon Township. 
In December 2020, GSL entered into a lease agreement with Moba, a machinery 
manufacturer for the egg industry. As part of the agreement, GSL agreed to build a commercial 
facility on the property for Moba’s operations. But the timeline was tight. The lease required 
GSL to “use [its] best reasonable efforts” to substantially complete the project and ensure Moba 
could take occupancy of the building by October 1, 2021 —just ten months away. R. 46 -2, 
PageID 1533. 
Around that same time, a GSL representative, Maria D’Agostini Lukosavich, discussed 
the Moba plan with Lyon Township officials. Lukosavich stressed that a “critical piece” of the 
Moba deal was “timing” because Moba “want[ed] to be occupied by September 2021.” R. 51 -2, 
PageID 2310. Lukosavich then met with Township officials for a “pre -application meeting.” 
R. 46-3, PageID 1691. GSL alleges that Township officials “g[ave] assurance” that the 
Township would assist in obtaining approvals “as soon as reasonably possible.” R. 30, PageID 
1043. 
No. 25-1394 GSL Holdings, LLC v. Charter Twp. of Lyon Twp., Mich. Page 3 

GSL got to work, securing the necessary permits and approvals from Lyon Township to 
begin construction. But there was trouble from the start: the property had no access to the public 
sanitary sewer, which meant that GSL needed to construct an on -site sewage-disposal system. 
And to accomplish that, the developer needed a septic permit from the Oakland County Health 
Division (OCHD). 
Securing the septic permit was no simple matter. Around 2018, GSL applied for a permit 
to install an on -site sewage system on the same property, but the OCHD denied its application. 
The OCHD advised GSL that it would not grant a septic permit unless the developer combined 
the property with an adjacent lot—which, as of early 2021, GSL still had not done. 
In January 2021, Lyon Township preliminarily approved GSL’s site plan for the Moba 
facility. The plan described the construction of an on -site sewage system, or “septic field,” in 
lieu of access to the public sewer system. R. 30 -4, PageID 1096. But the approval did not mean 
GSL could start construction; the Township requires developers to “secure all necessary permits 
from other agencies as applicable to the project” before the start of construction. Lyon Charter 
Township Code of Ordinances § 15-10(b). In other words, GSL still needed a septic permit from 
the OCHD before construction could commence. 
Over the next two months, GSL secured an engineering review and applied for a permit 
to develop the foundation and shell of the building. But as of March 1, 2021, GSL still had not 
applied for a septic permit, nor had it applied to combine the lots. 
Yet, at least one person at GSL believed Lyon Township was moving too slowly. On 
March 8, Lukosavich emailed the entire Township board of trustees, along with various 
administrators and consultants, to express her impatience with the Township. 
In response, the Township informed GSL that it would proceed with the building plan 
review—but only if GSL signed a hold -harmless agreement.1 The proposed agreement relieved 

1Lyon Township’s ordinances provide that after an applicant receives initial approval from the planning 
commission, the applicant must again submit plans to the Township’s engineering department. Lyon Charter 
Township Code of Ordinances §§ 15-7–15-10, 5.04. “When engineering construction plans have been approved, the 
applicant may apply for a building permit from the Township Building Department.” Id. § 15-10(b). The 
engineering department will not approve plans unless the developer provides “documentation from other 
No. 25-1394 GSL Holdings, LLC v. Charter Twp. of Lyon Twp., Mich. Page 4 

the Township of liability related to its review of GSL’s building plans. And it specified that GSL 
assumed the risk of loss with respect to the denial of building -plan or building-permit approvals. 
GSL2 and the Township executed the agreement later that day on March 8, 2021. The parties 
seemed to be making progress. 
Still, Lukosavich’s email troubled some individuals. Lyon Township’s attorney, Carol 
Rosati, responded to Lukosavich that it was “inappropriate” to “communicate directly with the 
members of the Township Board in this fashion,” explaining in a later email that such 
communications risked “a potential violation of [Michigan’s] Open Meetings Act.” R. 30 -11, 
PageID 1118; R. 30-12, PageID 1123. And Leslie Zawada, an outside engineering consultant for 
the Township, complained about Lukosavich’s email to one of her colleagues. 
On March 9, 2021, GSL finally submitted its application to the OCHD for the on -site 
sewage system described in the site plan. But GSL still had not applied to combine the lots. So 
on March 22, as before, the OCHD advised GSL that it would not consider GSL’s septic -permit 
application until it combined the two lots. Only after receiving the OCHD’s response did GSL 
apply to combine the lots. 
Meanwhile, the Township’s engineering department completed its second review of the 
project and instructed GSL to “incorporate the [listed] items into revised plans” and resubmit 
them. R. 11-4, PageID 516. It added that “[a] pre-construction meeting shall be held prior to the 
commencement of any on -site construction.” Id. at 517. The engineering department also 
understood that GSL required “separate preconstruction meetings for grading and utilities.” Id. 
It therefore separately listed tasks GSL had to complete “prior to scheduling the pre -construction 
meeting for GRADING” and tasks that had to be completed “prior to scheduling the pre -
construction meeting for UTILITIES.” Id. The “Utilities” category required GSL to obtain an 

agencies . . . indicating that the plans have received their approval.” Id. § 15-9(c). However, the Township 
sometimes allows a developer to simultaneously seek a building -department review while the engineering 
department reviews the site plans, provided that the developer signs a hold -harmless agreement, essentially 
promising not to sue the Township if the engineering department ultimately denies the application. 
2The agreement was signed by Lukosavich on behalf of Mode Development, Inc. In this opinion, “GSL” 
refers to GSL and any pertinent related entities. 
No. 25-1394 GSL Holdings, LLC v. Charter Twp. of Lyon Twp., Mich. Page 5 

Oakland County septic permit before scheduling a preconstruction meeting (and, by extension, 
starting non-grading building activity).3 
Throughout March, the lots remained separate and the septic -permit application remained 
pending. Yet according to Lukosavich, the Township notified her at the end of the month that a 
building permit was ready. Lukosavich claims to have received a call from Township building 
coordinator P.J. Andrews telling her that the shell and foundation building permits were ready to 
be picked up from the Township offices.4 
Whatever promises were made on that call, Lukosavich never picked up any permits. 
GSL says on appeal that it did not have a chance to pick up those permits “since the end of that 
week was Good Friday.” D. 32 at p.32. On April 5, Andrews emailed Lukosavich to explain 
that, “[p]er [Township supervisor] John Dolan, it has been decided not to issue the building 
permit until after your utility [pre -construction meeting].” R. 30 -15, PageID 1132. And that 
meeting could not be held until GSL obtained its septic permit. 
On May 3, in a last -ditch effort to keep the project alive, the Township proposed a 
second, distinct hold -harmless agreement. Under that agreement, the Township would allow 
GSL to begin construction without a septic permit if GSL “extend[ed] the public sanitary sewer . 
. . at [its] sole cost and expense” if it failed to obtain the permit. R. 30 -20, PageID 1150. 
According to GSL, this proposed agreement was both atypical and unduly burdensome. As a 
result, the parties never executed the second hold-harmless agreement. 
Needless to say, the facility would not be ready for Moba by October. Even so, GSL still 
had some options available. For instance, Moba had waived its termination rights under the 

3GSL contends that, earlier in March 2021, the engineering department indicated work on the foundation 
and shell could proceed without a septic permit. It relies on two pieces of evidence. On March 5, the engineering 
department emailed other Township officials saying GSL “has expressed needing a foundation permit issued by the 
first of April. . . . I do not have an objection if the Building Dept starts to review this and issues a foundation 
permit.” R. 51-17, PageID 2394. And Lukosavich testified that the engineering department “indicat[ed] that [it] had 
no issues on [its] end from issuing a footing permit.” R. 51 -6, PageID 2334. But these statements do not explicitly 
discuss a septic permit or whether GSL could begin building without one. 
4In its briefing on appeal, GSL says Lukosavich received the call on March 31.

GSL and Moba negotiated an agreement to terminate the lease.

2026 IL App (1st) 251951

 FIRST DIVISION
 November 9, 2026

 No. 1-25-1951
______________________________________________________________________________

 IN THE
 APPELLATE COURT OF ILLINOIS
 FIRST JUDICIAL DISTRICT
______________________________________________________________________________

BASIL M. HANTASH and DEBBIE HANTASH, ) Appeal from the
 ) Circuit Court of
 Plaintiffs-Appellants, ) Cook County
 )
 v. ) 25 L 1456
 )
AFFORDABLE PORTABLES, INC., d/b/a Philips ) Honorable
Interiors, an Illinois corporation, ) Jerry A. Esrig,
 ) Judge Presiding
 Defendant-Appellee. )
_____________________________________________________________________________

 PRESIDING JUSTICE ELLIS delivered the judgment of the court, with opinion.
 Justices Fitzgerald Smith and Cobbs concurred in the judgment and opinion.

 OPINION

¶1 The question here is whether a landlord may assign its right to collect past-due, unpaid

rent. We hold that it may. The circuit court ruled otherwise, relying on supreme court precedent

from 1872 as well as a more recent appellate decision. Our read of supreme court case law in the

modern era, however, convinces us that Illinois law permits the assignment of claims for unpaid

rent. We thus reverse the circuit court’s judgment and remand for further proceedings.

¶2 BACKGROUND

¶3 As this case terminated at the pleading stage, we draw our facts from the complaint and

take them as true. See Petta v. Christie Business Holdings Co., P.C., 2025 IL 130337, ¶ 3.

¶4 In 2002, defendant Affordable Portables, Inc., doing business as Philips Interiors, which

we will call “API,” leased commercial property on North Clark Street in Chicago (the
 No. 1-25-1951

“Property”). The original lessor was La Salle Bank, but the Property was sold several times

during the initial 20-year lease period. As of 2021, the Property was owned by 2600 N. Clark

Street, LLC.

¶5 Under the lease, API was required to pay, among other things, 38% of the Property’s real

estate tax obligation, utilities, and base rent. The complaint alleges that, while 2600 N. Clark

Street, LLC was the landlord, API failed to pay many of these rent charges.

¶6 In 2024, 2600 N. Clark Street, LLC assigned its right to collect this unpaid rent to

plaintiffs here, Debbie and Basil Hantash. (Debbie was the “managing member” of 2600 N.

Clark Street, LLC. She and Basil are married.) So in January 2025, Basil and Debbie Hantash

filed the lawsuit at issue here, a verified complaint to collect unpaid rent from API.

¶7 API moved to dismiss, among other reasons, claiming the Hantashes lacked standing to

recover unpaid rent owed to a previous landlord. The circuit court agreed, dismissing the

complaint “solely on the ground that the Court finds that the Plaintiffs lack standing.”

¶8 Basil and Debbie timely filed a joint notice of appeal (both individually named as

appellants). But only Basil, pro se, filed a brief.

¶9 ANALYSIS

¶ 10 I. Dismissal of Appeal

¶ 11 As an initial matter, API says we should dismiss this appeal because only Basil filed an

appellate brief. API argues that Debbie, though a “necessary party,” did not file a brief and thus

“abandoned” her appeal. We need to unpack a few matters to explain why API is incorrect.

¶ 12 First, both Basil and Debbie filed a notice of appeal, the only jurisdictional step necessary

to initiate appellate review. See People v. Smith, 228 Ill. 2d 95, 104 (2008). So we have

jurisdiction over both Basil’s and Debbie’s appeal as separate appellants.

 -2-
 No. 1-25-1951

¶ 13 It is true that only one appellant’s brief was filed in this case, and only Basil signed it. It

is likewise true that, as a non-attorney, Basil is free to represent himself on appeal, but he may

not represent anyone else. See Ratcliffe v. Apantaku, 318 Ill. App. 3d 621, 626 (2000).

¶ 14 Basil says this was a mere oversight, that Debbie intended to adopt Basil’s brief and

would be willing to file a motion to adopt it. But Debbie never told us that herself; as a technical

matter, Debbie has not said a word to this court. Just as Basil may not represent Debbie’s legal

interests before this court, likewise he may not speak for her.

¶ 15 So that leaves us with Basil filing a brief, and Debbie failing to do so. But it remains true,

as we said above, that we still have jurisdiction over Debbie’s appeal. And while it is true that we

may dismiss an appeal for failure to file an appellant’s brief (or the failure to file an adequate

one), that is a matter of our discretion, not a requirement. See First Capitol Mortgage Corp. v.

Talandis Construction Corp., 63 Ill. 2d 128, 131 (1976); Kozenczak v. Du Page County Officers

Electoral Board, 299 Ill. App. 3d 205, 208 (1998); Ill. S. Ct. R. 343, Committee Comments (rev.

Sept. 1, 1974).

¶ 16 In many cases, the lack of an appellant’s brief dooms our ability to consider the case.

How, after all, can we determine whether an appellant’s arguments carry the day when we don’t

know what they are? So while it remains in our discretion to dismiss the appeal, it is almost a

foregone conclusion that we would do so in that circumstance. Here, however, we have two

appellants, and Debbie’s interests are clearly aligned with those of her husband and co-assignee,

Basil, who has filed a brief providing a coherent argument for reversal. If he prevails on appeal,

so does she. We are not required to dismiss Debbie’s appeal, and we see no reason why we

should.

 -3-
 No. 1-25-1951

¶ 17 More importantly, there is absolutely no basis for dismissing the appeal in its entirety,

even as to Basil, who filed an appellant’s brief. The “necessary parties” doctrine API cites for

that proposition has no application here.

¶ 18 A necessary party is one whose participation in the litigation is required (1) to protect an

interest of the absent party that would be materially affected by the judgment, (2) to reach a

decision that protects the interests of those before the court, or (3) to allow for a complete

determination of the controversy. Emalfarb v. Krater, 266 Ill. App. 3d 243, 247 (1994). An order

entered without a necessary party is void. Id. This objection is typically raised at the trial court in

the prejudgment phase, usually as a basis for dismissal. See 735 ILCS 5/2-615(a) (West 2024).

Though disfavored, it may be raised for the first time on appeal, but the point of the argument

remains to void the original trial judgment. See Emalfarb, 266 Ill. App. 3d at 247.

¶ 19 API is using the doctrine not to challenge the judgment below but to scotch the appeal of

that judgment. With one exception, the “necessary parties” doctrine does not work that way in

the appellate court. A plaintiff at the trial level may sue whomever she must to include a

necessary party, but a potential appellant has no control over whether another appellant files an

appeal. It would be grossly unfair if an appellant were denied her day in (appellate) court simply

because a different appellant chose, for whatever reason—lack of money, settlement,

bankruptcy, etc.—not to prosecute an appeal.

¶ 20 To say nothing of the fact that, even if the doctrine applied in this context, API’s

argument would still fail. The “necessary parties” concept is a jurisdictional one; an order

entered without a necessary party is void for want of jurisdiction. Id. We have already explained

that we have jurisdiction over Debbie’s appeal, as she filed a notice of appeal.

¶ 21 The one exception to this discussion comes in the unique context of appeals of

 -4-
 No. 1-25-1951

administrative action, where state law often requires that all defendants be joined in the appeal.

See McGaughy v. Illinois Human Rights Comm’n, 165 Ill. 2d 1, 11 (1995); 735 ILCS 5/3-107(a)

(West 2024) (trial level); Ill. S. Ct. R. 335 (eff. July 1, 2017) (in appellate review of

administrative actions, “[t]he agency and all other parties of record shall be named

respondents.”). But administrative-action review is unique in that its authority derives not

directly from our constitution but from state law, and thus the requirements of state law dictate

the courts’ authority. McGaughy, 165 Ill. 2d at 6-7; Ill. Const. 1970, art. VI, §§ 6, 9.

¶ 22 That administrative-action exception does not apply here. API’s “necessary parties”

objection is unfounded. We see no basis to dismiss this appeal in whole or in part.

¶ 23 II. Assignment of Claim for Unpaid Rent

¶ 24 We now turn to the principal issue raised on appeal: may a property owner assign claims

for past unpaid rent to another party? In answering that question in the negative, the circuit court

relied on our supreme court’s 1872 decision in Kennedy v. Kennedy, 66 Ill. 190, 196 (1872),

which held that such claims are not assignable, as well as our appellate decision in 1002 E. 87th

Street, LLC v. Midway Broadcasting Corp., 2018 IL App (1st) 171691, ¶ 24, which quoted

Kennedy for that proposition in dictum. We explain below why this case law is inconsistent with

our supreme court’s modern view on the law of assignability of claims.

¶ 25 We start with a general discussion of the law and a clarification of terms. Unless the

parties contract otherwise, when a party is conveyed property that contains a lease, the lease runs

with the property, so the new property owner steps into the shoes of the previous one and

becomes the new landlord on the lease. Lipschultz v. Robertson, 407 Ill. 470, 474 (1950);

Midway Broadcasting, 2018 IL App (1st) 171691, ¶ 17. The new landlord obviously may now

receive any rent associated with the lease in the future and may sue for nonpayment of that rent.

 -5-
 No. 1-25-1951

See People ex rel. Hargrave v. Phillips, 394 Ill. 119, 123 (1946) (rights to future rent “follow the

land” and “pass with a sale or devise of the land.” (Internal quotation marks omitted.)); Kahn v.

Deerpark Investment Co., 115 Ill. App. 2d 121, 125-26 (1969) (same); Midway Broadcasting,

2018 IL App (1st) 171691, ¶ 17 (same); 735 ILCS 5/9-209 (West 2024).

¶ 26 That is not our issue. We are not talking about future rent. We are talking here about rent

already due and owing that has not been paid. That is what we mean when we refer to “past

unpaid rent” or “rent in arrears” or “accrued unpaid rent.” Here, the Hantashes are seeking

payment of rent that was owed to the previous owner/landlord, 2600 N. Clark Street, LLC. The

Hantashes, in other words, are not suing in their capacity as landlord; they are suing as assignees

of a claim originally held by 2600 North Clark Street as landlord.

¶ 27 That presents a different question, as claims for rent owed to the previous owner do not

run with the property, so to speak, when a new owner/landlord steps in. That has been true for

over a century. See Scully v. People, 104 Ill. 349, 351 (1882); Kennedy, 66 Ill. at 196 (“The sale

of the [property] carries with it rents to fall due, or that may subsequently accrue, under any

lease, unless reserved, but not rents already accrued.” (Emphasis added.)). It remains true today.

See Midway Broadcasting, 2018 IL App (1st) 171691, ¶ 17 (“[T]he new landlord does not have a

right to recover rent due from before it owned the property.”); A.M. Realty Western L.L.C. v.

MSMC Realty, L.L.C., 2012 IL App (1st) 121183, ¶ 45 (same).

¶ 28 Rather, a claim for unpaid rent is held by the landlord to whom the rent was owed, as an

actionable claim or “chose in action.” Phillips, 394 Ill. at 122 (“rent in arrears is a chose in

action”); Scully, 104 Ill. at 352 (“Rent arrear is a chose in action ***.” (Emphasis omitted.));

A.M. Realty, 2012 IL App (1st) 121183, ¶ 50 (“[R]ent that accrues prior to the termination of the

lease is a chose in action and is not assigned to future owners of the property.”). As such, the

 -6-
 No. 1-25-1951

landlord to whom the rent was owed may sue to collect that unpaid rent, either before or after the

property is conveyed to a new owner. A.M. Realty,

U.S. BANK TRUST, NATIONAL ASSOCIATION, not in its individual capacity but solely as

Appeal from the Circuit Court of Cook County. 
Honorable Edward N. Robles, Judge, Presiding. 
No. 22-CH-8760 

JUSTICE FITZGERALD SMITH delivered the judgment of the court. 
Presiding Justice Ellis and Justice Cobbs concurred in the judgment. 
ORDER 
¶ 1 Held: The trial court did not abuse its discretion by (1) ruling that defendant had waived 
all arguments for vacating the judgment of foreclosure by raising them for the first 
time in a motion to reconsider summary judgment; and (2) approving judicial sale 
where defendant failed to show he was prevented from raising challenges to the 
underlying foreclosure judgment in a timely manner. 

¶ 2 The defendant, Dean Holub, as Trustee of the Trust Agreement Dated May 24, 2000, 
and known as Trust Number 3707, appeals orders by which the trial court confirmed a judicial 
sale, denied his motion to va cate the judgment of foreclosure and dismiss this action, and denied 

- 2 - 
his motion for reconsideration. We affirm. 
¶ 3 BACKGROUND 
¶ 4 The facts pertinent to this appeal are undisputed and relatively straightforward. In May 
2007, Arthur Holub obtained a $50,000 home equity loan from Bank of America, N.A., secured 
by a mortgage on a single-family residence at 3707 South 59th Court in Cicero (subject property). 
When Arthur Holub signed the mortgage and note, he covenanted that he “is lawfully seised of the 
estate hereby conveyed and has the right to mortgage, grant and convey the Property.” He further 
asserted that he had all title and interest in the subject property and represented at closing that the 
mortgage would be a good and valid first mortgage free from all defenses. A pproximately seven 
years earlier, however, a deed in trust had been recorded in the office of the Cook County Recorder 
reflecting Arthur Holub’s conveyance of the subject property to the defendant trustee. No trust 
documents are contained in the record on appeal. The record indicates that Arthur Holub passed 
away on November 24, 2009. 
¶ 5 For apparently a decade following Arthur Holub’s death, monthly payments continued 
to be made upon the mortgage. This ended with the monthly payment due January 6, 2020, and 
the mortgage went into default thereafter. Bank of America, N.A., later assigned its interests under 
the mortgage to the plaintiff, U.S. Bank Trust, N.A., not in its individual capacity but solely as 
Owner Trustee for RCF 2 Acquisition Trust. 
¶ 6 The plaintiff initiated the present mortgage foreclosure action on September 2, 2022, 
when it filed a four-count complaint against the defendant and Felicola M. Esteban. Count I sought 
foreclosure of the mortgage and sale of the subject property pursuant to the Illinois Mortgage 
Foreclosure Law (735 ILCS 5/15-1101 et seq. (West 2022)). Count II sought to quiet title as to any 
interest Esteban had in the property and is not relevant to this appeal. Count III sought to have an 

- 3 - 
equitable lien imposed on the property, and count IV sought foreclosure of that equitable lien. 
¶ 7 We note that count I of the complaint, for statutory foreclosure, was pled in accordance 
with section 15-1504(a) of the Mortgage Foreclosure Law (id. § 15-1504(a)). Thus, its allegations 
were “deemed and construed to include allegations,” inter alia, “that the mortgage constitutes a 
valid, prior and paramount lien upon the indicated interest in the mortgaged real estate.” See id. 
§ 15-1504(c)(7). 
¶ 8 On March 1, 2023, the defendant, acting through counsel, filed an answer to the 
complaint. The defendant’s answer did not deny the allegation deemed and construed as included 
in count I that the mortgage const ituted a valid lien upon the indicated interest in the mortgaged 
real estate. It did not raise any affirmative defenses to the allegations of the complaint. 
¶ 9 On May 9, 2023, the plaintiff filed a motion for summary judgment against the 
defendant on all counts of the complaint. It asserted that the defendant’s answer had failed to raise 
any genuine issue of material fact. It was supported by the affidavit of Verlina Griffin, an employee 
of the plaintiff’s mortgage servicer. The relief sought was both the entry of summary judgment and 
a judgment of foreclosure and sale in favor of the plaintiff and against the defendant. The plaintiff 
also filed separate motions seeking orders specifically as to counts II, III, and IV of the complaint. 
¶ 10 The motion for summary judgment was entered and continued generally over the 
ensuing six months. Within this time, on October 19, 2023, the defendant’s counsel filed a motion 
for leave to amend his answer to add an affirmative defense. The affirmative defense raised in that 
proposed answer was that the mortgage was not valid because Arthur Holub had not been the 
owner of the subject property at the time he signed the mortgage in May 2007, having transferred 
his interest in the property to the defendant trustee s even years earlier. The trial court struck the 
defendant’s motion from the call when it was scheduled for presentment due to deficiencies in the 

- 4 - 
notice of motion. The motion was never rescheduled for presentment, and a later order issued by 
the trial court confirms that it was never granted. 
¶ 11 On January 11, 2024, the trial court entered a briefing schedule directing the defendant 
to file a response to the plaintiff’s motion for summary judgment within 45 days, i.e., by February 
25, 2024. However, the defendant never filed any response to the plaintiff’s motion for summary 
judgment. 
¶ 12 We note that a purported e-mail dated February 23, 2024, from the defendant’s attorney 
to the plaintiff’s attorney was attached as an exhibit to the plaintiff’s response to the defendant’s 
later-filed motion for reconsideration. In that e -mail, the defendant’s attorney affirmatively 
represented that the defendant was not intending to further contest the foreclosure and was “not 
filing a responsive pleading to your latest motion.” 
¶ 13 On May 9, 2024, the trial court entered a series of orders. One was an order granting 
the motion for summary judgment in favor of the plaintiff and against the defendant. That order 
did not delineate specific counts of the complaint upon which summary judgment was or was not 
entered. Second, the trial court entered an order of default against Esteban. Third, it entered a 
judgment of foreclosure and ordered that the subject property be sold at a judicial sale unless the 
sum of $60,069.70, plus interest and costs were paid by the expiration of the redemption period on 
August 9, 2024. Finally, it entered an order appointing a selling officer for the subject property. 
¶ 14 Although the trial court entered the above orders on May 9, 2024, it did not enter orders 
on the plaintiff’s separate motions specifically seeking orders of judgment on counts II, III, and IV 
of the complaint. Thus, on July 31, 2024, the plaintiff filed amended motions seeking orders as to 
those three counts specifically. 
¶ 15 On August 14, 2024, the plaintiff filed a motion for an order approving sale of the 

- 5 - 
subject property that had occurred on August 12, 2024. The purchaser of the subject property was 
identified as Greystone Appraisals Inc., and the purchase price was $141,000. 
¶ 16 On August 16, 2024, an additional appearance was filed on the defendant’s behalf by 
new counsel. That same day, the defendant’s new counsel filed on his behalf a motion to vacate 
the judgment of foreclosure and to dismiss the action with prejudice. That motion requested that 
the trial court reconsider the motion for summary judgment and deny it on the basis that the 
mortgage was invalid due to Arthur Holub having no interest in the subject property or right to 
mortgage it as of May 2007 when he obtained the mortgage. 
¶ 17 On August 22, 2024, the trial court entered three orders specifically granting judgment 
in the plaintiff’s favor on counts II, III, and IV of the complaint. 
¶ 18 On September 24, 2024, the defendant filed a response opposing the plaintiff’s motion 
for an order approving sale. He first argued that the mortgage, the judgment of foreclosure, and 
the resulting foreclosure sale were all void due to Arthur Holub’s lack of ownership interest in the 
subject property at the time he executed the mortgage. Second, he argued that there were no 
allegations in any of the pleadings that stated a legal basis for finding that an equitable lien existed. 
Third, he argued that the foreclosure sale was held improperly because it was conducted prior to 
any order establishing the existence of an equitable lien. Fourth, he argued that because there was 
no factual, legal, or equitable basis for the entry of a judgment of foreclosure and sale against the 
defendant or the subject property, conducting the judicial sale was unconscionable, fraudulent, and 
resulted in justice otherwise not being done under section 15-1508(b) of the Mortgage Foreclosure 
Law (id. § 15-1508(b)). On October 7, 2024, the defendant filed a reply brief in support of his 
motion to vacate and dismiss which essentially raised these same arguments as additional reasons 
why the trial court should reconsider its entry of summary judgment. And on October 8, 2024, the 

- 6 - 
defendant filed a “supplement motion” to dismiss on the grounds that Arthur Holub’s estate or 
special representative was a necessary party not named in the complaint, thus defeating subject 
matter jurisdiction. 
¶ 19 On January 17, 2025, the trial court entered a written order granting the plaintiff’s 
motion for an order approving sale and denying the defendant’s motion to vacate and dismiss. The 
trial court found that the defendant had waived any challenges involving the failure to name a 
necessary party, the invalidity of the underlying mortgage or note, or any other basis why the 
plaintiff was not entitled to the underlying judgment due to the defendant’s failure to raise these at 
any point prior to the plaintiff’s filing of the motion to approve the sale. The trial court noted that 
the defendant had been represented by counsel throughout these proceedings and had failed to 
raise any challenges to the complaint or to the plaintiff’s motion for summary judgment during the 
time he had to do so. The court added that the defendant’s arguments were not valid bases for a 
motion for reconsideration of summary judgment because they were all based upon facts and 
evidence that had been available to him throughout the time the case was being litigated. 
¶ 20 On February 18, 2025, the defendant filed another motion to reconsider. The defendant 
argued in this motion that trial court had erred by ruling that he had waived his right to seek to 
vacate the judgment of foreclosure or to object to the equitable lien. He argued that the failure of 
the complaint to state a legally cognizable cause of action was a challenge that could be raised at 
any time and not waived, and the complaint was legally insufficient as to both its statutory and 
equitable lien foreclosure claims . He also argued that he could not waive a challenge to the trial 
court’s subject matter jurisdiction, which he argued was absent on the basis that the plaintiff’s 
claim for equitable lien was untimely as brought more than five years after the date of origination 
of the loan. He argued that the trial cour

J-S27043-26 

NON-PRECEDENTIAL DECISION - SEE SUPERIOR COURT O.P. 65.37 

FIRST CITIZENS COMMUNITY BANK 

 v. 

SA LIVING FUND LLC, CRAIG L. 
GROSSMAN, AND AARON Z. COHEN 

 Appellants 
:

: 
IN THE SUPERIOR COURT OF 
 PENNSYLVANIA 

No. 2083 EDA 2025 

Appeal from the Order Entered July 9, 2025 
In the Court of Common Pleas of Philadelphia County Civil Division at 
No(s): 250302422 

BEFORE: BOWES, J., OLSON, J., and McLAUGHLIN, J. 
MEMORANDUM BY McLAUGHLIN, J.: FILED NOVEMBER 9, 2026 
 SA Living Fund LLC (“SA Living”), Craig L. Grossman, and Aaron Z. 
Cohen (collectively, “the SA Living Parties”) appeal from the Order denying 
their petition to open and/or strike the confessed judgment entered against 
them by First Citizens Community Bank (“FCCB”). We affirm. 
 The trial court summarized the factual background as follows: 
In July 2022, SA Living borrowed $3,850,000 for a period 
of 18 months, executing a loan agreement secured by 
mortgaged premises located at 827 Spring Garden Street, 
Philadelphia, subject to an extension option and 
modifications. The Note and Loan Agreement contained 
confession of judgment provisions. [] Cohen and Grossman 
individually guaranteed SA Living’s performance under the 
loan documents, signing a Guaranty and Suretyship 
Agreement, which also contained a confession of judgment 
provision. The initial term of the loan was for a period of 18 
months. 
In March 2024, [the SA Living Parties] exercised the 
option to extend the maturity date one month to April 26, 
J-S27043-26 
- 2 - 
2024, paying an extension fee of $9,625 and a legal fee of 
$750. The first modification also contained a confession of 
judgment provision. In November 2024, [the SA Living 
Parties] sought a second modification to the loan agreement 
whereby they agreed to make a payment of $103,433.33 to 
[FCCB] to bring the loan current and to make an additional 
prepayment of interest for the upcoming year. [FCCB] 
agreed to extend the maturity date to October 2029 unless 
it opted to call the loan sooner. The second modification 
contained a confession of judgment provision. 
Trial Ct. Op., filed Jan. 15, 2026, at 1-2.1 
In January 2025, FCCB sent a letter to the SA Living Parties detailing 
the loan history, including the second modification, wherein the SA Living 
Parties agreed to pay $103,433.33 to bring the loan current and $100,000.00, 
which would be held in reserve to satisfy the future monthly principal and 
interest payments due. Answer to Pet. to Strike and/or Open, filed May 28, 
2025, at Exh. 1. The letter continued that the SA Living Parties had failed to 
make the full amount of payments due under the second modification, with 
an outstanding balance of $18,463.33 owed for the modification payments. 
Id. It further stated that the SA Living Parties owed $30,010.55 for the 
principal and interest payment that had been due on January 1, 2025. The 
letter pointed out that the failure to pay was an event of default under the 
loan. Id. It provided SA Living with 15 days to cure the defect. Id. In March 
2025, FCCB filed a complaint for a confessed judgment, and the prothonotary 
entered a confessed judgment. 
____________________________________________ 
1 FCCB is the successor by merger of Huntingdon Valley Bank, which was the 
original lender. 
J-S27043-26 
- 3 - 
 The SA Living Parties filed a petition to strike and/or open the confessed 
judgment. The SA Living Parties claimed the complaint was facially defective 
because FCCB alleged in a conclusory manner that the SA Living Parties were 
in default without specifying what the alleged default was, when it occurred, 
and how it ripened into an event of default. They further claimed they had 
valid defenses and disputed the money amount sought. 
At a hearing, the SA Living Parties’ counsel discussed good faith and fair 
dealing, and Grossman testified as to the negotiations. N.T., 7/9/2025, at 7-
9, 16. Further, FCCB agreed that the calculations in the complaint were 
incorrect and requested that the court “grant the bank leave to amend to file 
an amended complaint with amended judgment.” Id. at 31. The court denied 
the petition to strike and/or open judgment and ordered FCCB to file a motion 
to reassess damages.2 The SA Living Parties filed a notice of appeal. 
 The SA Living Parties raise the following issues: 
Question 1: Did the Trial Court err in denying [the SA Living 
Parties’] Petition to Strike, or in the alternative to Open, the 
confessed judgment where [FCCB’s] [c]omplaint failed to 
allege facts establishing that an Event of Default had 
occurred and was continuing as required by the underlying 
Loan documents and Pennsylvania Rules of Civil Procedure 
2952(a)(6) and 1019? 
Question 2: Did the Trial Court err in denying [the SA Living 
Parties’] Petition to Open the confessed judgment where 
[the SA Living Parties] presented evidence of a meritorious 
defense that [FCCB’s] calculations of the sums due were 
patently and materially erroneous—evidence so compelling 
____________________________________________ 
2 FCCB filed the motion to reassess damages. The court deferred ruling on the 
motion until after disposition of the appeal. Order, filed Aug. 8, 2025. 
J-S27043-26 
- 4 - 
that the Trial Court itself directed [FCCB] to file a Motion to 
Reassess Damages? 
Question 3: Did the Trial Court err in denying [the SA Living 
Parties’] Petition to Open the confessed judgment where 
[the SA Living Parties] presented colorable evidence 
sufficient to submit to a jury that [FCCB] breached the 
implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing? 
The SA Living Parties’ Br. at 5 (suggested answers omitted). 
 The SA Living Parties first contend the court erred in failing to strike the 
judgment. It claims the loan documents require that an Event of Default has 
occurred and be continuing before FCCB can exercise the warrants of attorney. 
They point out the complaint alleged SA Living “failed to remit the required 
payments under the Loan documents and is now in default” and Cohen and 
Grossman “have failed to remit the required payments under the Loan 
documents, guaranteeing SA Living’s performance under the Loan documents, 
and they are now in default.” Id. at 15 (quoting Complaint, filed Mar. 18, 
2025, at ¶¶ 45-46). They note the complaint does not specify what payments 
were allegedly missed, when they were due, what the amount was, or whether 
and for how long the failure was continuing. The SA Living Parties further claim 
the complaint did not allege that an Event of Default, as defined by the loan 
documents, occurred and is continuing. They conclude, “The bare allegation 
that [SA Living] is ‘now in default’ is conclusory, fails Rule 2952(a)(6)’s 
specificity requirement, and ignores the contractually-defined trigger upon 
which the warrants of attorney are conditioned.” Id. 
 The SA Living Parties further claim the complaint does not allege any 
acceleration. They note the loan was not scheduled to be due until October 1, 
J-S27043-26 
- 5 - 
2029, and maintain that the balance could have been due only if the loan was 
accelerated. 
 The SA Living Parties maintain the January 2025 letter was not evidence 
that an Event of Default had occurred and was continuing. They contend it 
was sent more than two months before the Confession of Judgment, was silent 
as to acceleration, and did not declare the entire balance immediately due and 
payable. They claim that “because the conditions precedent set forth in the 
warrants of attorney were not alleged, much less established, on the face of 
the complaint, the confessed judgment must be stricken.” Id. at 17. 
“We review a trial court’s order denying a petition to strike a confessed 
judgment to determine whether the record is sufficient to sustain the 
judgment.” Graystone Bank v. Grove Estates LP, 58 A.3d 1277, 1281 
(Pa.Super. 2012) (quoting Osprey Portfolio, LLC v. Izett, 32 A.3d 793, 795 
(Pa.Super. 2011)). “A petition to strike a judgment is a common[-]law 
proceeding [that] operates as a demurrer to the record.” Stoltzfus v. Green 
Line Labs, LLC, 303 A.3d 447, 452 (Pa.Super. 2023) (citation omitted; 
alterations in Stoltzfus). A court may grant a petition to strike a judgment 
“only for a fatal defect or irregularity appearing on the face of the record.” Id. 
at 452-53 (quoting Dime Bank v. Andrews, 115 A.3d 358, 364 (Pa.Super. 
2015)). When determining whether “there are fatal defects on the face of the 
record . . . , a court may only look at what was in the record when the 
judgment was entered.” Id. (quoting Dime Bank, 115 A.3d at 364). “[I]f any 
defect disclosed by the record ‘is one that can be remedied by an amendment 
J-S27043-26 
- 6 - 
of the record or other action, nunc pro tunc, the judgment should not be 
stricken off.’” Id. (quoting Dime Bank, 115 A.3d at 364). 
The trial court concluded: 
[The SA Living Parties’] statement of matters complained of 
on appeal states that the court erred in not opening the 
judgment because the complaint “failed to allege facts 
establishing that an Event of Default had occurred and was 
continuing.” The complaint outlines terms to which [the SA 
Living Parties] had agreed to obtain the second modification 
and alleges that [the SA Living Parties] did not make those 
payments and was thereby in default. It is not heavy on 
details and does not mention the contents of the January 
15, 2025 letter. However, the response to the Petition to 
Open included the letter and it was entered into the record 
at the hearing. The submissions and the testimony 
demonstrate that [the SA Living Parties] had not fully met 
the terms to which they had agreed and had no factual basis 
to assert a defense on that basis. 
Trial Ct. Op. at 4. 
 In this issue, the SA Living Parties challenged the denial of their motion 
to strike. The trial court, however, reviewed not only the complaint and 
documents attached thereto, but also the testimony and evidence submitted 
in response to the petition to open and/or strike. This was error, as when 
addressing a motion to strike a court may only review documents of record at 
the time judgment was entered. See Stoltzfus, 303 A.3d at 452. 
 However, based on the record when FCCB confessed judgment, we 
conclude the court that the error was harmless because the court ultimately 
properly denied the petition to strike. Pennsylvania Rule of Civil Procedure 
J-S27043-26 
- 7 - 
2952 governs the contents of a complaint in a confession of judgment action 
and provides: 
(a) The complaint shall contain the following: 
(1) the names and last known addresses of the parties; 
. . . 
(2) the original or a photostatic copy or like reproduction 
of the instrument showing the defendant’s signature; if 
the original is not attached, an averment that the copy 
attached is a true and correct reproduction of the 
original; if neither the original nor a reproduction can be 
attached, an explanation why they are not available; 
. . . 
(3) an averment that judgment is not being entered by 
confession against a natural person in connection with a 
consumer credit transaction; 
(4) a statement of any assignment of the instrument; 
(5) either a statement that judgment has not been 
entered on the instrument in any jurisdiction or if it has 
been entered an identification of the proceedings; 
. . . 
(6) if the judgment may be entered only after a 
default or the occurrence of a condition precedent, 
an averment of the default or of the occurrence of 
the condition precedent; 
(7) an itemized computation of the amount then due, 
based on matters outside the instrument if necessary, 
which may include interest and attorneys’ fees 
authorized by the instrument; 
(8) a demand for judgment as authorized by the warrant; 
. . . 
(10) signature and verification in accordance with the 
rules relating to a civil action.

leads.caseName: Brittany Hoak v. Left Back Properties, LLC
leads.text:
RENDERED: NOVEMBER 6, 2026; 10:00 A.M. 
TO BE PUBLISHED 

Commonwealth of Kentucky 
Court of Appeals 

NO. 2026-CA-0102-MR 

BRITTANY HOAK APPELLANT 

v. 
APPEAL FROM JEFFERSON CIRCUIT COURT 
HONORABLE SUSAN SCHULTZ GIBSON, JUDGE 
ACTION NO. 24-CI-000390 

LEFT BACK PROPERTIES, LLC APPELLEE 

OPINION 
AFFIRMING 

** ** ** ** ** 

BEFORE: COMBS, A. JONES, AND MOYNAHAN, JUDGES. 
COMBS, JUDGE: Brittany Hoak was bitten by a dog on premises leased by Left 
Back Properties to Fermin Alvarado and occupied (at the time of the incident) by 
nine others, including Sixto Alvarado, Jennifer Mitchell, and Hoak. Hoak appeals 
the Jefferson Circuit Court’s decision granting summary judgment with respect to 
the strict liability and common law negligence claims she asserted against Left 
Back Properties, LLC (“Left Back Properties”). Having examined the record and 
reviewed the applicable law, we affirm. 

 -2- 
 On the afternoon of November 7, 2023, Hoak entered the backyard of 
property rented to Fermin Alvarado by Left Back Properties. As she crossed the 
yard to access a side gate, Hoak was attacked by a pit bull terrier that lived with 
her and several others in the garage located at the back of the premises. Hoak’s 
face and arm were badly injured. She also suffered a fractured jaw that required 
emergency surgery at University of Louisville Hospital. As an owner of the dog, 
Sixto Alvarado was cited by animal control officers. 
 On January 17, 2024, Hoak filed a civil action against Sixto Alvarado, 
Jennifer Mitchell, and Left Back Properties in Jefferson Circuit Court. (Alvarado 
and Mitchell were never served with process.) In her complaint, Hoak alleged that 
the defendants were liable for injuries she sustained as a result of the dog bite 
incident based upon theories of strict liability and common law negligence. 
Written discovery was served along with the complaint. 
 On May 17, 2024, Left Back Properties filed a motion to dismiss the 
claims against it for failure to state a claim for which relief could be granted. See 
CR1 12.02. By its order entered August 8, 2024, the Jefferson Circuit Court denied 
the motion on the basis that the “case is still in its infancy,” giving Hoak an 
opportunity to conduct further discovery. 

1 Kentucky Rules of Civil Procedure. 

 -3- 
 On October 30, 2025, Left Back Properties filed a motion for 
summary judgment. Although Left Back Properties admitted that it owned the 
property leased by Fermin Alvarado, it explained that it did not know that a pit bull 
terrier was being kept on the premises and could not have known that the dog had 
dangerous propensities. Consequently, it argued that as a matter of law, it could 
not be held liable for Hoak’s damages on a theory of common law negligence. 
 With respect to Hoak’s statutory strict liability claim, Left Back 
Properties argued that a landowner could be deemed a dog owner for purposes of 
liability under the provisions of KRS2 258.235 only where it both owned and 
occupied the premises where the dog was kept. Because Left Back Properties did 
not occupy the premises leased to Fermin Alvarado, it contended that it was 
entitled to judgment as a matter of law. 
 Hoak filed an extensive response. She argued that Left Back 
Properties qualified as a statutory owner of the pit bull terrier by virtue of its visits 
to -- and inspection of -- the property rented to Fermin Alvarado; that genuine 
issues of material fact remained with respect to whether Left Back Properties knew 
of the dog and its vicious propensities; and that further discovery was necessary. 

2 Kentucky Revised Statutes. 

 -4- 
 The circuit court granted the motion of Left Back Properties for 
summary judgment. In its order entered December 23, 2025, the court concluded 
as follows: 
Despite being given the opportunity to conduct discovery 
after this Court’s Memorandum and Order, entered 
August 8, 2024, [Hoak] has submitted no affirmative 
evidence which supports her claims that Left Back is 
statutorily liable for the alleged dog attack, or that Left 
Back knew of the dog and its vicious tendencies. As a 
result, there remain no genuine issues of material fact and 
Left Back is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. 

This appeal followed. 
 On appeal, Hoak argues that the circuit court erred by granting 
summary judgment with respect to her claims. She also contends that the circuit 
court abused its discretion by granting summary judgment prematurely where more 
time for discovery was needed. 
 Summary judgment is appropriate where “the pleadings, depositions, 
answers to interrogatories, stipulations, and admissions on file, together with the 
affidavits, if any, show that there is no genuine issue as to any material fact and 
that the moving party is entitled to a judgment as a matter of law.” CR 56.03. 
 An appellate court’s role in reviewing a summary judgment is to 
determine whether the trial court erred by concluding that no genuine issue of 
material fact existed and that the moving party was entitled to judgment as a matter 
of law. Scifres v. Kraft, 916 S.W.2d 779, 781 (Ky. App. 1996). Because factual 

 -5- 
findings are not at issue, a trial court’s decision to grant summary judgment is 
reviewed de novo. Pinkston v. Audubon Area Community Services, Inc., 210 
S.W.3d 188, 189 (Ky. App. 2006) (citing Blevins v. Moran, 12 S.W.3d 698, 700 
(Ky. App. 2000)). 
 Summary judgment is properly granted only where the party opposing 
the motion has been given adequate opportunity to complete discovery and then 
fails to offer controverting evidence. Suter v. Mazyck, 226 S.W.3d 837, 841 (Ky. 
App. 2007). However, it is not necessary to show that the respondent has actually 
completed discovery -- but only that she has had an opportunity to do so. Hartford 
Ins. Group v. Citizens Fidelity Bank & Trust Co., 579 S.W.2d 628, 630 (Ky. App. 
1979). Whether a party has had enough time and opportunity “must be determined 
within the context of the individual case” -- with more complex cases requiring 
more time. Suter, 226 S.W.3d at 842. Ultimately, there must be a limitation on the 
time the parties have to complete discovery. Id. at 844. “The trial court’s 
determination that a sufficient amount of time has passed and that it can properly 
take up the summary judgment motion for a ruling is reviewed for an abuse of 
discretion.” Key v. CitiMortgage, Inc., 686 S.W.3d 630, 636 (Ky. App. 2023) 
(citing Blankenship v. Collier, 302 S.W.3d 665, 668 (Ky. 2010)). 
 First, we must determine whether Hoak was afforded sufficient 
opportunity to complete discovery. This was a straightforward tort action. When 

 -6- 
she filed her complaint on January 17, 2024, it was accompanied by written 
discovery. Several months later, the trial court denied the motion of Left Back 
Properties for dismissal, thus giving Hoak further opportunity to conduct 
discovery. It was nearly two years after discovery began when the trial court 
granted summary judgment. While Hoak explains that numerous depositions 
remain to be taken (in part because the individual defendants could not be located), 
she does not explain why depositions of other witnesses were not scheduled in the 
many months after discovery commenced. Moreover, she does not explain what 
steps, if any, were ever taken to ensure the participation of Sixto Alvarado and 
Jennifer Mitchell in the action. Under the circumstances, the trial court did not 
abuse its discretion by determining that Hoak had adequate opportunity to conduct 
discovery and that sufficient time had passed for it to rule on the summary 
judgment motion in the final days of 2025. 
 Next, we consider Hoak’s argument that the trial court erred by 
granting summary judgment with respect to her strict liability claim. KRS 258.235 
provides that “any owner” whose dog is found to have caused injury to a person is 
liable for damages. Where applied to the proprietorship of a dog, KRS 
258.095(5)(b)3. defines “owner” to include every person who “[p]ermits the dog to 
remain on or about premises owned and occupied by him or her . . . .” (Emphasis 
added.) 

 -7- 
 Hoak contends that Left Back Properties is responsible for her 
damages under this provision because the landlord is deemed an “owner” of the 
dog pursuant to the definition included in KRS 258.095(5)(b)3. Hoak observes 
that Left Back Properties retained a right to enter the property in its lease 
agreement (upon adequate notice). She notes that evidence existed indicating that 
Left Back’s representative visited the property (on a single occasion) to collect the 
rent and to observe the state of the backyard. Therefore, she argues that Left Back 
Properties qualifies as both an owner and an occupier of the premises. 
 The trial court correctly rejected this reasoning. The court explained 
that prior to its amendment in 2017, the statute imposed strict liability upon anyone 
who owned or occupied the premises. However, in deliberate response to a court 
case (as will be noted below), the legislature amended the statute to require that the 
landowner also “occupy” the premises by replacing or with and. By that change 
in conjunctions, the legislature intended to limit a landlord’s exposure to strict 
liability. The trial court opined that a landlord who does not reside on the premises 
does not meet the statutory definition. It concluded that no evidence of record 
indicated that Left Back Properties both owned and occupied the premises where 

 -8- 
Hoak lived and the dog was kept.3 Therefore, Left Back could not be classified as 
an “owner” pursuant to the provision imposing strict liability. 
 Just months before the circuit court granted the motion of Left Back 
Properties for summary judgment, the Supreme Court of Kentucky addressed the 
changes that our dog-bite strict liability statutes have undergone in recent years. In 
Deramos v. Anderson Communities, Inc., 709 S.W.3d 197, 200–01 (Ky. 2025), it 
observed as follows: 
In 2012, the Court decided Benningfield ex rel. 
Benningfield v. Zinsmeister, 367 S.W.3d 561, 562 (Ky. 
2012), and held that a landlord could be liable to a third 
party for injuries caused by a tenant’s dog. On June 29, 
2017, the General Assembly redefined the statutory 
definition of dog owner. In relevant part, the now-
existing version of KRS 258.095(5)(b)[3.] defines a dog 
owner as a person who “permits the dog to remain on or 
about premises owned and occupied by him or her . . . .” 
(Emphasis added.) Therefore, landowners are only 
considered dog owners for strict liability purposes if they 
both own and occupy the premises where the dog-related 
injury occurs. 

The General Assembly has commanded: “[a]ll 
statutes of this state shall be liberally construed with a 
view to promote their objects and carry out the intent of 
the legislature . . . .” KRS 446.080(1). Generally, by 
creating a strict liability statute, the legislature has 
expressed that dog owners shall be strictly responsible 
for injuries caused by their dogs. However, by replacing 
the “owned or occupied” language with “owned and 

3 We note in passing that deposition testimony indicates that Hoak routinely cared for the dog by 
feeding it, letting it outside, cleaning up after it, and letting it sleep with her. This activity could 
arguably result in Hoak’s being classified as a putative owner of the dog. 

 -9- 
occupied,” especially in light of the Benningfield 
decision, the legislature has effectively reduced the 
imposition of strict liability on landlords for injuries 
caused by a tenant’s dog. 

“[W]e presume that the legislature is aware of the 
state of the law when it enacts a statute, including the 
judicial construction of prior enactments.” Indep. Bank 
v. Welch, 636 S.W.3d 528, 535 (Ky. 2021) (citation 
omitted). Here, this awareness includes this Court’s 
interpretation in Benningfield that a landlord can be a 
statutory owner of a dog for strict liability
