JUDGE WHITE delivered the Opinion of the Court.
 WHITE, JUDGE:

 Petitioner Fountain Place, LLC (“Fountain Place”) appeals the Circuit Court

of Logan County’s July 18, 2025, order granting a motion to dismiss filed by Respondents

City of Logan, West Virginia (the “City”) and City of Logan Development Authority (the

“Development Authority”) (collectively, the “Logan Respondents”). The issue on appeal

concerns enforceability of a 1997 contract between Fountain Place’s predecessor-in-

interest and the Logan Respondents which was renewed by Fountain Place in 2017. For

reasons stated below, we affirm the judgment of the lower court and remand for further

proceedings.1

 I. FACTUAL AND PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND

 The contract in question was a Development Agreement between the Logan

Respondents and Fountain Place’s predecessor-in-interest, Monterra. Sometime prior to

 1
 None of the parties question the finality of this ruling for purposes of appellate
review even though certain counterclaims brought by the City against Fountain Place
remain pending and the circuit court did not certify this matter for immediate review under
Rule 54(b) of the West Virginia Rules of Civil Procedure. Nonetheless, because this is a
jurisdictional question, we have independently reviewed this issue and determined that the
ruling of the circuit court approximates a final order pursuant to Syl. Pt. 2, Durm v. Heck’s,
Inc., 184 W. Va. 562, 401 S.E.2d 908 (1991). See generally Antero Res. Corp. v. Pike, 251
W. Va. 522, 529, 914 S.E.2d 757, 764 (Ct. App. 2025) (finding finality despite absence of
Rule 54(b) language where a motion for summary judgment resolved all allegations in the
complaint even though counterclaims for trespass and conversion were still pending). In
finding that we have jurisdiction, we note that the lower court’s order disposes of all of the
claims against the Logan Respondents, and that no similar claims against other defendants
are currently pending.

 1
 January 1, 1995, Monterra began work to develop a shopping center in Logan County (the

“Property”). The property where Monterra intended to develop the proposed shopping

center was located within an unincorporated area of Logan County.

 To encourage and facilitate the completion of the shopping center, the City

established the Development Authority. The City and Development Authority then jointly

entered into the subject Development Agreement in 1997 with Monterra (the

“Development Agreement”). Under the Development Agreement, Monterra would not

object to the City annexing the Property. In exchange for Monterra’s acquiescence in the

annexation of the Property, the City and Development Authority were to remit to Monterra,

or its successors or assigns, an amount equal to 57% of the annual revenue raised by the

City from business and occupancy taxes (“B&O Taxes”) collected from businesses and

occupants operating at the planned shopping center.

 The Logan Respondents were to create a “Special Allocation Fund” (the

“Fund”), “pledge and apply” the moneys not yet paid to the Fund, and pay Fountain Place

from that Fund. The agreement by the City and Development Authority to remit 57% of

the B&O Taxes arising from the Property was for an initial term of twenty years (the “Initial

Term”) but could be extended by Monterra or its assigns at its or their sole option for an

additional ten-year period (the “Renewal Term”), to begin at the conclusion of the Initial

Term. The payments by the City and Development Authority to Monterra and/or its

successors or assigns over the Initial Term and, if applicable, the Renewal Term, were in

 2
 consideration of Fountain Place’s cooperation regarding the annexation of the Property2

and were to incentivize and facilitate the development of the Property as a shopping center.

Monterra continued to develop the Property after the Development Agreement was

executed. When Fountain Place acquired the Property, it finished building the shopping

center, which still operates on the Property as the “Fountain Place shopping center,” or

“Fountain Place Mall.”

 The Development Agreement provides that it “shall be binding upon and

inure to the benefit of the [p]arties [thereto] and their respective authorized successors and

assigns.” Due in part to the immense cost of the project, which involved considerable

excavation, Monterra declared bankruptcy in 1999. By Order of the United States

Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of West Virginia, all rights and title to the

Development Agreement (and the payments due to Monterra by the City and Development

Authority thereunder) were assigned, without objection, to Fountain Place. Under the

Development Agreement, Fountain Place collected annual payments from the Logan

Respondents in the amount of 57% of the total B&O Taxes collected from the Fountain

Place Property for several years after it replaced Monterra.

 2
 In addition to receiving annual payments of 57% of the B&O taxes collected from
businesses operating on the subject property, Monterra and its successors and assigns were
excused from paying any B&O taxes related to construction, rental, and leasing activities
for the subject property. To date, neither Monterra nor Fountain Place have paid any B&O
taxes related to the shopping mall property.

 3
  Sometime in or around 2013, the Development Authority dissolved;3 but

Fountain Place continued to receive annual payments directly from the City. On June 28,

2016, Fountain Place informed the City in writing of its decision to renew the Development

Agreement for an additional ten years, until July 22, 2027. The City did not object to

Fountain Place’s exercise of its renewal option and continued to make payments directly

to Fountain Place through May 2021, when the City decided that it was not legally

obligated to do so.

 On August 9, 2023, Fountain Place filed an action for breach of contract and

declaratory judgment in the Circuit Court of Logan County. The Logan Respondents

moved to dismiss the complaint under Rule 12(b)(6) of the West Virginia Rules of Civil

Procedure. On July 18, 2025, the circuit court issued an order granting the motion to

dismiss on the grounds that the Development Agreement created an unconstitutional

“indebtedness” under Article X, Section 8 of the West Virginia Constitution; the City was

statutorily immune from the liabilities of the Development Authority, which had dissolved

in 2013; and the Logan Respondents were not estopped from contesting the lawfulness of

 3
 It is unclear from the record whether the City intentionally dissolved the
Development Authority, or it simply withered away. According to the City, one member of
the Development Authority may have died while other members moved away. In any event,
by 2013 the Authority was no longer active, and the parties agree that the authority was
dissolved, although they disagree as to exactly how and why that occurred.

 4
 the development agreement even though they had made payments under it for many years.4

Fountain Place appeals from this order.5

 II. STANDARD OF REVIEW

 “Appellate review of a circuit court’s order granting a motion to dismiss a

complaint is de novo.” Syl. Pt. 2, State ex rel. McGraw v. Scott Runyan Pontiac-Buick, Inc.,

194 W. Va. 770, 461 S.E.2d 516 (1995); see also State ex rel. Perdue v. Nationwide Life

Ins. Co., 236 W. Va. 1, 5-6, 777 S.E.2d 11, 15-16 (2015). The interpretation of a statute is

subject to de novo review. Motto v. CSX Transp., Inc., 220 W. Va. 412, 415, 647 S.E.2d

848, 851 (2007). “Constitutional challenges relating to a statute are reviewed pursuant to a

de novo standard of review.” Morris v. Crown Equip. Corp., 219 W. Va. 347, 352, 633

S.E.2d 292, 297 (2006).

 III. DISCUSSION

 4
 The circuit court also held that continued payments under the Development
Agreement would conflict with West Virginia Code § 7-12-2 (1986) which states that “[t]he
purposes for which the authority is created are to promote, develop and advance the
business prosperity and economic welfare of the municipality or county for which it is
created[.]” In this case, Fountain Place is no longer building or maintaining the shopping
center. The money it receives from the City is now used to support activities outside of the
City limits. Fountain Place argues that the City continues to benefit from the shopping
center it developed, but we need not resolve this issue given our other rulings.
 5
 The State of West Virginia filed an amicus curiae brief in support of the Logan
Respondents. We acknowledge the contribution of the State and thank it for its assistance.

 5
  The Logan Respondents rely in part on Article X, Section 8 of the West

Virginia Constitution which limits the ability of municipalities to assume indebtedness and

requires the approval of three fifths of all votes cast for or against the proposed measure.6

In this case, the Development Agreement was not submitted for public approval by the

voters. Because we find West Virginia Code § 7-12-8 and 7-12-13 (1986) and our

jurisprudence concerning estoppel to be dispositive, we decline to address this

constitutional issue. See Cogar v. Sommerville, 180 W. Va. 714, 716, 379 S.E.2d 764, 766

(1989) (“established law… compels us to avoid deciding constitutional issues whenever

 6
 Article X, Section 8 of the West Virginia Constitution provides:
 No county, city, school district, or municipal corporation,
 except in cases where such corporations have already
 authorized their bonds to be issued, shall hereafter be allowed
 to become indebted, in any manner, or for any purpose, to an
 amount, including existing indebtedness, in the aggregate,
 exceeding five per centum on the value of the taxable property
 therein to be ascertained by the last assessment for state and
 county taxes, previous to the incurring of such indebtedness;
 nor without, at the same time, providing for the collection of
 a direct annual tax on all taxable property therein, in the ratio,
 as between the several classes or types of such taxable
 property, specified in section one of this article, separate and
 apart from and in addition to all other taxes for all other
 purposes, sufficient to pay, annually, the interest on such debt,
 and the principal thereof, within, and not exceeding thirty-four
 years

FACTUAL AND PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND) 
OnDecember27, 2005, PlaintiffsDarrellBerryandConstanceLafayette (Plaintiffs)

Before the instant suit was filed, the Plaintiffs defaulted on the promissory note

authorizingexecutoryprocessandalsoissueda writ of seizureandsaleof the mortgaged
property. However, the sheriffs sale was continually delayed and cancelledby various
lawsuits and bankruptcy proceedingsflied by the Plaintiffs. 
Nevertheless, allegingWellsFargodid not follow the properprocedurein the 2017
ExecutoryProcessSuit, on October7, 2022, the Plaintiffs, proceedingpro se, filed the
instantsuit seekinginjunctiverelief and damagesunderSuit No. 724,405 in the 19th3DC
the 2022 Injunction Suit). In their petition, the Plaintiffs named several defendants,

This Court lodged the appeal of the LSF10/ U.S. Bank judgment under docket

Jurisdiction; a Motionto StayAppellateProceedingsPendingSupervisoryReview; Motion

pending Supreme Court writ ruling); and a Motion for Judicial Notice of Absence of

with the merits of the appeal. 
DISCUSSION
This Court' s appellate jurisdiction extends to final judgments and to interlocutory
judgments when expressly allowed by law. See La. C. C. P. arts. 1841, 2083( A) and ( C). 
We have reviewed the LSF10/ U. S. Bank judgment. We conclude the reasoning applied
by the Berry 0688 Court equally applies herein. That is, the LSF10/ U.S. Bank judgment
is interlocutory and non -appealable. Further, after reviewing the factors set forth in
Herlitz Construction Company, Inc, v. Hotel Investors of New Iberia, Inc, 396 So. 2d 878
La. 1981) ( per curiam), we decline to review the LSF10/ U. S. Bank judgment under our
supervisory jurisdiction at this time. The Plaintiffs' claims against LSF10 and U. S. Bank
have been dismissed with prejudice by a separately signed July 1, 2024 judgment, which
granted those defendants' exceptions of no cause of action and prescription. The
Plaintiffs appealed that judgment under this Court' s docket number 2026 CA 0496 and

reasoningappliedby the Berm 0688Courtapplies. That is, based on this Court' s lack of
appellate jurisdiction, as well as our decision not to convert the appeal to an application

CONCLUSION
For the above reasons, we grant the rule to show cause and dismiss the instant
appeal. We deny the pendingmotionsfiled by Darrell Berry and ConstanceLafayette.

injunction seeking to arrest the seizure and sale of the property and requesting

On April 29, 2020, U. S. Bank filed a motion for summary judgment

JUSTICE PUCINSKI delivered the judgment of the court, with opinion. 
Justices Hyman and Evans concurred in the judgment and opinion. 

OPINION 

¶ 1 This action under the Administrative Review Law (735 ILCS 5/3-101 et seq. (West 2022)) 
stems from the decision of the City of Chicago Department of Public Health (CDPH) to deny a 
permit sought by appellant General III, LLC (General III) to operate a large recycling facility on 
the southeast side of Chicago. After General III sought review in the City of Chicago Department 
1-24-1683 
-2- 

of Administrative Hearings (DOAH), an administrative law judge (ALJ) vacated the permit denial. 
CDPH sought administrative review, after which the circuit court reversed the ALJ’s decision and 
reinstated the permit denial. General III then sought relief in this court. 
¶ 2 For the following reasons, we agree with the circuit court that the ALJ made errors of law 
in the course of vacating the permit denial. Thus, we affirm the circuit court, reverse the ALJ’s 
decision, and reinstate the CDPH’s denial of the permit. 
 I. BACKGROUND 
¶ 3 This matter stems from the February 2022 decision by the Commissioner of CDPH to deny 
a permit to operate a new large recycling facility on the southeast side of Chicago. Before we delve 
into the facts, we find it helpful to review the regulatory scheme that governs the powers of the 
CDPH and the permitting process for recycling facilities. 
¶ 4 A. CDPH Powers Under the Code 
¶ 5 First, we review the provisions of the Municipal Code of Chicago (Code) governing the 
CDPH, which are contained in Chapter 2-112 of the Code. Chicago Municipal Code § 2-112-005 
et seq. (amended Feb. 24, 2021). Section 2 -112-010 of the Code establishes the CDPH and 
specifies that it shall be administered by a Commissioner, who is either a licensed physician or a 
person with an advanced degree in a field related to public health. Chicago Municipal Code § 2-
112-010 (amended March 20, 2024). The Code states: “All matters pertaining to the administration 
of the staff of the [CD PH] and the proper protection and promotion of public health shall be in 
charge of the Commissioner of Public Health.” Chicago Municipal Code § 2-112-030 (amended 
February 24, 2021). 
¶ 6 At the relevant time, section 2 -112-110 specified the Commissioner’s authority to issue 
permits under Chapter 11- 4 of the Code (the Chicago Environmental Protection and Control 
1-24-1683 
-3- 

Ordinance). Chicago Municipal Code § 2-112- 110(b)(9) (amended Feb. 24, 2021) (since 
amended); Chicago Municipal Code § 11-4-010 et seq.(amended Oct. 27, 2021). Section 2-112-
110 of the Code set forth several additional powers of the Commissioner, including the power to 
“conduct studies, investigations and research, including joint cooperative investigation and 
research with public and private agencies and organizations” and the power to “advise, consult and 
cooperate with other agencies of the state and federal governments.” Chicago Municipal Code § 2-
112-110(b)(12), (13) (amended Feb. 24, 2021) (since amended) .1 Additionally, section 2-112-
110(c) gave the Commissioner power to do what “may be necessary” for the “proper protection 
and promotion of public health.” Id. § 2-112-110( c); Chicago Municipal Code § 2-112-030 
(amended Feb. 24, 2021). 
¶ 7 The Code further authorizes the Commissioner “to issue rules necessary or proper for the 
administration or enforcement of health ordinances.” Chicago Municipal Code § 2-112-070 
(amended Feb. 24, 2021) (subsequently amended Dec. 20, 2025). 
¶ 8 B. Code Provisions and Rules Regarding Recycling Permits 
¶ 9 This case also requires familiarity with provisions of Chapter 11-4 of the Code, the Chicago 
Environmental Protection and Control Ordinance, pertaining to recycling facilities. 
¶ 10 Chapter 11-4, Article XX (sections 11-4-2510 to 11-4-2680) is entitled “Recycling Facility 
and Urban Farm Accessory Composting Permits.” Chicago Municipal Code §§ 11-4-2510 to 11-
4-2680. Section 11-4-2660 of the Code states that the Commissioner “shall promulgate rules and 

1Analogous language now appears in section 2-112-100(c) of the Code. Chicago Municipal Code § 2-
112-100(c) (amended Nov. 15, 2023) (“The Commissioner shall encourage and conduct such studies, 
investigations and research as in his judgment will promote and improve public health. Such activity may 
be carried out jointly with public or private entities.”). 
1-24-1683 
-4- 

regulations necessary to implement the provi sions of this Article XX.” Chicago Municipal Code 
§ 11-4-2660 (amended May 6, 2015). 
¶ 11 Section 11-4-2530 specifies that an application for a recycling facility must be made “to 
the Commissioner in a manner specified by the Commissioner for such purpose.” Chicago 
Municipal Code § 11-4-2530 (amended July 29, 2015) (subsequently amended Nov. 15, 2023) . 
That section identifies certain minimum information that must be provided but also states that the 
applicant must provide “ [a]ny other information requested by the Commissioner.” Id. § 11-4-
2530(I). 
¶ 12 Pursuant to its rulemaking authority, the Commissioner has issued two sets of rules 
pertinent to recycling facilities. First, the Commissioner issued “Recycling Facility Permits 
Rules and Regulations” in March 2014 (2014 Rules). Chi. Dep’t of Pub. Health, Recycling 
Facility Permits (Mar. 19, 2014), 
https://www.chicago.gov/content/dam/city/depts/dol/rulesandregs/RECYCLINGFACILITYPER
MITSFINAL.pdf [https://perma.cc/HUT5-P5AU]. 
¶ 13 Pertinent to this appeal, Rule 3.0 of the 2014 Rules sets forth “Conditions of Permit 
Issuance,” including that an application must pass a “compliance history evaluation” described in 
Rule 4.0. Id. In turn, Rule 4.0 states that, before granting a permit for a recycling facility, the 
Commissioner “will conduct an evaluation of the applicant’s prior experience in recycling or junk 
facility operations or other waste handling operations.” Id. Under Rule 4.0, the Commissioner may 
deny a permit based on an applicant’s violations of laws, regulations, standards, permit conditions, 
or ordinances in the past three years or if conditions at a previously permitted facility “pose a 
material threat to continued compliance” with any such laws, regulations, standards, permit 
conditions, or ordinances. Id. 
1-24-1683 
-5- 

¶ 14 The Commissioner issued a second set of rules, titled “Rules for Large Recycling 
Facilities” (LRF Rules), in June 2020. Chi. Dep’t of Pub. Health, Rules for Large Recycling 
Facilities (June 5, 2020), https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/dol/rules-and-regulations-
portal/rules-for-large-recycling-facilities.html#docaccess [https://perma.cc/7AXU-JVKH]. The 
LRF Rules set forth additional requirements for the operation of a “Large Recycling Facility”, 
which was defined to mean a “ Facility that is authorized to accept 1,000 tons or more per day of 
Recyclable Materials, operates a metal Shredder that Processes vehicles that has a rated capacity 
of greater than 25 tons per hour, or utilizes Mechanical Sorting Equipment in the Processing of 
ASR [Auto Shredder Residue].” Id. There is no dispute that the facility underlying the instant 
appeal meets the definition of a Large Recycling Facility. 
¶ 15 The Code states that the Commissioner may deny an application for a permit “where such 
application does not meet all applicable requirem ents set forth in the Code.” Chicago Municipal 
Code § 11-4-040(a) (amended July 29, 2015) (subsequently amended Nov. 15, 2023) . It also 
provides that “[t]he Commissioner may impose reasonable permit conditions to protect the public 
health, safety or welfare of the city.” Id. § 11-4-040(e). 
¶ 16 Elsewhere, section 11 -4-2525 of the Code states that “ [n]o permit shall be renewed or 
issued to” an applicant “whose permit issued under this article has been revoked for cause within 
the past three years” or to entities with a 25% or larger ownership stake in a party whose permit 
was revoked for cause within that time frame. Chicago Municipal Code § 11-4-2525 (added Apr. 
9, 2008). 
¶ 17 The Code contemplates review of a CDPH permit denial by the DOAH. A fter denial of a 
permit application, the applicant may demand a hearing within 15 days, after which the 
“Commissioner shall initiate an administrative hearing at the Department of Administrative 
1-24-1683 
-6- 

Hearings, Environmental Safety and Consumer Affairs Hearings Division.” Chicago Municipal 
Code § 11-4-040(d) (amended July 29, 2015) (subsequently amended Nov. 15, 2023). Upon the 
conclusion of the DOAH hearing, the “administrative law officer shall have the authority to affirm 
or vacate the Commissioner’s denial decision.” Id. 
¶ 18 C. Prior Operations at the Site of the Proposed Facility 
¶ 19 For several decades , General Iron Industries Inc. (General Iron) owned and operated a 
metal scrap recycling business in the Lincoln Park neighborhood of Chicago. Beginning around 
2015, the City advised General Iron that it desired the closing of the operations in Lincoln Park. 
¶ 20 By July 2018, General Iron had agreed to sell certain of its assets to Reserve Management 
Group (RMG ). There is no dispute that RMG is an affiliate of General III , with overlapping 
ownership. Specifically, General III is 80 percent owned by another LLC, General II, which, in 
turn, is owned by two holding companies, RMG Investment Group and RMG Development Group 
II. As stated by the circuit court, this relationship indicates that RMG entities own 80 percent of 
General III; General III does not dispute this point. 
¶ 21 Notably, for many years preceding the permit application at issue, RMG and affiliated 
entities owned and operated four recycling facilities at a 175-acre site at 116th Street and Burley 
Avenue on the south side of Chicago, referred to as the “Burley site.” This appeal concer ns an 
application to operate a large recycling facility on the Burley site. 
¶ 22 In February 2019, General II I applied to the Chicago Zoning Board of Appeals (Zoning 
Board) for a special use permit. Following a public hearing, in April 2019, the Zoning Board issued 
findings and authorized the permit application. 
¶ 23 In September 2019, the City entered into an agreement with General Iron, General Metals, 
LLC, and RMG, titled “TERM SHEET REGARDING GENERAL IRON/RMG INTERIM 
1-24-1683 
-7- 

OPERATING PLAN, CESSATION OF NORTHSIDE OPERATIONS, AND SOUTHSIDE 
TRANSITION.” It recited that RMG and General Iron agreed to cease the Lincoln Park metal 
recycling operations, and “RMG intends to transition to a new met al recycling operation to be 
developed” at the Burley site. The City agreed to “reasonably cooperate * * * in achieving the 
efficient, expeditious transition” of operations to the Burley site, “including reasonable assistance 
with processing and review of license and permit applications, and scheduling of public hearings.” 
However, the City specified that it would “enforce its ordinances, rules, regulations, licenses,

leads.caseName: Halabi v. Columbus Plaza Venture
leads.text:
2026 IL App (1st) 252022-U 
No. 1-25-2022 
Order filed November 6, 2026 
NOTICE: This order was filed under Illinois Supreme Court Rule 23(b) and is not 
precedential except in the limited circumstances allowed under Rule 23(e)(1). 

IN THE 
APPELLATE COURT OF ILLINOIS 
FIRST DISTRICT, SIXTH DIVISION 

BASSEM EL HALABI, Plaintiff-Appellant, 
v. 
COLUMBUS PLAZA VENTURE LLC, Defendant-Appellee. 
Appeal from the Circuit Court of Cook County. 
Honorable Arlene Y . Coleman Romeo, Judge, Presiding. 
No. 24-M1-134060 

JUSTICE PUCINSKI delivered the judgment of the court. 
Presiding Justice Gamrath and Justice Evans concurred in the judgment. 
ORDER 
¶ 1 Held: T he trial court’s judgment in defendant’s favor on plaintiff’s breach of contract 
claim was not against the manifest weight of the evidence. 

¶ 2 Plaintiff Bassem El Halabi appeals pro se from the trial court’s order entering judgment in 
defendant Columbus Plaza Venture LLC ’s favor on plaintiff’s breach of contract complaint . 
Plaintiff alleged that defendant breached because they failed to maintain plaintiff’s rented 
apartment in a habitable condition. On appeal, plaintiff argues that the judgment was against the 
manifest weight of the evidence where defendant failed to permanently repair defect ive windows 
which caused “direct and foreseeable” increased electricity billing. We affirm. 

- 2 - 
¶ 3 I. BACKGROUND 
¶ 4 The record on appeal includes a common law record and bystander’s reports submitted by 
plaintiff and the court in accordance with Illinois Supreme Court Rule 323(c) (eff. July 1, 2017). 
¶ 5 On December 31, 2024, plaintiff filed pro se a small claims breach of contract complaint 
against defendant. Plaintiff alleged that defendant failed to repair a “preexisting issue” with the 
windows in plaintiff’s apartment which , plaintiff alleged, violated the Chicago Residential 
Landlord and Tenant Ordinance (RLTO) requirement to maintain the property in a habitable 
condition. See Chicago Municipal Code § 5-12-070 (amended Nov. 6, 1991). Plaintiff requested 
$2,279 as reimbursement for additional heating expenses, legal fees, and compensation for 
“emotional distress.” 
¶ 6 On September 3, 2025, the matter proceeded to a bench trial. 
¶ 7 Plaintiff testified that he signed a lease with defendant to rent an apartment from June 2023 
to June 2024. The apartment had a combined HV AC unit, and plaintiff was instructed to maintain 
a temperature of 62 degrees Fahrenheit to prevent high electricity bills and the pipes from freezing 
and bursting in the winter . During a walk -through inspection of the apartment upon move in, 
plaintiff noticed “air leakage” and sealant damage on the living room and bedroom windows. No 
one acted when he first complained about the windows in June 2023. He claimed that under the 
RLTO, management was required to repair the issue within 14 days. Plaintiff conceded that a third-
party contractor completed a “small repair” and placed sealant on the windows. 
¶ 8 Plaintiff experienced “no problem” in the summer. His electricity bill averaged $47 from 
June 2023 to September 2023 but increased to $220 in October 2023. Plaintiff stopped paying his 
electricity bill that same month. Plaintiff argued that defendant’s instruction to continuously run 
the HV AC system caused the “sharp rise” in the electricity bill. He also argued that his bill was 

- 3 - 
higher than that of his neighbors and submitted reports from ComEd comparing his electricity 
consumption to his neighbors’ consumption. 
¶ 9 Amy Fischer, defendant’s on-site community manager, appeared on behalf of defendant. 
She testified that plaintiff leased one of the property’s larger units and was advised of the heating 
requirements when he signed the lease. Plaintiff submitted work orders for the windows “a few 
times.” For one order, plaintiff denied maintenance workers acce ss to his apartment because he 
was not given proper notice. A third- party contractor inspected the windows and repaired the 
sealant on the windows twice. Defendant replaced and resealed the windows in November 2023 
and December 2023. Plaintiff continued to complain about his electricity bill. 
¶ 10 Fischer testified that under the RLTO, plaintiff was required to give 14-day written notice 
to defendant’s management company regarding the issue with the windows. Plaintiff failed to 
provide the required notice and only submitted a work order , which management subsequently 
addressed. I n an email dated June 6, 2024, plaintiff asked management to stop scheduling 
appointments for workers to reevaluate the problem and refused to identify exactly where air was 
leaking into the apartment after workers had caulked the windows. 
¶ 11 According to Fischer , larger units commonly had higher electricity bills depending on 
tenant needs. Plaintiff failed to use the recommended HV AC settings in his apartment and stated 
that he only operated the HV AC unit when he was home to conserve energy. 
¶ 12 Defendant submitted an email communication from June 11, 2024, between Fischer and a 
ComEd employee where Fischer inquired about a possible reason for plaintiff’s increased bill. The 
ComEd employee replied, “I would say the HV AC is where he is getting hit.” Fischer testified that 
other possible reasons for plaintiff’s increased electricity bill could have be en the change in 
seasons and his nonpayment of the bill after a certain time. 

- 4 - 
¶ 13 The trial court entered judgment in defendant’s favor, finding that plaintiff failed to prove 
by a preponderance of the evidence that defendant failed to repair the windows or that the condition 
of the windows was the sole reason for plaintiff’s increased electricity billing. 
¶ 14 Plaintiff timely appealed. 
¶ 15 On June 3, 2026, we entered an order taking this case for consideration on the record and 
plaintiff’s pro se brief only. See First Capital Mortgage Corp. v. Talandis Construction Corp., 63 
Ill. 2d 128, 133 (1976) (“[I]f the record is simple and the claimed errors are such that the court can 
easily decide them without the aid of an appellee’s brief, the court of review should decide the 
merits of the appeal.”). 
¶ 16 II. ANALYSIS 
¶ 17 On appeal, plaintiff contends that the trial court’s judgment in defendant’s favor was against 
the manifest weight of the evidence where plaintiff showed that defendant failed to permanently 
repair his apartment’s defective windows which caused “direct and foreseeable” increased 
electricity billing. 
¶ 18 A judgment is against the manifest weight of the evidence “only when the findings appear 
to be unreasonable, arbitrary, or not based on evidence, or when an opposite conclusion is 
apparent.” Vaughn v. City of Carbondale, 2016 IL 119181, ¶ 23. This is so because “the trial judge, 
as a trier of fact, is in a superior position to observe witnesses, judge their credibility, and determine 
the weight their testimony should receive .” Battaglia v. 736 N. Clark Corp., 2015 IL App (1st) 
142437, ¶ 23. 
¶ 19 Section 5-12-070 of the RLTO provides that “[t]he landlord shall maintain the premises in 
compliance with all applicable provisions of the municipal code and shall promptly make any and 
all repairs necessary to fulfill this obligation.” Chicago Municipal Code § 5-12-070 (amended Nov. 

- 5 - 
6, 1991). Section 5-12-110 of the RLTO extends the landlord’s obligation to include a duty to 
maintain windows in “ sound condition” and the failure to do so constitutes “material 
noncompliance” with the above provision. Id. § 5-12-110 (amended Sept. 6, 2017). The landlord’s 
“material noncompliance” allows the tenant to tender written notice to the landlord “specifying the 
acts *** constituting the material noncompliance and specifying that the rental agreement will 
terminate on a date not less than 14 days after receipt of the notice by the landlord, unless the 
material noncompliance is remedied by the landlord within the time period specified in the notice.” 
Id. § 5-12-110(a) (amended Sept. 6, 2017). 
¶ 20 If the landlord fails to remedy the material noncompliance “within the time period so 
specified in the notice, the rental agreement shall terminate, and the tenant shall deliver possession 
of the dwelling unit to the landlord within 30 days after the expiration of the time period specified 
in the notice.” Id. The tenant may also recover damages resulting from the landlord’s material 
noncompliance. Id. § 5-12-110(e) (amended Sept. 6, 2017). 
¶ 21 Here, the trial evidence established that plaintiff failed to provide defendant with the 
required written notice regarding any issue with the windows. Instead, plaintiff merely submitted 
work orders , which defendant completed. Additionally, plaintiff conceded that a third -party 
contractor inspected and repaired the windows , including repairing the sealant around the 
windows. Defendant also replaced and resealed the windows in November 2023 and December 
2023. As such, despite plaintiff’s contentions, he failed to show that defendant failed to repair the 
windows or that the court erred in concluding that plaintiff failed to prove this contention. 
¶ 22 Moreover, Fischer testified that in response to one work order, plaintiff denied access to 
the apartment for “lack of notice” and, in June 2024, requested that management stop scheduling 
appointments for workers to evaluate the issue and refused to specify exactly where air was leaking 

- 6 - 
from the windows after they were caulked. Additionally, Fischer testified that plaintiff could have 
experienced increased electricity bill ing due to the size of his apartment, the change in seasons, 
his failure to maintain the recommended HV AC settings, and his nonpayment of the bill after a 
certain time. Based on the above, the court found that plaintiff failed to prove that the condition of 
the windows was the sole reason for his increased electricity billing. See People v. Daniel, 2022 
IL App (1st) 182604, ¶ 102 (the trier of fact’s role is to “assess the credibility of the witnesses, 
weigh the evidence presented, resolve conflicts in the evidence, and draw reasonable inferences 
from the evidence”). 
¶ 23 Based on the evidence in the record , a rational factfinder could determine that plaintiff 
failed to prove that the condition of the windows was the sole reason for plaintiff’s increased 
electricity billing and that defendant failed to materially comply with the RLTO . Therefore, the 
trial court’s ruling in defendant’s favor was not against the manifest weight of the evidence. See 
Vaughn, 2016 IL 119181, ¶ 23. 
¶ 24 III. CONCLUSION 
¶ 25 For the foregoing reasons, we affirm the judgment of the circuit court of Cook County. 
¶ 26 Affirmed.

 Hannah Wyble; Lori Vlach; Gerald Kuhn, in his individual capacity; The City of
 Omaha

 Defendants - Appellees
 ____________

 Appeal from United States District Court
 for the District of Nebraska - Omaha
 ____________

 Submitted: March 18, 2026
 Filed: November 6, 2026
 ____________

Before COLLOTON, Chief Judge, GRUENDER and KOBES, Circuit Judges.
 ____________

KOBES, Circuit Judge.

 The City of Omaha closed the Yale Park Apartment Complex for building-
code violations. Yale Park’s owner AB Realty, LLC and tenants Kay and Janea
Anderson sued the City, Omaha’s Assistant Director of Human Rights Gerald Kuhn,
Housing Inspectors Scott Lane and Kevin Mulcahy, and citizens Hannah Wyble and
 Lori Vlach under 42 U.S.C. § 1983. AB Realty, LLC and the Andersons1 appeal the
dismissal of their Fourth, Fifth, and Fourteenth Amendment claims. Reviewing de
novo, we affirm. Meinen v. Bi-State Dev. Agency, 101 F.4th 947, 950 (8th Cir. 2024)
(standard of review).

 I.

 We describe the facts alleged by AB Realty and established by the exhibits
attached to or referenced in the complaint. See Miller v. Redwood Toxicology Lab’y,
Inc., 688 F.3d 928, 931 (8th Cir. 2012) (“[We] may consider some materials that are
part of the public record or do not contradict the complaint, as well as materials that
are necessarily embraced by the pleadings.” (citation omitted)).

 During the summer of 2018, housing advocates Wyble and Vlack started
talking to Yale Park tenants about their living conditions and took pictures of the
building. They offered to document building code violations, helped tenants fill out
complaint forms, and sent information about violations and complaints to the City—
which began planning Yale Park’s closure. Omaha’s Chief Housing Inspector Lane
applied for and received a warrant to inspect and search Yale Park, relying mostly
on Wyble and Vlack’s information. Lane’s application cited suspected health and
safety violations in 84 units. It contained factual errors, including a false statement
that Kay denied Lane’s request to enter and inspect the building. Nonprofits and
local media knew that the City planned to close Yale Park, but AB Realty and Kay
did not.

 1
 Janea Anderson is a member and manager of AB Realty, LLC. Kay
Anderson disputes his role in the company, but a state-court jury found he was either
Yale Park’s owner or building manager. State v. Anderson, 10 N.W.3d 334, 360,
362 (Neb. 2024). As the district court noted, the “plaintiffs routinely fail to
adequately distinguish between themselves as individual plaintiffs and the rights
they each assert . . . repeatedly refer[ing] to themselves as a group and blend[ing]
their rights and interests together.” Where their allegations and arguments overlap
we refer to them collectively as “AB Realty.”
 -2-
  The City executed the warrant on September 20, 2018. Police and housing
inspectors searched the property and tenants were forced to relocate. A few days
later, the City mailed AB Realty a list of alleged code violations, citing carbon
dioxide leaks, holes in the roof, non-functioning heat, exposed electrical wiring,
broken windows, faulty plumbing, and moldy circuit breakers. The City ordered
that Yale Park could not reopen until the violations were cured. AB Realty started
work on repairs but wanted to challenge the code violations and the closure of the
building. The City referred them to the Property Management Appeals Board, which
handles building code disputes, and AB Realty appealed to the Board in January
2019.

 Meanwhile the City mailed AB Realty notices of around 2,000 total violations
and prosecuted Kay for misdemeanor violations of the City’s property maintenance
code. After finishing repairs, AB Realty reopened Yale Park in the spring of 2021
and filed this lawsuit. The district court2 granted the defendant’s motion to dismiss
in part and stayed the case pending the resolution of Kay’s criminal case. After a
jury found Kay guilty on a few counts but acquitted him of most, see State v.
Anderson, 10 N.W.3d 334, 346 (Neb. 2024), cert. denied sub nom. Anderson v.
Nebraska, 145 S. Ct. 1331 (2025); see also Carter v. Ludwick, 139 F.4th 982, 987
(8th Cir. 2025) (taking judicial notice of related state supreme court opinion), the
district court dismissed the remaining claims.

 II.

 AB Realty first argues the search warrant was invalid because Inspector Lane
lied about asking for permission to enter Yale Park and falsely alleged that police
were called to the complex, that the City had conducted inspections, that Kay used
“threat tactics” against tenants, and that a gas leak caused an explosion. According

 2
 The Honorable Laurie Smith Camp, United States District Judge for the
District of Nebraska, now deceased, granted in part the motion to dismiss. The
Honorable Robert F. Rossiter, Jr., Chief Judge, United States District Court for the
District of Nebraska, dismissed the remaining claims.
 -3-
 to AB Realty this rendered the warrant invalid under Franks v. Delaware, 438 U.S.
154, 155–56 (1978), which made the search unconstitutional, see, e.g., Cronin v.
Peterson, 982 F.3d 1187, 1195 (8th Cir. 2020).

 To establish a Franks violation, AB Realty must show that (1) Lane
deliberately, knowingly, or recklessly made false statements in the supporting
affidavit and (2) “the affidavit’s remaining content is insufficient to provide probable
cause.” Williams v. City of Alexander, 772 F.3d 1307, 1311 (8th Cir. 2014) (citation
omitted). Probable cause for administrative inspection warrants “may be based on
specific evidence of an existing violation or a showing that reasonable legislative or
administrative standards for conducting an inspection are satisfied with respect to a
particular establishment.” United States v. Jamieson-McKames Pharms., Inc., 651
F.2d 532, 541 (8th Cir. 1981) (cleaned up); see also Camara v. Mun. Ct. of S.F., 387
U.S. 523, 538 (1967).

 Even excluding the information disputed by AB Realty, the warrant
application established probable cause for the inspection warrant. Lane wrote that
he received code violation complaints for 84 of the 100 units and referenced holes
in the building’s roof, untreated natural gas leaks, and Kay’s admission that he has
been “lackadaisical” in completing maintenance requests. See Anderson, 10
N.W.3d. at 356–57 (finding the revised warrant still supported a probable cause
finding in Kay’s criminal case). That was enough for probable cause.

 Pointing to state law that allows inspection warrants to issue “only upon
showing that consent to entry for inspection purposes has been refused,” Neb. Rev.
Stat. § 29-832, AB Realty argues that the warrant was deficient because Lane never
asked for consent. The Nebraska statute is beside the point; a violation of state law
alone does not state a § 1983 claim. Stevenson v. Blytheville Sch. Dist. #5, 800 F.3d
955, 965 (8th Cir. 2015) (“Section 1983 guards and vindicates federal rights alone.”
(citation omitted)); Holloway v. Reeves, 277 F.3d 1035, 1038 (8th Cir. 2002) (“[A]
suit under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 can remedy only a violation of federal rights, and so any
violations of rights guaranteed by local or state laws are irrelevant for present
 -4-
 purposes.” (citation omitted)). “[W]hether state law authorized the search [is]
irrelevant” because “state law [does] not alter the content of the Fourth
Amendment.” Virginia v. Moore, 553 U.S. 164, 171–72 (2008).

 III.

 According to AB Realty, “[t]he Defendants effectively deprived the Plaintiffs
of virtually all significant due process.” To state a procedural due process claim,
AB Realty “must demonstrate that the state deprived [them] of some ‘life, liberty, or
property’ interest” and “then establish that the state deprived [them] of that interest
without sufficient ‘process.’” reVamped LLC v. City of Pipestone, 163 F.4th 462,
466 (8th Cir. 2025) (citation omitted), cert. denied, 146 S. Ct. 2676 (2026). And AB
Realty must plead “factual content that allows the court to draw the reasonable
inference that the defendant is liable for the misconduct alleged.” Ashcroft v. Iqbal,
556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009). “[L]egal conclusions” or “[t]hreadbare recitals of the
elements of a cause of action, supported by mere conclusory statements,” is not
enough. Id.

 Reading AB Realty’s second amended complaint, we cannot decipher who is
allegedly responsible for what due process violation. Among other things, it alleges
that Wyble and Vlanch collected “invalid complaints” used to get the warrant; that
the City closed the entire building rather than individual units; that all the tenants
were evicted; that “Danger Closed” signs were wrongly posted on the buildings; that
Yale Park was not allowed to reopen before every purported violation was corrected;
that repairs were “delayed or impeded,” and that AB Realty was denigrated to
potential contractors. These scattershot allegations involve different defendants and
distinct interests, which change depending on which plaintiff is asserting them. See
Devines v. Maier, 665 F.2d 138, 142 (7th Cir. 1981) (discussing the difference
between landlord and tenant rights); see also State ex rel. Wagner v. Evnen, 948
N.W.2d 244, 257 (Neb. 2020) (per curiam) (noting the difference “between the
nature of rights held by an individual and by a business or other legal entity”).

 -5-
  Since AB Realty has failed to identify what constitutionally protected interests
are at stake, see reVamped, 163 F.4th at 466, and who violated their due process
rights and how, we cannot assess what process was constitutionally due, see Dover
Elevator Co. v. Ark. State Univ., 64 F.3d 442, 445–46 (8th Cir. 1995) (“Analysis of
either a procedural or substantive due process claim must begin with an examination
of the interest allegedly violated.”); Temple v. Mercier, 127 F.4th 709, 714 (8th Cir.
2025) (“[T]he extent of procedural safeguards required depends on the nature of the
interest at stake.”); see, e.g., Rochling v. Dep’t of Veterans Affs., 725 F.3d 927, 932
(8th Cir. 2013) (dismissing a due process claim because plaintiffs “speculative and
conclusory” allegations did not sufficiently state a deprivation of a constitutionally
protected interest), and we affirm the dismissal of these claims.3

 IV.

 AB Realty finally alleges that “[t]he City’s actions constitute an effective and
inverse taking, causing damage to AB Realty’s real property rights.” It is not clear
what that means. 4 Under the Fifth Amendment, there are two kinds of takings: per
se takings and regulatory takings. Hawkeye Commodity Promotions, Inc. v. Vilsack,
486 F.3d 430, 440 (8th Cir. 2007). AB Realty has not clarified which kind they are
alleging and, like the district court, we are not convinced they properly pleaded
either.

 3
 Since AB Realty’s claim fails the first step of our due process inquiry, we do
not address their additional arguments that the City’s failure to follow its procedure
for issuing code citations violates due process and that the City is liable for Wyble
and Vlanch’s alleged due process violations even though they are private citizens.
See Rochling, 725 F.3d at 931 (“A procedural due process analysis has two steps,”
and “[t]he plaintiff must first show deprivation of a ‘constitutionally protected life,
liberty or property interest.’” (citation omitted)).
 4
 If AB Realty means inverse condemnation, that is a state-law cause of action
to remedy an alleged taking, not a type of taking. See, e.g., Am. Family Ins. v. City
of Minneapolis, 836 F.3d 918, 923 (8th Cir. 2016) (discussing Minnesota’s inverse
condemnation procedure).
 -6-
  At times, AB Realty seems to raise a per se takings claim. The operative
complaint says

leads.text:
IN THE COMMONWEALTH COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA

Bethlehem Landfill Company, :
 Appellant :
 :
 v. :
 :
Lower Saucon Township, Lower :
Saucon Township Council, Priscilla :
Deleon, Laura Ray, and Victoria :
Opthof-Cordaro in their official :
capacities as elected councilpersons :
for Lower Saucon Township, and :
Steven Goudsouzian in his official :
capacity as Lower Saucon Township : No. 737 C.D. 2025
Solicitor : Argued: October 13, 2026

BEFORE: HONORABLE ANNE E. COVEY, Judge
 HONORABLE STACY WALLACE, Judge
 HONORABLE MARY HANNAH LEAVITT, Senior Judge

OPINION BY
JUDGE COVEY FILED: November 6, 2026

 Bethlehem Landfill Company (BLC) appeals from the Northampton
County Common Pleas Court’s (trial court) May 14, 2025 order (as amended May
15, 2025) overruling in part, and sustaining in part with leave to file an amended
complaint, Lower Saucon Township’s (Township),1 the Township’s Council’s
(Council), the Township’s councilpersons Priscilla deLeon’s (deLeon), Laura Ray’s
(Ray), and Victoria Opthof-Cordaro’s (Opthof-Cordaro) (collectively, Township
Defendants), and the Township’s solicitor Steven Goudsouzian’s (Solicitor)
(collectively, Appellees) Preliminary Objections to BLC’s Complaint for Sunshine
Act Violation and Declaratory Judgment and Injunctive Relief against the Township,

 1
 The Township is a second class township. On November 6, 1973, the citizens of the
Township voted to adopt an optional plan of government pursuant to the Home Rule Charter and
Optional Plans Law, 53 Pa.C.S. §§ 2901-3171, and to be governed under the Council-Manager
plan beginning January 5, 1976.
 the Council, and the Township Defendants and Solicitor in their official capacities
(Complaint). BLC presents five issues for this Court’s review: (1) whether this
Court has jurisdiction over this appeal; (2) whether the trial court erred by dismissing
Counts IV and V of BLC’s Complaint; (3) whether the trial court erred by dismissing
Counts I, II, and III of the Complaint when it was not clear and free from doubt that
BLC failed to state a claim therein; (4) whether the trial court erred by dismissing
Counts I, II, and III of the Complaint with prejudice based on an improper
determination that the Township Defendants’ alleged secret vote was properly
ratified on May 1, 2024; and (5) whether the trial court erred by dismissing Counts
I, II, and III of the Complaint with prejudice as moot based on its finding that the
BLC failed to appeal from the Council’s May 1, 2024 ratification motion. After
review, this Court quashes the appeal.

 Background
 BLC owns and operates a municipal solid waste landfill located in the
Township at 2335 Applebutter Road, Bethlehem, Pennsylvania (Landfill).2 deLeon
was a Township resident and Council president. Ray was a Township resident and
Council Vice President. Opthof-Cordaro was a Township resident and Council
member. Solicitor was the Township’s appointed municipal solicitor.
 In the process of obtaining federal, state, and local approvals necessary
to effectuate a planned expansion of the Landfill (Landfill Expansion), BLC
requested that the Township rezone 275.7 acres of Township land (the Property),
including the proposed Landfill Expansion area from the Township’s Rural
Agricultural (RA) zoning designation to the Light Industrial (LI) zoning designation.
In addition, because the Property encompassed in the Landfill Expansion was

 2
 BLC is a Texas business corporation organized and existing under Delaware law.
 2
 encumbered by two separate instruments in favor of the Township filed with the
Northampton County Recorder of Deeds at Volume 1994-6, Page 10281 and
Volume 1994-6, Page 102074 (collectively, 1994 Recorded Documents), that would
preclude development of the Landfill Expansion on certain portions of the Property,
BLC also requested that the Township release or terminate the 1994 Recorded
Documents to allow for the Landfill Expansion.
 On August 14, 2023, Bruce and Ginger Petrie, Andrew and Tina-Louise
Krasnansky, Robert and Elizabeth Blasko, and Robert and Cynthia McKellin
(collectively, the Petrie Plaintiffs) filed a complaint in the trial court seeking the
following declaratory judgment and injunctive relief against the Township and BLC:
(1) a declaration that because the Property is subject to what is commonly referred
to as the Donated or Dedicated Property Act (DDPA),3 BLC may not utilize it for
purposes inconsistent with the 1994 Recorded Documents without approval of the
trial court’s Orphans’ Court division (Orphans’ Court);4 (2) a declaration that the
Township is subject to the DDPA and may not rezone the Property in a manner
inconsistent with the 1994 Recorded Documents without Orphans’ Court approval;
(3) an injunction enjoining the Township from adopting proposed Ordinance No.
2023-05, that would change the Property’s zoning designation from RA to LI and
change a landfill and waste disposal facility use from one permitted by special
exception to one permitted by right in the LI Zoning District, without Orphans’ Court
approval; and (4) an injunction enjoining the Township from terminating the 1994
Recorded Documents (Petrie Litigation).5 The Township and BLC jointly defended
the Petrie Litigation.

 3
 Act of December 15, 1959, P.L. 1772, 53 P.S. §§ 3381-3386.
 4
 Under the DDPA, the Orphans’ Court has jurisdiction over donated property held by a
municipality in public trust for use as a public facility. See Section 4 of the DDPA, 53 P.S. § 3384.
 5
 The Petrie Plaintiffs initiated the Petrie Litigation at trial court Docket No. C-48-CV-
2023-6089.
 3
  On August 30, 2023, Council - then consisting of Jason Banonis
(Banonis), Mark Inglis (Inglis), Sandra Yerger (Yerger), Thomas Carocci (Carocci)
and deLeon - took three actions related to the Landfill Expansion. First, Council, by
a 4-1 vote - with all members, except for deLeon, voting in favor - authorized the
release of the 1994 Recorded Documents in exchange for grants of new and entirely
separate conservation easements from BLC on two properties formerly subject to
the 1994 Recorded Documents, as well as on other surrounding properties, totaling
approximately 193 acres of land. Second, Council, by a 3-2 vote - with Banonis,
Inglis, and Carocci in favor, and deLeon and Yerger opposed - adopted Ordinance
No. 2023-05, thereby changing the Property’s zoning designation from RA to LI and
allowing a landfill and waste disposal facility use as one permitted by right in the LI
Zoning District. Third, Council, by a 4-1 vote - with all members, except deLeon,
voting in favor - adopted and approved an Amended and Restated Host Community
Agreement6 with BLC. Thereafter, BLC filed with the Township its Phase V
Preliminary Land Development & Lot Consolidation Plan seeking approval for
Landfill Expansion onto portions of the Property (Preliminary Land Development
Plan). On December 6, 2023, Council, by 3-2 vote - with Banonis, Inglis, and
Carocci in favor, and deLeon and Yerger opposed - granted conditional approval of
the Preliminary Land Development Plan.
 In the November 7, 2023 municipal election, Township residents re-
elected deLeon, and elected Ray and Opthof-Cordaro to replace Inglis and Yerger
on Council. Before Ray and Opthof-Cordaro took office on January 2, 2024,
Opthof-Cordaro made clear her intention to reverse Council’s position on the
Landfill Expansion and to have the Township join with the Petrie Plaintiffs in the
Petrie Litigation in opposing the Landfill Expansion. Although the Township and

 6
 The record does not further describe the Amended and Restated Host Community
Agreement.
 4
 BLC filed joint preliminary objections to the complaint in the Petrie Litigation, after
the Petrie Plaintiffs filed an amended complaint in January 2024, the Township
neither joined BLC’s preliminary objections to the amended complaint, nor filed an
answer to the amended complaint. Instead, on April 15, 2024, Solicitor filed a brief
joining the Petrie Plaintiffs and intervenors’ preliminary objections to BLC’s
preliminary objections (Joinder Brief). See Reproduced Record (R.R.) at 155a-156a.
 At Council’s April 17, 2024 meeting, Banonis and Carocci confirmed
that Council had not, either in public or in executive session, voted on the
Township’s position change in the Petrie Litigation, nor did Council vote to
authorize or direct Solicitor to file the Joinder Brief. Thus, BLC objected to the
Township’s reversal in policy and filing of the Joinder Brief, arguing that either the
Township Defendants took official action not voted upon at a public meeting in
violation of the Sunshine Act, or Solicitor acted without Council’s permission,
which was beyond his power under Section 5-12 of the Code of the Township of
Lower Saucon (Township Code).7
 At Council’s May 1, 2024 meeting, Banonis and Carocci again
confirmed that Council had not voted on the Township’s realignment in the Petrie
Litigation, either in public or in executive session, before Solicitor filed the Joinder
Brief. Nevertheless, Council considered a motion to authorize Solicitor to ratify the
Township’s Joinder Brief in the Petrie Litigation (Ratification Motion). Before
Council voted on the Ratification Motion, BLC declared that because the
Ratification Motion was not on Council’s May 1, 2024 meeting agenda, and no
motion had been made to include it before the meeting commenced, Council’s vote
thereon would further violate the Sunshine Act. Therefore, BLC objected to
Council’s adoption of the Ratification Motion and demanded that Opthof-Cordaro

 7
 https://ecode360.com/6772414 (last visited Nov. 5, 2026).
 5
 recuse herself from voting on Landfill Expansion issues generally, and the
Ratification Motion in particular, due to her obvious bias and pecuniary conflicts of
interest.8 Opthof-Cordaro refused to recuse herself, and Council passed the
Ratification Motion by a vote of 3-2, with Opthof-Cordaro, Ray, and deLeon in
favor, and Banonis and Carocci opposed.
 On May 15, 2024, BLC filed the Complaint in the trial court: (1)
alleging that Appellees violated the Sunshine Act by taking official action to reverse
the Township’s position in the Petrie Litigation at a meeting that was not open to the
public (Count I); (2) claiming that Appellees violated the Sunshine Act by depriving
the public of the statutory prior notice of its vote on the Ratification Motion (Count
II); (3) seeking a declaration that the Joinder Brief in the Petrie Litigation was null
and void because Solicitor filed it without the express permission of a Council
majority (Count III); (4) seeking a declaration that Opthof-Cordaro has conflicts of
interest that preclude her from voting on matters related to the Landfill Expansion
(Count IV); (5) seeking an injunction preventing Opthof-Cordaro from participating
in any future Council vote relating to the Landfill Expansion (Count V); and (6)
alleging a promissory estoppel claim against Appellees regarding the Township’s
previous promise to release the 1994 Recorded Documents (Count VI). See R.R. at
4a-159a. Regarding Counts I and II, BLC asked the trial court to declare Council’s
Joinder Brief null and void, require the Township to rescind the Joinder Brief, and
enjoin the Township from re-filing it or otherwise taking action to reverse the
